Automatic analysis of semantic similarity in comparable text through syntactic tree matching One of the central tasks in natural language processing today is the analysis of meaning and semantic similarity. This includes the challenging task of finding similarity between expressions in the natural language of various forms, be it sentences, phrases, or words. A particular and important case of this is the comparison of texts in questions such as "What is the translation of a given text sentence into a different language?" or "What does a given short text summary say (in simpler language) about the text it summarizes?". The latter question is very similar to the task of generating comparables (short summaries alongside a full text) in search results. In comparative linguistics studies on texts in different languages, the comparison is typically done with the help of dictionaries, glossaries, or bilingual lexicons. However, these methods have limitations, as among semantic relations beyond simple translation there can be many other types of relations - "Two sentences are paraphrases", "A short sentence summarizes a longer paragraph", or "Sentence 1 implies Sentence 2 and adds new information" - which cannot be captured rigidly by these traditional approaches. Furthermore, if we consider texts belonging to different domains or genres - say, a news article or a business report - translating the text would often be insufficient, if even applicable, to find similarity relations. For such different texts in the same language, we specifically wish to find semantic rather than textual similarity. In the literature on the acquisition and representation of meaning in computational models (formal semantics), the theory of "semantic similarity" or "meaning comparison" studies the formal (not necessarily computational) properties of expressions that can guarantee one expression can in principle be "interpreted" based on another, without necessarily being a translation or paraphrase. However, such formal treatment usually relies on formal language theory and would be hard to apply to natural language processing tasks that require scalable algorithms on large and diverse textual data. Our approach to analyzing semantic similarity in texts, especially within comparable texts side-by-side, focuses on exploiting the syntactic structure of the language. The idea is that semantically related expressions are likely to share common syntactic patterns, even if their surface forms appear very different. Specifically, given two comparable texts in the same language, we first build syntactic trees for both texts (using standard NLP parsing tools), and then attempt to match pairs of corresponding subtrees in the two trees.

Supervised topic models can be broadly classified into two types: (1) those using an aggregate-level likelihood (Dunl; 2010), and (2) those using a per-instance likelihood (Surdeanu and Lam; 2012; Asuncion et al.; 2009). The latter kind – instance-level questions are preferred in practical applications – seems to be more suitable for improving numerical model interpretability. However, logistic (or sigmoid) likelihood (which is most of the time associated with instance-level questions) comes with two key challenges for practical applications: 1. It may over-weight response variables due to the knowledge of document word counts, and 2. Existing variational inference (VI) methods need to make strong mean-field assumption, which may underestimate true posteriors and limit derived inferences. Plus, as Gillespie and Hopkins (2012) pointed out, "Two significant [Bayesian] hurdles [using logistic likelihoods] are the lack of analytical forms of all required factorizations for variational inference, and the lack of a direct connection between forward and backward passes resulting in difficult inference". In this paper, we tackle these two major challenges for supervised topic models or more generally cluster assignments with logistic likelihoods. 1. A side view from the optimization lens: balance between the different parts of the expected log-likelihood The logistic assumed under the model may seem simple but hides the complexity of uncertainty estimation at the instance level within a model, which we can't ignore. Issues stems from the design of inference: (1) the inference for supervised task aims to approximate the posterior, but it's done by marginalizing in batches or as a group (i.e., per document) instead of per-instance; (2) "proper treatment" of the likely doesn't come naturally with the aggregate-level likelihood (and the implicit assumptions of which would influence the derivation of the inference algorithms). We introduce a regularization constant (K) that inserts side of measured variables into the objective function. We derive the inequality of the log-likelihood components and introduce a balance criterion for uncertainty estimation. This criterion allows us to jointly optimize the log-likelihood of both the supervised and topic models part, and hence the response variables are not over-weighted by the word counts. 2. A variational inference method that avoids making strict mean-field assumption: We propose a Gibbs sampling algorithm with auxiliary variables for Dirichlet hyperparameters. By introducing auxiliary Polya-Gamma variables for the mixtures and collapsing out the Dirichlet variables, we bypass the log-likelihood factorization barriers of the mean-field assumption.

Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms for subject-object-verb (SOV) languages is challenging due to their grammatical structure differing significantly from those found in English and many other European languages. By applying a dependency parser to extracted source language sentences, our approach identifies and reorders subject and object phrases according to their grammatical roles, which are then used to guide the reordering in the target language. This method can be seen as a form of knowledge-based reordering that uses linguistic structures to inform semantic roles beyond simple part-of-speech tagging or frequency-based reordering. The organization of this paper is as follows. First, we introduce a problem statement explaining the challenges of working with SOV order languages, and how current SMT systems can suffer from inadequate handling of grammatical structure. Following this, we outline our proposed solution for achieving better reordering through the use of a dependency parser. For each SOV language analyzed, we detail the specificities of their grammar and how our approach can address the unique challenges associated with those languages. We then describe the experimental setup and the quantitative evaluation methodology used to assess the improvements to translation quality, based on the BLEU score metric. Results for five SOV languages are compared with both current state-of-the-art SMT systems, and systems using alternative reordering methods, such as surface reordering based solely on word order, and a control baseline using no reordering at all. For ease of comparison and to ensure that improvements are not due to chance or unrelated factors, we use a detailed error analysis that identifies particular grammatical structures and source sentences that may be more significantly affected by our method. For languages such as Japanese, we highlight how our method specifically addresses challenges in distinguishing subjects and zero-obligation objects, a common feature in SOV languages where the direct object can be omitted.

Such an operation relies heavily on the notion of probability over partial descriptions of the structures, i.e., prefixes. Prefix probabilities measure the likelihood of a structure beginnings with a given sequence of symbols, without completing the structure. Providing efficient and accurate methods for computing these probabilities can profoundly impact the performance of algorithms that rely on p-SCFSs for this purpose. One such application is the nucleus sampling (Brown et al., 1992) which specifically requires prefix probabilities, while another is the minimized expected risk decoding in n-gram models over SCFGs (Stoyanchev et al., 2010), though this latter application typically handles the probability distribution over all complete sentences more directly. Prior work has presented methods for suffix probabilities in SCFGs (Heintze, 1983) and p-SCFSs (Stoyanchev and Knight, 2009; 2010; 2013). However, the problem of computing prefix probabilities, which can be more complex due to the potential for recurring initial prefixes of invalid partial structures in SCFGs, has received less attention. The necessity for a comprehensive and systematic approach to compute prefix probabilities is now explicitly acknowledged (Stoyanchev et al., 2010). However, practical methods leveraging changing the grammar to a more tractable form (essentially normal forms), while theoretically advanced, are computationally intensive and not generalizable to all grammar formulations. This paper presents a novel method for computing prefix probabilities for p-SCFSs that is both efficient and general in its applicability. Our approach avoids the complexities and inefficiencies associated with prior methods by leveraging a simple, yet elegant, transformation of the grammar and then utilizing standard techniques for working with normal forms. The proposed method thus combines the best of both worlds: flexibility in supporting a wide variety of grammars with computational efficiency.

Training structured prediction models can be computationally expensive, and this prohibits many researchers from using state-of-the-art structured learning algorithms. The accelerated training of structured models would enable a wide range of novel applications, from learning comprehensive statistical models of natural language phenomena to classifying medical images. One key algorithm for training structured prediction models is the structured perceptron (Collins, 2002;Bui et al., 2008). The structured perceptron works by iteratively refining its model parameters based on current mispredictions. In practice, this algorithm is often combined with inexact search for inference. For example, an exact backwards pass through a dynamic programming (DP) algorithm can be too expensive, so instead inference is performed with lazy beam search. Beam search uses a set of ``candidate'' predictions in each iteration. It continuously modifies the candidates by applying inference among the chosen candidates, and expanding the set of candidates by either adding the best new answer found, or pruning the worst answers. This leads to exploration of possible predictions, but its computational cost is linear in the number of candidates, which can be exponentially large in the structured case. For similar reasons, various applications of beam search have proposed pruning or simply truncating their search at fixed or even dynamic lengths. While these simplifications reduce this overhead, truncation or pruning may overly restrict the search space and hence can significantly hurt accuracy. In structured perceptron with beam search, one can label the candidate sets with the current model prediction and then use the algorithm's rule for training. A key insight from (Collins and Roark, 2004) is that simply applying this rule can still lead to convergence: they propose an early-update rule for beam search, which is faster than exact learning but has never been analyzed from a theoretical standpoint. In fact, the community has come to rely on it as a heuristic and the progress that has been made on structured learning has been due in large part to the design of structured perceptron algorithms. The question that arises is the following: under what assumptions can a laser-like search algorithm of the beam variety be used in combination with a structured perceptron update rule to obtain convergence to a local solution? In this paper, we describe a systematic extension of the structured perceptron algorithm to compensate for inexact search. Our proposed methods can be thought of as ``violation-fixing'' algorithms for structured learning.

Linguistic style can be broadly interpreted as the unique way in which an individual expresses his or her thoughts and feelings. It can be manifested through various aspects of language such as lexical choice, syntactic structure, idiomatic expressions, and discourse markers. The phenomenon of individuals adjusting their linguistic styles to adapt to the communication style of the other, known as linguistic style accommodation, has long been recognized as one of the most pivotal communication behaviors in various domains such as interpersonal communication, media, and even social media. The theory of communication accommodation, as proposed by Giles and co-authors in (Giles et al., 1991), is indeed a cornerstone in understanding how and why individuals engage in such behavior, and its implications for social influence, power dynamics, and even social identity. This theory's relevance extends well into the online realm, particularly in the context of online debates and discussions among strangers. Online debates, facilitated by social media platforms, forums, or discussion boards, provide a unique venue to observe and analyze how individuals accommodate their linguistic style when interacting with others, whether in agreement or disagreement. The anonymity, yet public nature, of these debates, allows for a level of transparency in communication styles that might not be as readily observable in face-to-face interactions. Moreover, the permanence and often the asynchronous nature of online communications facilitate a more reflective view of the accommodation process, as individuals may have time to "cool off" and rephrase their thoughts, while the textual form locks in evidence of the transactional moves at play. Furthermore, studying linguistic style accommodation in online debates can provide insights into how individuals negotiate power, establish (or challenge) social identities, and perhaps most importantly, how they attempt to build common ground or affirm in-group or out-group affiliations through language (Giles et al., 1991;Spencer-Oatey, 2000). The dynamics of accommodation can also reveal the implicit rules or norms of interaction within particular online communities, highlight potential instances of power-play or domination (e.g., when one party consistently dominates the conversation or dictates the communication style), or, conversely, instances of yielding or appealing to the other's style for mutual understanding or influence. However, analyzing linguistic style accommodation in online debates presents several challenges. From technical perspectives, extracting and measuring changing patterns in linguistic style across large amounts of text data can be computationally intensive and requires advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques.

The sheer expressiveness and linguistic rigor of CCG make it an attractive choice for tasks requiring detailed syntax analysis, such as text interpretation, information extraction, and even machine translation (Steedman, 2001;Peters et al., 2012). However, the same attributes that make CCG so compelling also introduce computational challenges. The CCG formalism employs a matrix (or "base") of lexical semantic features combined through function application in a way that defies traditional parsing techniques designed for context-free or phrase-structure grammars. This leads to exploration of vast semantic space, particularly when compared to standard techniques for parsing natural language, which often rely on syntactic parsing with a focus on surface grammatical structure. ### 1.1 Parsing Challenges in CCG The computational burden imposed by the CCG formalism is two-fold. First, the matrix representation and the combinatory nature of lexical features render brute-force parsing infeasible. Traditional parsing techniques, such as CKY for constituent structures, need to be augmented or entirely replaced with methods capable of navigating the complex, hierarchical space of CCG derivations. Second, the expressiveness of CCG equates to a vast number of possible derivations for any given sentence. While this allows CCG to capture nuanced semantic structures that other formalisms cannot, it also means that traditional search techniques like backtracking can get easily stuck in local optima or fail to explore the entire search space due to its immense size. ### 1.2 Approaches to Efficient Parsing of CCG Over the years, researchers have proposed several methods to reduce the computational overhead associated with CCG parsing. #### 1.2.1 Adaptive Supertagging One of the most popular and effective approaches is adaptive supertagging (Sudo et al., 2008). This technique relies on a separate stage prior to parsing where a model trained on a large corpus of sentences predicts a subset of lexical categories (supertags) for each word in the sentence. The predicted supertags guide the parser by limiting the search space to a predefined set of lexical categories that are deemed appropriate for the majority of words in the sentence. This approach has proven effective in reducing the number of edges the parser needs to consider during parsing (Gildea, 2002), thus significantly decreasing the computational effort.

Training neural network parsers typically involves updating two sets of weights: one for the neural input's representation via embeddings or matrix multiplications, and another for the transition and parsing decision rules (e.g., using RNNs, CNNs, or MLPs) that decide the next action to take or token to parse next. Current research has shown that improved input questions can improve parser predictions (Levy & Goldberg, 2014, Hyun et al., 2016, Pennacchiotti et al., 2015), but less attention has been paid to how to effectively train the parsing decision weights given a fixed set of input features. This is particularly relevant in transition-based parsing, which takes a sequence of decisions (non-local actions) to form the final result (e.g., a dependency parse), and thus the neural network needs to decide both which among possible actions to perform and in what order. The recent trend of adopting "structure" in neural network parser training refers to aligning the parser's decisions with some notion of linguistic structure, whether during pre-training or during fine-tuning. Standard training of such parsers often involves similar components as in sequence prediction (Seq2seq or encoder-decoder), where the next parsing decision or output token depends on the current state (e.g., a vector representing the symbols seen so far) and may be different depending on the expected action. A traditional approach would train using the error of the final predicted label (e.g., the dependency parse tree) to backpropagate through the decision variables. However, this can lead to inefficiencies and suboptimal decision making when the previous decisions taken are significantly wrong, leading to an "explosion in error" as demonstrated by (Johansson & Mooney, 2008). The structured perceptron model, originally designed for discriminative training in structured prediction (Taskar et al., 2004; Tsochantaridis et al., 2004), addresses the problem of efficiently and optimally training structured output together with structured decision-making. The structured perceptron uses a staged loss function that locally optimizes each step of the decision-making process (e.g., which edge to add next in transition-based parsing). It sequentially updates the entire decision path according to an additive function, ensuring that the updated decisions can be appropriately re-evaluated based on the current subset of available actions. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of structured perceptron training as a fine-tuning step for neural network transition-based parsing given a pre-trained neural network representation of the input. We expect this structured fine-tuning step to improve the parser's ability to make correct parsing decisions given the vast knowledge and features encapsulated by the pre-trained neural input.

This paper presents a novel method to measure similarities between TV programs based on semantic relations. These relations are automatically extracted from the web, offering a large, up-to-date, and diverse source for capturing the myriad connections between concepts. The method uses summary nouns as nodes in a graph, with edges representing semantic relations between them. For example, the concepts of "Drama" and "Theater" might be connected due to common associations in pop culture or definitions.

While character relationships can be useful to model at the level of a single point in time (e.g. for predicting character feelings during a scene), it can be particularly informative to model how these relationships change over time, revealing, for example, a narrative arc in which two characters start as friends and end as enemies. Several studies have looked at dynamic trends in character relationships (Hwang and DiPaola, 2011; Duan et al., 2013), but they typically rely on hand-crafted features and annotated labels, which limits the scalability of these approaches. In contrast, recent advances in deep learning enable unsupervised learning of increasingly nuanced representations of natural language text (e.g. Kingma and Welling, 2013 or Kim, 2014), which this paper leverages to develop an unsupervised neural model for characterizing and learning dynamic character relationship trajectories. Unlike traditional topic modeling approaches, the model proposed in this paper learns to identify sets of time-dependent relationship features and to predict the trajectory over these features for each relationship across an entire novel or story. The resulting model equips studies in computational literary analysis with a new tool, allowing for large-scale exploration of evolving relationships and character interaction patterns. To evaluate our model, we use crowdsourced annotations on character relationships and compare our model to baselines from unsupervised learning in natural language processing. We also explore the relationship between the model's learned features and annotations from existing literary studies. This paper’s model can be seen as an unsupervised extension of existing methods in character analysis. For example, previous work focused on extracting latent features from character relationship networks (Veale and Hao, 2017) or creating hand-built features from co-occurrence and topic analysis (Rogne and van Veen, 2016). Our approach differs by learning these features directly from text data and simultaneously capturing time-dependent dynamics, allowing it to handle unstructured narrative data. The structure of our model is such that each relationship between two characters is associated with a description of their evolving relationship over time, manifested as a trajectory through a learned space of relationship features.

Our method is designed to capture the sequential structure of text while accounting for both the actual position of words and the similarity of their sequential relationships. Training natural language understanding (NLU) models for task-oriented dialogue systems using real conversation data is often challenging due to data scarcity. In particular, NLU modules are often trained on relatively small amounts of annotated data which may not fully cover the various linguistic phenomena and dialogues involved in the voice-user interface. A particular issue is the limited vocabulary and language expression – in face questions or commands asked by users may be expressed in a variety of ways and the models have to learn to understand these different expressions that have the same meaning (alternatives), or be able to generalize beyond what they observed during training. To overcome this data scarcity problem, we explore data augmentation techniques. Our aim is to generate diverse training samples to help NLU models to improve their understanding of natural language inputs. Sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models are a powerful tool for natural language generation and summarization. They can be used to generate alternative expressions based on sample from real conversations. Traditional Seq2Seq model only focuses on individual utterance without considering its relationship with other utterances in the same dialogue. In task-oriented dialogue systems, however, dialogues are sequential and thus semantically related. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to data augmentation by leveraging Seq2Seq model to generate other semantically equivalent or related sentences based on the same semantic goal of given context. One key contribution of our approach is that it includes a different aspect of the training corpus. Unlike traditional data augmentation methods, while the latter typically generate additional samples based on single examples, our approach uses the whole corpus to provide plausible alternative sentences. Our model generates an augmented dataset through analyzing how similar (in terms of semantic content) sentences vary in their syntactic structure, allowing it to model more different representations in the augmented dataset. We specifically incorporate a diversity rank mechanism in our Seq2Seq model. This mechanism compels the model to generate diverse utterances with respect to the candidates it has previously seen and the structure that they might represent. Further, to make our approach effective, we introduce a novel token-level embedding of dialogues. This embedding takes into account the nuances of dialogue structure and the fact that different matched pairs of interlocutor statements can express the same underlying meaning. For instance, "I'd like to find a vegetarian restaurant" and "Do you have any recommendations for places with vegetarian options?" convey the same meaning even though they use different words and structures.

In these cases, the missing arguments are semantically defined through the predicate (e.g., “buy” = “passive” implies buyers and buyers’ beneficiaries as arguments), and presumably or even definitely present in the text, so that this argument can be found somewhere in the text or in the wider narrative context (e.g., assuming Mary and his mom are assumed to buy the tickets for themselves). Named Entity Recognition (NER) in electronic health records (EHRs) is an important preprocessing step for downstream clinical applications. However, training a universal NER system requires a large annotated dataset, which is tedious and expensive. Moreover, medical NER has been shown to be specialty sensitive (Roberts et al., 2017). Different specialties exhibit varying clinical terminologies and writing styles (Cohen and Roessler, 2001). Thus, a NER system trained on a large dataset of records from one specialty may perform poorly when applied to another specialty. To overcome this data scarcity problem, Transfer Learning (TL) has been increasingly employed. However, training a TL system requires labeled data to transfer from. Thus, TL requires a certain amount of specialized training data for a domain. Cross-specialty NER, where a trained NER model can be applied to any medical specialty with little or no additional specialized training data, would greatly facilitate the widespread adoption of NER technology in EHR systems. On the other hand, there has been little work on cross-specialty NER. The key challenges for cross-specialty NER are: 1.   Specialty variance  : Different medical specialties exhibit varied terminologies or rarer terms. A NER system trained on one specialty may have difficulty recognizing entities from another specialty. 2.   Data scarcity  : All specialties may not have labeled data, while the distributed and heterogeneous structure of EHRs make it hard to gather and share data across specialties. 3.   Transferability  : The knowledge or features learned for one specialty (e.g., from specific clinical conditions or drugs) may not apply well to another specialty. For example, drug names for neurology may not overlap much with those for cardiology. 4.   Specialty classification  : In practice, records are often not labeled with their specialty. While specialty is the implicit category, how to use such information effectively is still an open question. A promising approach is to utilize labeled data from one or more side domains (specialties) to help a target specialty, which we term "Double Transfer Learning" (DTL). DTL assumes that either explicitly or implicitly, each record possesses its own specialty label. DTL leverages labeled data from side domains to benefit the target specialty by transfer learning (either features or parameters or both), while also respecting the fact that different specialties exhibit different characteristics (i.e., "double transfer"). Our proposed Label-aware Double Transfer Learning (La-DTL) addresses the first two challenges: -   Feature representation transfer  : We develop a novel label-aware feature representation transfer technique that allows the model to exploit discriminative features from side domains while minimizing unnecessary influence from information irrelevant to the target.

Judgment metrics, which incorporate comprehensive human evaluations, are used as primary measures of summarization performance within TAC competitions. A particular challenge in the TAC summarization track – as in questions of evaluation in general – is the need to measure the relative performance of summarization systems while making minimal assumptions about the judgments that they will face. However, recent research has criticized the report card, suggesting that it is not appropriate from a statistical standpoint (Keller and Lapata, 2012). The main issue is sample dependency: the value of the report card metric on a new set of judgments varies substantially depending on the specific collection of document/ summary pairs used for its calculation. This is undesirable because it reduces the predictive accuracy of the evaluation metric when it is applied to new data. To address this concern, we propose an alternative metric that is both statistically appropriate and more effective at distinguishing between human evaluators and machine systems. In this paper, we first revisit the foundations of the report card metric and discuss the statistical assumptions that it implies. We then introduce a novel metric based on the probability of observing the machine over human evaluation within a given document-set, followed by an empirical study using data from the 2015 TAC summarization track (Etzioni et al., 2015). The new metric provides a more reliable and discrimination-accurate way of ranking summarization systems, and demonstrates improvements in confidence over the report card when human judgment doesn’t come close to machine performance. The analysis is grounded in analysis of variance (ANOVA) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve construction, using bootstrapping techniques for statistical inference. This extends the ongoing evaluation methods in the TAC competition, aiming for a future where we are able to evaluate summarization systems in a way that is both statistically robust and informative for end-users. We structure our report as follows. While the first section provides a detailed overview of the existing report card metric and discusses its statistical foundations, it also critiques the vulnerabilities that stem from these foundations. Our critique highlights the sample dependency and issues in discriminating machine versus human performance.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, while such data is available for some languages today, for many languages there is scarcity of annotated data. Inducing a parser or a grammar from unannotated text has various applications, including parsing languages where no annotation exists, improving the coverage and robustness of parsers on languages with limited annotated corpora, as well as cross-linguistic and zero-shot learning (Abu-Fariha and Li, 2016; Arora et al., 2017). These range from early rule-based systems (Church, 1989; Srinivas and Knight, 1994) through to more recent work using Parametric Sentential Context-Free Grammars (PSCFG; Curran and Clark, 2007; Goldberg and Nivre, 2009), Latent Anomaly Grammars (LAG; Chen and Manning, 2014), and various deep learning models (Dyer et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Peng and Dyer, 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Sanh et al., 2016; Williamson et al., 2016; Modi et al., 2017; Shaw et al., 2018). State-of-the-art data-driven parsers come close to or even exceed the accuracy of handcrafted or current supervised parsers (Hockenmaier and Schuetze, 2005; Nivre, 2017) in specific domains or languages. However, they can also be perceived as somewhat ad-hoc models that do not necessarily capture the underlying structures the way that handcrafted or manually tuned grammars do (Nivre, 2018). Some of the recent models (e.g., Xing et al., 2015; Peng and Dyer, 2016; Peng et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Ghods and Goldsmith, 2018; Dyer et al., 2018; Wand et al., 2018; Huang and Nivre, 2019) still show deficits across languages or in fine-grained operations. For instance, while parser performance during head prediction (e.g., for nouns and pronouns) often tops 90%, performance across clausal relations (those relating to sentences or clauses) is lower. Moreover, even with a perfect low-level parser that could perfectly predict all heads and local dependencies (i.e., from a given word to its dependent), it remains mostly unclear how to configure that parser to scale to larger operations (Frazer and VanDyke, 2017). Such internal configurations often involve handcrafted sub-systems such as non-local annotation rules or shortcuts.

Automatically Classifying Edit Categories in Wikipedia Revisions Over the past decade, Wikipedia's online encyclopedia has grown into a major repository of knowledge, maintained and cultivated by its worldwide community of volunteer editors. The collaborative nature of Wikipedia gives rise to a need for tools that can assist in improving the quality and consistency of the content. One relevant task in this domain is edit categorization: identifying the goals and intentions behind individual edits and classifying them according to predefined categories (e.g., 'minor text formatting', 'fact correction', or 'vandalism'). The ability to automatically label edits can greatly aid in facilitating review, assessing article quality, and detecting content disputes. The categorizations of edits can be based on textual changes (e.g., corrected spelling, vocabulary) or meta-data (e.g., addition or removal of references). Sentiment analysis (Hutto and DiMicco, 2011), authorship analysis (Das et al., 2013), and edit type classification (Wang and Zhang, 2015) have been explored within this context. However, the task of comprehensive edit categorization remains challenging due to the variety and subtlety of potential intention markers. Human-annotated datasets for edit categorization are limited or non-existent; hence, the development of automatic systems is a pressing and novel challenge. Our paper introduces a different perspective to the problem by analyzing the possibility of predicting edit categories from the textual and meta-data evidence of the edit itself, as well its revision history. Our algorithm employs features derived from variables such as: 1.   Textual Differences (TD)  : A comparison between the original and revised content, extracting information such as word count changes, text-based feature frequencies, and semantic changes based on WordNet or embedding models. 2.   Meta-data and Structural Analysis (MSA)  : Extraction of information related to the edit's context, such as user data, edit time, location of changes within the textual structure (e.g., head section or footnote), and the article's general editing patterns. 3.   Language Properties (LP)  : Analysis of linguistic characteristics, including readability scores (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid or Gunning-Fog), grammatical correctness, and style (e.g., formality level or emotional appeal). We use a supervised machine learning approach to combine and weigh these features for the task of multi-labeled edit categorization. Our chosen supervised learning model is a combination of multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for its ability to learn complex relationships and logistic regression for interpretability and real-world application ease. Our methodology involves training on a curated dataset of about 10,000 labeled edits, tagged with 21 categories from a manually designed taxonomy based on Wikipedia's current categorization schemes plus derived categories.

Sentiment analysis is a line of research among semantic analysis methods that can indicate the attitude of a text towards certain objects. As discussed below, we hypothesize that answers to why-questions often correlate with the sentiment of the question and answer text. Word classes refer to a set of semantically defined word categories, such as names of persons, organizations, and locations. They have been used for achieving sophisticated linguistic analysis, including role or slot filling (Bergsma et al., 2000). In QA, these word classes have shown to significantly aid answer selection through techniques like Modality-based Answer Voting (Garcia and Schneider, 2005). We extend this approach, exploring whether the role and sentiment of entities (represented through word classes) within the answer can be used to predict why answers more accurately. To our knowledge, our work is the first study that uses sentiment analysis specifically for why-question answering. Although sentiment analysis has been applied to factoid QA (Cao et al., 2011) and other tasks (Pang and Lee, 2008), to date, no one has combined it with word classes for the task of answering why-questions. Our approach aims to address a few key challenges. 1.   Relevance Prediction  : Given a why-question, we need to predict answers that explain the question's phenomenon. Often, wrong answers will be irrelevant or contradictory to the question's sentiment. Accurate sentiment analysis could help us filter such answers. 2.   Causality and Key Entities Identification  : Sentiment can hint at the nature of a causal relationship. For instance, if the question asks "why did the stock market crash?", a potentially informative answer would involve entities and events with negative sentiment.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental medium of contemporary communication, fostering online discussions on various social issues. As an important source of firsthand and instant information, tweets enable deep insight into current events and public opinions. Significantly, individual tweets can carry controversial voice indispensable for political or other forms of discourse. Hence, a compelling research direction is questions such as "What is the stance of a user towards a certain topic?" (Mukherjee et al., 2012). In language of computer science, the task at hand is to classify tweets according to their alignment or stance with respect to a given topic. This problem falls under the category of knowledge intensive natural language processing, and more broadly within social sciences, it’s a subject of social media analysis. As recent studies have shown, the alignment of users' stances with respect to a topic can be informative for understanding various social phenomena, ranging from political polarization to public opinion formation (Pang and Lee, 2008;Henelius et al., 2014). Furthermore, stance classification can be also useful for several user-facing applications, such as information filtering, opinion profiling, or trusted advice retrieval (Mukherjee et al., 2013). Different approaches have been proposed for stance classification of this sort. One of the earliest works relied on lexical features such as positive/negative sentiment expressions, bias words, or polarizing words while another approach employed lexicon-based methods in combination with syntactic dependency parsing features (Chang et al., 2012). Advances in deep learning models for text classification (Yang et al., 2016;, Rajpurkar et al., 2016;, Devlin et al., 2019) have also been applied to this task. All these models require a large amount of labeled tweets to train the model and the stance that they learn to predict might be tied to the particular context and features presented during training. Often, collecting the needed volume of labeled data is laborious and expensive, especially when the task requires annotating the stance towards a certain topic rather than just sentiment polarity. Therefore, researchers have also explored weakly supervised approaches which can deal with less or no labeled data, but instead use proxy labels or changing the stance prediction task into one that is more feasible to learn from less supervision (Mukherjee et al., 2013;, Bansal et al., 2015). Moreover, incorporating structured information such as information about social relationships among users has been demonstrated to show improvement in the accuracy of stance classification (Wang et al., 2014;, Chiu and Poon, 2017), though these previous works typically use such information as additional features rather than as a core reasoning mechanism.

Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM) is a new language modeling technique that captures syntax and semantics of natural language by representing a sentence as a latent tree encoding word roles. The core idea of LTLM is the encoding of a sentence as a latent tree structure where nodes represent word roles. A particular word can occupy different roles depending on the context of the corresponding sentence. The role assignments encourage the embedding and generalization of syntactic and semantic relations between words. The model can represent abstract links that may not necessarily correspond to tree structures actually present in the language. Table 1 (left) outlines the major challenges of LTLM and ways to address them. The knowledge of language we want to model is inherently ambiguous and lazy retrieved – unlike many computer programs, verbal communication often makes implicit reference to shared context and prior knowledge. This ambiguity presents a challenge to any model aiming to encode the structure of language in a sample from a language distribution. Another difficulty we address is the fact that natural language structure is indefinitely pliable: any given sequence of words can be interpreted in countless ways, as much as it can be very unequivocal in its meaning. Our model approaches these challenges from multiple angles. Firstly, it employs Gibbs sampling to estimate the roles of the words in the given sentence. This sampling process is guided by the model's parameters that are learned through exposure to the training data. The process results in an assignment of roles that captures the intricate dependencies and patterns in the data in a way that a simple n-gram or even the most advanced n-gram model augmented by features or carefully selected word embeddings are unable to capture. We then take advantage of the tree structure learned during this sampling process to predict the next word as a combination of predicting the role of the next word and the contexts corresponding to that role. While the role assignments likely doesn’t represent a tangible, observable linguistic structure (and the structure that emerges might not correspond to any known linguistic typology), it allows the model to generalize over varied syntactic and semantic configurations. This flexibility of representation is particularly useful in resolving ambiguity and capturing the blurred boundaries between syntactically similar but semantically distinct sequences. We use dynamic programming to ensure that we find the most probable tree given the observed sentence, but we also use a faster algorithm based on Gibbs sampling.

In this paper, we explore the use of tables as a knowledge base for automatic question answering. We specifically investigate whether it is possible to exploit the semi-structured structure of tables to answer questions, and whether these structures allow us to achieve or even surpass the performance of both unstructured and more heavily structured knowledge bases, like those represented by knowledge graph groundings of natural language or by shallow structures like RDF (Resource Description Framework) triples. This framework must include methods for (1) creating or acquiring tables (2) annotating those tables with metadata or structuring them through in-table or external schema for question answering, (3) converting tables and their contexts into queryable and interpretable entities for automated analysis, and (4) determining how table structures can be used to reason about questions. Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Phrase structure parsing is an essential step in natural language processing applications; it is often involved in higher-level tasks such as named entity recognition, question answering, information extraction, and machine translation (Eisner, 2003; Charniak, 1997). Phrase structure questions have been tackled using context-free grammars (CFGs) and principled ways of making them more compact and tractable have been explored (Fraser and Hanson, 1990; Ratnaparkhi, 1997). However, due to the pervasive phenomena of word structure complexity in several natural languages, particularly those that are morphologically rich (but also many others) such as German, Dutch, Polish, and Russian (Haspelmath, 1996; Baker, 2001), context-free grammar (CFG) -based phrase structure parsing approaches that operate directly on words and use simple lexical descriptions of words have been found to be inadequate (Schmid, 2000). The problem of morphological richness in these languages can be traced back to issues in both the regularity and complexity of the structure of words. A simple word may have several derivations, so that this word can be represented as symbols appearing in several lexical rules. The different derivations may be shallowly related (but often assumed to be the same word in a syntactic context in a phrase structure grammar). However, several derivations also may be derived from very different morphemes or through relatively complex affixation (e.g., German (re-)Hypothetical Vārian (-bar suffix can appear at any level of derivation)). One could resort to context-sensitive grammars (CSGs) to deal with such complexity (Kaplan and Kay, 1994), but the computational and the linguistic burden of doing so would be quite high, including the understanding and the construction of such grammars (e.g., creating generalizations about the invalidity of certain structure combinations). To mitigate the issue of morphological richness without resorting to full-fledged context-sensitive grammars or to explicitly represent all possible word forms as lexical items, lexicalized parsing and grammar formalisms emerged (Lasnik and Uriagereka, 1994; Collins, 1999). These techniques store lexical information for words in the grammar itself. For example, a base form can be associated with a set of possible prefixes, suffixes, or infixes; the structure of these affixes can then be expanded and combined with the base form. Collins (2003) proposed a fast and discriminative algorithm to parse with these formalisms, but unfortunately its inherently non-deterministic nature leads to efficiency issues. Lexicalized parsing still needs to produce efficient parsers. In this paper, we present a novel parser that takes advantage of the generalizations provided by lexicalized grammars but mitigates the issue of non-determinism.

Training parallel corpora is one of the key ingredients in statistical machine translation (SMT) (Koehn, 2005). Conventionally parallel corpora are collected from various public and proprietary sources (e.g., book translations), organizations (e.g., EU parliament proceedings), and specialized institutes (e.g., United Nations). For many language pairs, questions remain as to whether these traditional sources are sufficiently large for state-of-the-art SMT systems or "gold" enough to produce the best translations. There is of course the issue of domain overlap, i.e., texts coming from different domains can create out-of-domain characteristics that can deplete translation quality when trained on limited resources (Toral and Way, 2010;Bojar et al., 2011). Consequently, efforts have been made to enlarge existing parallel corpora by re-releasing the raw data, weighted boosting sample selection (Das and Smith, 2004), and web sources (Wubben et al., 2008). However, these approaches are still restricted to parallel sources and thus fail to expose the statistical MT system to larger volumes of in-domain training data. This paper introduces a novel approach to mine parallel sentences from the web or any other large scale text collections, using a combination of a carefully designed web search query and an automatic document alignment based approach. We present an initial empirical evaluation of this novel approach, while the system is still in its development stage. Striking substantial improvement over several baseline approaches, we identify the core variables responsible for these results and carefully analyze how distinct web mining approaches perform. The MT task focused in this study is limited to German-English translation. We believe, however, that the proposed mining methodology can be generalised to other language pairs and help to increase "in-domain" training data leading to stronger SMT systems. But it is not just "mining" that we investigate: we also examine the quality and adequacy of the obtained parallel data in SMT. We discuss general methods to evaluate measured variables such as lexical overlap, sentence level, and paraphrasing compatibility. The paper is structured as follows: we initially present the methodology and its rationale before we dive deep into the evaluation. We then describe the technical implementation of the entire system and the set up of the large-scale experimental evaluation. Finally, we analyze the evaluation results and draw conclusions that are both generalizable to other language/purpose pairs and specific to the German-English domain. We suggest potential future directions at the end of the paper.

Variation in referring expressions (REs) is a fundamental property of human language that can have significant effects on how successful the pragmatic interaction is. Human communication would not function without the ability to refer, using both proper names and descriptive terms. Most current text generation technology, however, resorts to deterministic or relatively simplistic ways of producing REs, often relying on questions or status updates as basis for the content and often using only one form of referring expression (e.g., a proper name) to reference the same entity, even if the text is longer or includes multiple REs. While it is important that generated REs keeps changing as needed, it is also important to ensure that the variability in referring expressions, if any, is not interrupted in ways that seem to human readers as inexplicable and disruptive to the flow of the text. This paper presents an approach to text generation that produces REs that exhibit human-like variation in their form and continuity. The presented method follows from previous work on using statistical and machine learning models to generate human-like referring expressions (Jansen et al., 2009a; 2009b; Jansen and Weld, 2011; Lioutikov et al., 2013; Jansen et al., 2015). Specifically, it uses a statistical model to predict when a newly introduced concept (e.g., a character in a story) should be named rather than described, and what label to use if more than one is possible (i.e., the coreference model). It further extends this to create variation by using distinct (and equidistant) pseudonyms for the character as story progresses, using phonological variation to create in-story character names. This is key to the present study and a focus on this paper, which will highlight how model analysis yields insights into socio-linguistic variations and the computational analysis and generation of such. For this, we introduce variation models to highlight variation on all levels of expression (e.g., the choice of pronouns or proper names, or synonyms) and a method to create REs that keep referring to the same entity in a human-like manner yet with variation, even within very short texts. Replicating human behavior in text generation has great appeal, but changing the form of referential expressions (referential form variation, or RFV) has a series of additional implications for the generation system. The most important challenges is that a generated text can easily lose readability and coherence when such variation is added without proper management.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter and Facebook, are now used as key information sources for almost any type of news. These platforms have also become important communication channels for government institutions, NGO, and businesses. While events can be extracted well on microblogging platforms, extracting events from mainstream media sources is relatively easier due to the more consistent language usage and journalistic questions (e.g., who, what, where, when, and why). A major issue with social media data, however, is the lack of context and informal nature, as the brevity of sentences and the use of non-standard language can hinder even well-performing general event extractors. Additionally, due to the knowledge constraints in social media, certain events may be not well tracked or frequently misidentified. These problems need to be addressed to have a powerful event extractor that can handle heterogeneous online sources to extract meaningful events. Unsupervised knowledge enrichment in the scope of event extraction has recently gained interest. Most existing approaches that leverage external sources have focused on associating certain information with entity/relation mentions (e.g., Lee et al. (2015); Bordes et al. (2013)) and claim this information can also help for event extraction. However, these approaches lack focus on the event-level knowledge needed for this task. One example is Entity Linking (EL) to Wikipedia, as in the work by Thomas et al. (2015), which can label an event with more structured and substantial information than simple entity linking, but still does not provide the event-level insights or contextually rich information (e.g., whether the event is a crisis event or an expected event like an election) that can in itself contribute as a feature to event identification or understanding the event type and roles. Existing generic event extractors that can also tackle social media data, such as Nadeem et al. (2016) and Nadeem et al. (2015), do incorporate some features that consider the general nature of the source, such as the readability score and the presence of named entities, but are not specifically designed to handle cross-genre data or to explicitly incorporate cross-genre knowledge as features to improve event extraction performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to incorporate external sources — particularly from traditional/mainstream media — into event extraction to enrich the event extraction model. The approach aims to leverage these external sources to: (i) provide contextual information, (ii) fill in missing information, and (iii) validate extracted events to handle uncertainty or potential misinformation in social media.

Certainly, here is my answer: Abstractive text summarization of news requires first and foremost a way of representing events. Imagine every event as a cluster of patterns and every pattern as a way of expressing this event (e.g., " party " could be expressed through patterns like " celebrated the party ", " was at the party ", etc.). A questions remains which kind of patterns should be used and how to find those patterns. A good event representation should help the abstractive model to generate sentences that cover all of the content of the source document, i.e. presenting key information about important entities and events in an order that makes sense, while omitting less important information. One way to construct this pattern set is to assemble a set of training summaries and try to extract templates by clustering or extracting features from the sentences. This method, however, is problematic: (1) semantic features beyond simple part-of-speech tags and similarity measures can be hard to model, and (2) the structure of event patterns is most of the time highly complex and its size and variety make looking for patterns challenging. Our work aspires to build event patterns empirically, through a similar method as the popular web search engine ranking algorithm. We try to find event patterns by looking what oracles (in this case humans) would say given a set of news articles as input, and use these ground-truth abstractive summaries to create a memory of possible event patterns. A key insight behind our approach is that in good summaries the occurrence and expressions of events (pattern clusters) are followed by variables (pattern stems), making them relatively easily distinct from one another, while the details (specific sentences taken as an example) are presented in multiple different ways in different summaries, making for a large space of grammatical ways of expressing the same message. To this end, we need two things: a dataset of good abstractive summaries and the computational means to the search that large space for the best matches. The dataset we use comes from the document-level CNN/DailyMail summarization task (Hermann et al., 2015), which, as of the time of our research, included approx. 300 000 training examples (source document summary pairs). We leverage human abstractive summaries to create a collection of event patterns. For each training example, we build an open information extraction (OpenIE) style pattern – a simplified representation of the summary sentence in which entities of interest (defined broadly in our case) are left as variables (e.g., " celebrated the party ") and other parts are constants (e.g., " X married Y ").

Early work in this area includes the seminal paper of Fillmore (1968) and various extensions (Fillmore, 1976;Gawne and Rosenbach, 2016), questions such as "What is the typical order and set of participants/events in a story of type X"? However, much work in this area keeps coming backwards due to a reliance on hand-built and limited knowledge bases or to word senses, which are often not available in less resourced languages or verbal domains. As recent work on event extraction from text has shown (e.g., Pradhan et al., 2012), there is much to be gained from adopting fully unsupervised approaches that induce events and their participants from raw text data. We want to be able to do this without any prior knowledge and without reliance on limited knowledge bases. Many of these systems build on the FrameNet project (Fillmore and Baker, 2001), relying on both hand-crafted frames and Forth-like bracketing of core arguments and peripheral roles. However, these systems typically operate over a small set of shallowly annotated frames, and assumed prior knowledge about event structures. They cannot easily scale to more generic and unstructured narrative schemata, the core object of our interest. Issues of scalability and robustness to noise (e.g., to tagging errors) also remain as significant open questions. Our approach breaks new ground in several ways, synthesizing concepts and ideas from several areas. It simultaneously learns both narrative schemas and the "prototype" roles that fill the arguments of these schemas (e.g., the set "JUDGE, SUSPECT, POLICE" for the arrests schema, as mentioned in the abstract above). The approach is unsupervised and relies only on coreferring arguments and surface predicate information. The idea is that certain arguments tend to co-occur in chains of verbs, and that by clustering similar predicates that share similar sets of core and peripheral arguments, we can reconstruct a narrative structure. Our system uses a new clustering technique that allows us to robustly cluster role types (such as "JUDGE", "SUSPECT", and "POLICE") without relying on WordNet or other semantic resources, relying instead on co-occurrence patterns of such role labels in the context of their verbs. We are essentially building a latent role-type representation based on co-occurrence patterns and use this to predict the argument roles we observe in a corpus.

Training and Evaluating Pragmatic Enriched Word Embeddings for Natural Language Understanding (Word Embeddings with Pragmatic Information for NLU) One of the core challenges in Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks such as machine translation, question answering, and text summarization, is the ability to capture the pragmatic information and nuances of language, beyond the literal meaning of words and sentences. Traditional word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec and GloVe) capture general semantic meanings and syntactic roles but lack the ability to incorporate pragmatic information, such as implicature, presupposition, speech act, and conversational implicature (Clark, 1992;Ginzburg, 2012). This limitation is especially critical in human-like language understanding where such pragmatic inferences often play a crucial role. Pragmatic word embeddings (PWE) attempt to capture this missing component by ensuring that the embedded representation of a word reflects not only its semantic meaning but also how it should be interpreted in context (Pu and Xing, 2018). This paper presents a thorough examination and implementation of creative methods to enrich word embeddings with pragmatic information, focusing on three approaches: enriching embeddings with corpus-based pragmatic information, incorporating linguistic pragmatics within the embedding learning framework, and utilizing neural models to learn context-aware pragmatic embeddings. Our primary contribution is not only to create enhanced word embeddings that encode pragmatic information, but also to develop empirical metrics and benchmarks for evaluating the acquisition and preservation of pragmatic understanding in the resulting embeddings. Our experiments demonstrate that such enriched embeddings significantly improve performance in NLU tasks that heavily rely on pragmatic understanding, such as conversation summarization and reading comprehension. ### 1. Introduction In recent years, recommendation systems have become an important technology for helping users discover information and products that match their needs and preferences. There are several methods to build recommendation systems, and most of them rely on numerical data – e.g., purchase history, ratings, and behavioral records. A problem with these numerical data-based systems is that they miss out on valuable information that is embedded in free, natural language form text, such as product reviews and user comments. These text reviews can carry diverse and expressive characteristics that can be particularly useful in understanding users and items. Capitalizing on this textual information is not without challenges – unlike numerical data, text is heterogeneous, and its meaning can be context-dependent. Traditional methods of text mining and natural language processing (NLP) have been used to extract aspect-level features and sentiment from such text. These approaches are well-documented in the literature and have been applied to a variety of tasks, including sentiment analysis and topic modeling. However, these traditional methods lack in a direct connection to recommendation systems that can exploit these text features. Most often, the features extracted from text reviews are not incorporated in a way that fully leverages their value within the main recommendation framework. One problem is that feature engineering for text is typically based on surface-level indicators, like counting positive and negative words, counting the presence of specific keywords, etc. These features may not capture the deep nuances within the text, nor do they effectively reflect the intricate relationships between sentiments, topics, entities (e.g., features and attributes), and user preferences as expressed through their choice of words and sentences. A more recent approach to representational learning from text has been the successful application of distributed representations and "embedding" techniques. Originally designed for machine translation and language modeling (e.g., "Word2Vec" (Mikolov et al., 2013), "GloVe" (Pennington et al., 2014)), these methods learn compact, dense vector representations for words and phrases that capture their meanings in a semantic space. This concept has been extended to other domains, including recommendation systems, and it holds potential to address the challenge of changing the representation from surface-level indicators to more meaningful, vector-based representations that can effectively capture semantic information from text. Anaphora resolution is one of the key tasks in natural language analysis to understand the context's dependency. In particular, associative anaphora, together with zero anaphora, has been identified as a key challenge for the natural language processing (NLP) community, because the antecedent for associative anaphora, unlike regular anaphora, cannot be directly corresponding to the anaphora. This paper presents a probabilistic model to address the associative anaphora resolution in Japanese, based on the idea of treating associative anaphora similarly as zero anaphora, and thereby presenting a joint resolution for both types of anaphora jointly. Experimental results demonstrate that our model not only performs well in associative anaphora resolution but also creates an improvement over the individual resolution of zero anaphora and associative anaphora. Anaphora resolution is a challenging task in natural language processing as it requires understanding the context in which the referring expression is used to identify the intended anaphoric antecedent. Anaphora can be broadly classified into two main types: binding and bridging (Johns and Resnik, 1997). Binding anaphora refers to expressions which can be bound (i.e. linked) to antecedent referents, while bridging or non-binding anaphora refers to expressions which refer to concepts that are identified by the context rather than directly linked to a specific antecedent. Among bridging anaphora, zero anaphora and associative anaphora are two types that are particularly challenging to resolve because the coreference link between an anaphor and its antecedent is often indirect and can involve inference about the meaning of the sentence as a whole, rather than direct matching of text in the sentence as with binding anaphora (Daniel Alai, 2013). Zero anaphora is the simplest type of bridging anaphora where the antecedent is the implicit subject of the sentence or implied based on the general knowledge of the discourse. For instance, in "The result of the chess game was the king's victory," the anaphor "the king" is a zero anaphor because its antecedent is the implied subject of "the result." The antecedent is not explicitly referred to in the sentence, but can be inferred from the common knowledge about the conventional structure of sentences and the conventional sense of certain terms. Associative anaphora meanwhile, is a more complex phenomenon where the anaphor is linked to the antecedent through a chain of associations rather than a direct co-reference relationship. The association can be between the terms in the sentence itself or could even involve some common knowledge or shared context that allows the hearer or reader to infer which antecedent is being referred to, even if that antecedent is not directly mentioned or co-referenced in the sentence.

Training embeddings using unsupervised pretext tasks has seen much success in NLP, where these embeddings are then used as word representations for downstream tasks (Peters et al., 2018; Subramanian et al., 2018; Radford et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2018; Sastry et al., 2018). Pre-training of embeddings helps generalization to new tasks and reduces the need for language-specific resources, as the embeddings are learned on large unlabeled corpora. In this paper, we extend the idea of using unsupervised task-agnostic training objectives to word representations, but with a focus on leveraging these pre-training objectives within the training pipeline of a supervised NLP task. Sentence embedding models like the Skip-Thought Encoder (Kiros et al., 2015) precompute fixed sentence representations on large amounts of unlabeled text and use those as input to task-specific classifiers, but these do not allow for further learning and adaptation of the embeddings in the context of the specific task. In neural models, it is often the case that the word embeddings are fixed early in the training process, used as initializations, and then fine-tuned on the downstream task. However, if these embeddings were allowed to continue training throughout the process of optimizing for the task while still being regularized by some unsupervised task-agnostic objectives, we conjecture that the resulting embeddings could become more expressive and better suited for the specific task (e.g., capture both task specific and general word characteristics). This idea aligns with previous work that has benefited from continued distillation of generative models (Hinton et al., 2015; Salimans et al., 2016). But it is different from existing work in that we do not use a pre-trained model to distill on, but design a structured training objective that the entire model (tasks side and embeddings side together) can train on. We focus on the task of temporal relation classification, which is useful in clinical or scientific domains where temporal relations between events are crucial for understanding the narrative and meaning in technical texts. Specifically, we target the extraction of narrative containment relations (referring to events that occurred before another event) because of its difficulty and importance for subsequent temporal reasoning tasks (e.g., scheduling, anomaly detection). Our proposed approach allows the embeddings to be fine-tuned not only with supervisory signals from the labels but also with an auxiliary unsupervised loss. The unsupervised loss acts on the word embeddings and encourages them to align with the vast unlabeled data used for pretraining.

Furthermore, looking for semantics paths such as equivalent concepts (synonyms) or related concepts (hyponyms and hypernyms) may not provide enough information to understand their inter-relation or derivation. A intuitively way to overcome the shortage of common words and scarcity symbols provided by both sentences is to leverage different levels of the knowledge structures. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) contain a wealth of information which if properly leveraged can have a significant impact on healthcare delivery and research. Among the several tasks which can be performed on EHRs, information extraction is one of the most fundamental. Information extraction from EHRs can include extracting particular facts, such as medication taken, diagnosis, treatment plans, clinical status, radiology reports, or notes made by healthcare professionals. The extracted information can then be used for a variety of purposes, such as constructing patient histories, conducting clinical trials, or monitoring drug safety (Kohane and Thurm, 2012). This task is often formulated as sequence labeling, where the objective is to annotate the medical events (medications, symptoms, etc.) with their attributes (e.g., dosage, duration of symptoms) present in the unstructured text of EHRs. This task presents several challenges. One of the main challenges is the variety in the linguistic expression of these events. For example, a medical event such as ‘hypertension’ can be mentioned in different ways in EHRs such as ‘HBP’, ‘high blood pressure’, ‘HTN’, etc. Furthermore, the EHR text usually contains multiple referential objects (such as patient, doctor, medication, etc.) which may have common names and make it problematic for identifying the correct event. Another challenge is the need to recognize contextual information. For example, while the word ‘stomach’ in isolation may refer to the body part, in the context ‘stomach pain’ it refers to a symptom. One of the most popular current approaches for sequence labeling is the Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) framework (Lafferty et al., 2001). CRFs are probabilistic graphical models that are well-suited for sequence analysis problems such as labeling sequential data (e.g., medical events and their attributes in EHRs). CRFs consider a fixed-size context window (e.g., 15 words before and after the current word of interest) for modeling sequential dependencies. However, the fixed window size can be a limitation as it may not capture longer-range dependencies or context which are often rich in clinical information. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), which have been successful in modeling sequential structure over long distances (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). In this paper, we explored the use of Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks (Bi-RNNs) for medical event detection in EHRs. The main idea of using Bi-RNNs here is that the forward direction of the network can capture the context preceding the event and the backward direction the context following it.

Entity Linking (EL) is the task of identifying entities mentioned in unstructured text and linking them to a canonical KG. The effectiveness of EL is crucial to downstream tasks such as question answering, information retrieval, and information extraction, and has various applications including entity disambiguation and duplicate detection. A particular challenge in the EL task is the ambiguity of textual mentions corresponding to multiple entities. Traditional methods for EL rely on string-based matching and handcrafted features, which can often fail to capture the complex representation of an entity, especially when there is a mismatch in word usage (e.g., variation in mention words) or an out-of-vocabulary (OOV) scenario (e.g., new word, long phrase). Recent advances in deep learning and representation learning have enabled more effective representation and learning of language features. Specifically in EL, neural network-based methods have shown strong performance. However, the performance of these systems can be limited due to the lack of information required to disambiguate ambiguous entities. Most current neural EL systems are limited to a single mention and do not explicitly factor in the types and fine-grained descriptions of entities available in the knowledge base (KB). Furthermore, these systems are usually trained on top of KB entity descriptions and weights extracted from the mention contexts or word representations. They are often tightly coupled with this context, which means they might not perform well if these contexts are different from the ones they were trained on. The Modular Entity Captioning System (MECS) introduces the use of structured descriptions and types to improve EL performance, but it requires training data matching individual descriptions to entity names, which is not always feasible, especially for OOV entities or domains without sufficient training data. Another approach is Entity Vector in Memory (EVM), which builds an embedding of entities through aggregating all contexts they appear in and their descriptions through a model. However, EVM also requires explicit candidates and contextual information from user queries which are not always available or might be noisy, and also aggregates over all contexts of an entity which can miss the specificity needed for different queries or scenarios. In this paper, we address the limitations of current EL systems by proposing a neural architecture that jointly encodes multiple sources of entity information explicitly and implicitly. The architecture we present incorporates EL with joint entity and context encoding to holistically represent entities and their mentions.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has been shown to outperform traditional phrase-based systems by modeling the entire sentence as a joint probability distribution over source and target sentences (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015). While the NMT approach captures the sentence semantics better than its predecessors, questions remain as to whether and how NMT models could be equipped to leverage document-level contextual information, which can often significantly improve the quality of translations (Denkowski and Lavie, 2014;Graham and Neubig, 2017;Chen et al., 2016;Nguyen et al., 2017). Previous research has reported that incorporating contextual information into NMT can lead to improved performance. Sentence-level contextual features, derived directly from the source sentence before decoding, can be used to estimate the similarity between source sentences (Liu et al., 2017;Wang and Zhang, 2017;Jia et al., 2017a). Another line of work addresses the document-level context by including sentences in the document preceding the target sentence in the encoder or by using referential features (Wei et al., 2016;Tu et al., 2016;Yuan et al., 2017). These techniques typically use assumed context while the NMT models need to learn the appropriate way of using the contextual information to increase translation quality (Chen et al., 2017b;Sanchez et al., 2017). However, extracting, representing, and integrating document-level contextual information into the neural translation framework presents several challenges (1) An effective and efficient method must be employed to represent and highlight contextual information at the document level (2) The NMT model must learn how the document-level context might influence the translation and this can be unsuitable for global features such as word occurrence counts (Liu et al., 2016;Li et al., 2016) (3) The model should ideally learn to focus on useful parts of the document-level context by dynamically determining which parts are relevant for the translation and (4) The document-level attention mechanism should also respect the dependency structure within the document (Huang et al., 2016). Fortunately, attention mechanisms can be used to handle such issues in NMT. The attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2015) in NMT focuses on the relevant words in the source sentence. Attention can be used to dynamically focus on different aspects of the source sentence during decoding. However, to capture document-level contexts, the attention mechanism needs a mechanism to focus on the relevant parts of the document or sentences. In this paper, we propose to use hierarchical attention network for document-level neural machine translation.
