Latent-variable PCFGs (LVPFs) are a variant of strict (or context-free) PCFGs (PCFGs) that have become an important technique in Natural Language Processing (NLP). These models extend the original PCFG by allowing the hidden state of some non-terminal symbols to determine the particular grammar rule used by that symbol, opening up new possibilities for modeling complex linguistic phenomena and context-dependent choices between surface structures. This paper proposes a new, fully general and provably correct learning algorithm for LVPF, of which the core contribution is combining independent-best-rule structure and probabilistic matrix decomposition. The proposed algorithm keeps the computational complexity manageable. We support our theoretical results by several experiments, showing that, on a variety of tasks, the proposed algorithm is both effective and efficient in practice. Background: The traditional PCFG model posits that a sentence is derived by applying production rules from the grammar in a weighted, but deterministic way. However, the "independence" assumption that PCFG learning algorithms typically use -- namely, that the choice of the non-terminal symbol at any given position is independent of the choices at surrounding positions in the sentence -- is broken in many cases of interest. For instance, in German, Past tense for the verb "sprechen" (to talk) is used intuitively in progressive constructions ("I have been talking") but not in generic past ("I talked"). This kind of "latent-variable" choice should often be captured by the non-terminal's state. Latent-variable PCFGs make this possible, by assigning to the non-terminal symbols a latent variable that can have several possible values (e.g., one for generic past and one for progressive), and letting the learned probabilities reflect the choice between different values of the state. Assuming that the structure of the grammar is represented by a set V of non-terminal symbols and a set R of rules: v → w_1, ..., w_k (parameters for which are given as probability distributions; typically the parameterization is by log-probabilities or structured log-linear features). A typical LVPF assigns to each v in V a latent variable z, taking values v_1, ..., v_M (with M possibly much larger than the size of V), and for each candidate production rule v → w and value v_z of the latent variable, a probability distribution over R. We write η(z; v → w) to denote such a distribution, approximated by some function p(v_z | v → w) and a base probability p(v_z | v).

Training neural models to generate natural language from structured data is an exciting research area with recent breakthroughs in domains such as dialogue generation (Sordoni et al., 2015), image captioning (Vinyals et al., 2015), and text summarization (Nallapati et al., 2016). A key challenge in these applications is dealing with the constraints and structures of the input data, while still producing idiomatic and fluent language that makes sense to a human language consumer. In text generation with structured data, this means presenting structured data facts to a model that can keeps its "state" of representation dynamically over time. An emerging standard approach to text generation is using a recurrent neural network (RNN) to read input data step by step, with outputs conditioned on the sequence of inputs read so far (Sutskever et al., 2014), but this ignores the value of the "structure" of the input. As a result, many models add certain information about the data structure into its inputs at every step, for example, by handling each data field in a separate RNN (Koehn, 2004; Li et al., 2016), or by varying word representations based on their origin within the structured data (Serban et al., 2016). The approach we take in this paper is to allow the model to incorporate the entire structured data record into its current state, represented as a vector. This vector is then the core input to an RNN used for decoding (Sutskever et al., 2014) that is conditioned on, and summarises the record. We also propose a way of encoding each word in a way that depends on the structured contexts in which that word may occur in a database. We apply our model to biographical text generation, a domain with the structure that input facts about a person may be organized into various fields. This means if one structured fact has "date of birth: 1946" in the field "birthdate", and another has "place of birth: Chicago" in the field "birth city", we can use these two facts together in one sentence, or separate and refer to them sequentially. Because a biography is a natural form that typically uses such structured data to generate a coherent narrative, it is a natural fit for our proposed approach. Moreover, this domain allows us to capture a wide variety of real-world facts and linguistic phenomena such as ordinals (e.g., "her first daughter"), locations (e.g., born in and education in places), relationships (e.g., married to, co-founder with), and career progression (e.g., "from 2005 to 2010, she was CEO of XYZ").

As expected, content words (e.g., nouns, adjectives, and verbs) dominate in our dataset while function words (e.g., prepositions and pronouns) have much lower frequencies. Sentences that have been structured to capture both relationships among semantic entities and syntactic dependencies allow us to estimate how specific part-of-speech tags contribute to the representation and distinctions among words and constructions containing these tags. We want to understand if and how each part-of-speech tag adds unique value to the representation of a word, whether it marks a similar or different distribution across potential arguments or fills a different role between typed entities. We perform both global and local cluster analyses using the embeddings of individual POS tags on the identified symbols. We use Riordan matrices (Riordan et al., 1962), assumed under the random matrix theory, to study the local singular values of a collection of embeddings (Gu, 2013). This method allows us to quantify how distinctively each part-of-speech tag (as a category) contributes to the structure of the embedding space. For example, verbs and nouns are typically syntactically and semantically different roles in sentences. If they are represented distinctly in the embedding space, their embeddings (as a set) are expected to have distinguishable singular value distributions. If the distribution of their singular values is similar, it may indicate that the embedding of the less frequent or the less distinctive part-of-speech category tends to be blurred by the embedding of another more dominant tag in the same cluster. Different distributions among POS tags could imply that some tags are more consistently contributing to disambiguating word meanings than others, or changing the distribution of shared meaning within the words they are associated with. The normalized second smallest singular value (σ(2)) is chosen because it helps to capture significant structure in the distribution of the given set of POS tags.

Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Word knowledge is a fundamental component of language acquisition and understanding. It has been traditionally divided into lexical knowledge (i.e., word meaning, sounds, and orthography) and syntactic knowledge (i.e., word organization within sentences). In educational contexts, it is common to categorize words according to their difficulty or familiarity level. However, this traditional way of understanding word difficulty lacks nuance and fails to capture the complexities of language learning. For example, while a word might be known to be difficult due to its complexity, it might still be unknown to some individuals even if they are at a higher language proficiency level due to lack of knowledge or familiarity with a specific domain. This mismatch creates a challenge for educators who need precise information about the language competency of their students. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach to model word knowledge as a continuous, developmental property, which we term “word maturity.” Unlike traditional difficulty measures, word maturity acknowledges that the understanding of a word can grow and evolve over various stages of language acquisition—ranging from elementary school students to advanced language learners. The concept of word maturity marks a departure from the traditional view of word knowledge as a static, binary property (i.e., a word or word concept is either firmly established within one's vocabulary or it is not), toward a more dynamic and stage-based understanding of word knowledge. A key challenge in this paradigm shift lies in the development of computational methods that can effectively estimate word maturity. While substantial research has focused on defining, classifying, and using variables such as word frequency (e.g., via Google N-gram studies), MTLD (Meaningful Text Level Difficulty), or reading ease measures in education, these approaches often simplify word knowledge into scalar values without accounting for the developmental complexities of language acquisition. To model word maturity, we leverage techniques from natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning, which have demonstrated success in modeling textual data and understanding language acquisition processes (Miller and Charles, 2013;Baroni, 2015;Li, 2017). Specifically, we employ Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) as a foundational component of our framework. LSA and its variants have been used to analyze word and document semantics and are well-suited to model the latent relationships within a large corpus of texts (Landauer and Dumais, 1997). LSA uses singular value decomposition (SVD) on a term-document matrix to project high-dimensional lexical data into a lower-dimensional space capturing the semantic relationships between words.

Social media platforms, such as Reddit, provide a wealth of public discussions and first-person expressions online. These discussions can reveal insights into beliefs, attitudes, and values held by the users participating in these forums. One particular aspect of interest is dogmatism. In psychological theory, dogmatism refers to the inclination towards the acceptance of a group's or individual's questions or status of being infallible or absolute (Rokeach, 1960). It often encompasses traits like intolerance towards opposing views, overconfidence, and the use of absolute terms. Recognizable signs of dogmatism in communication include absolute language ("This is how it is"), intolerance for dissent ("You clearly don’t understand"), and a lack of acknowledgement of cognitive operations ("Those who think otherwise are obviously mistaken"). Dogmatically inclined individuals may appear in discussions across various online communities, even those dedicated to seemingly unrelated topics. Detecting dogmatism in online discourse can potentially allow us to better understand how this belief trait manifests in online communication and intermingle with socio-political and ideological dynamics. Our work sets out to identify linguistic and behavioral signs of dogmatism in social media discourse and build predictive models that can discern dogmatic comments. Drawing on psychological theories, we identify or re-conceive several key aspects of dogmatism which can be represented through linguistic indicators, such as the use of absolute language, the reliance on authority statements without evidence, and the lack of signalled cognitive processing. We formulate hypotheses about the relationship between these features and dogmatism based on the literature. To validate these hypotheses, we develop a corpus of Reddit comments annotated for dogmatism using mixed-model annotation, combining summarization from annotators and machine learning approaches as a form of quality control (human-in-the-loop). We focus on comments that are "pro" a particular stance on a topic (e.g., candidates in an election, "pro" vs. "against" a particular policy), to highlight tendencies towards rigidity and intolerance when arguing in favor of the held position. The dogmatism evaluation for each post is a continuous variable, allowing for the identification of a spectrum rather than binary outcomes. This annotation step is key, as it enables us to ground our computational models in humanly understood characteristics of dogmatic language use. We build a set of statistical models using our annotated dataset. These models incorporate a range of advanced features – from basic Bag-of-Words (BoW) to more nuanced representations such as contextual word embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec or BERT-based embeddings) and structural features like textual length, sentence structure complexity.

While several works have tackled coherence, they use different approaches which make it unrealistic to compare their results. For instance, one work (Hovy and Rambow, 2001) introduced an algorithm for measuring the coherence between sentences in a given text based on semantic and discourse relations between words and sentences. Hovy (2002) introduced a metric based on mutual information and gave an operational meaning to coherence based on it. Another work extracted stylistic characteristics of text and evaluated how much they contributed to the perception of coherence among human raters (Kim and Hovy, 2004). Kim and Hovy's work suggests that sentence length distribution plays a significant role in coherence. While Kim and Hovy's work did perform well in classification but it ignores the role of the author's intention in writing. They gave a purely qualitative interpretation of the results of their human evaluation, but its objectivity is limited. Our work, however, is based on the hypothesis that syntax marks intent and is indicative of coherence. We believe that the intentional discourse structure in text is best captured by syntactic or grammatical patterns. Our work utilizes a large corpus annotated with syntactic patterns and measures their correlations with both automatic and human evaluations of coherence. We hypothesize that text which exhibits certain syntactic patterns, while another may show other patterns. If the sets of syntactic patterns significantly correlate with coherence or incoherence evaluations, this would suggest that syntax can serve as a proxy for the communicative goal of a sentence and therefore for the coherence of a discourse. We presented our model on a dataset of news articles and academic papers. The key distinction between the two datasets was that they were annotated and evaluated differently. News articles were human-rated for their coherence and also annotated with the intentional discourse structure (e.g. which sentences are 'new information', 'background', 'summary'). We also introduced a new dataset of news articles that were labeled for measured variables such as the Gunning-Fog, Flesch-Kincaid and Flesch Reading Ease readability scores. These scores provide information on sentence complexity, which we also hypothesize correlates with coherence. From these we hoped to see if changing the complexity of sentences correlated with our coherence model. For academic papers, we provided a more qualitative analysis.

Certainly, here is my answer: Presenting unstructured message collections without context's consideration during processing is a common task in conversational and communication systems. This includes the challenging task of grouping talked about topics (i.e., conversations), especially when individual dialogues overlap (known as interleaving). A particular and challenging case of this is group chat – a combination questions, answers, statements and conversations intertwined and often overlapping. This paper proposes a novel context-based message expansion (CBME) technique which preprocesses incoming messages to better preserve the conversation's context, and thereby enhances disentanglement. Traditional methods mainly keeps individual messages untouched, or applies lightweight processing (like POS tags) to them, and bases on these creates structures (candidates for conversation) such as dynamic graphs (Tanev et al., 2007;Hosanagar, 2007;Tanev et al., 2009;Birgi et al., 2010) or tries to connect words/events/phrases (Gallegos, 2010). While such approaches might suffice when conversations are independent or have good separation cues (e.g., threading or explicit delimiters), they perform poorly in contexts or datasets where interconversation overlap is common or context cues are weak or non-anchored in syntax. Our approach differs in the sense that we first expand each message to incorporate the explicit and implicit context around it. This expansion is performed at the message level to increase the algorithm's perception of context variables such as: 1. Sentiment inference: By applying a basic sentiment tagger (e.g., VADER, Hutto & Gilbert, 2014) on each message, we can add sentiment information, which can often relate strongly to the "emotional state" of the conversation. 2. Emotion candidates: If the sentiment is inconsistent across messages, we can use an expanded lookup of emotion words to compensate, allowing for more structured analysis during expansion. 3. Deeper semantic processing via NER: Using Named Entity Recognition (e.g., SpaCy), we can add context terms related to people, organizations or other explicitly mentioned entities, which often play significant roles in conversation topics. 4. Relation generation: While concepts like coreference resolution generally require dependency parsing, our simpler strategy might involve detecting certain key phrases (like "let’s talk about") which suggest a conversation shift/pivot or boundaries. 5. State tracking for structure: We suggest expanding messages by appending or zero-order Markov models of the last few sent messages, to give a simple form of "conversation state" which almost acts like a context vector for the message. 6. Social cues: If available, social cues (e.g., role/affiliation in a group, or closeness metrics like centrality in a social network) can be added as tokens in the expanded message, providing deeper background on the user's clout or role in the conversation.

Training embeddings directly from unparallel corpora is a prohibitive task due to the lack of word-to-word parallel pairs. However, training embeddings based on bilingual dictionaries is also challenging as the mere use of dictionaries may not fully capture the various nuances and idiomatic expressions within the language. Bilingual dictionaries are, after all, mere collections of translations of individual words or phrases, and do not provide the contextual information that is necessary for the successful training of distributed word representations (Mikolov et al., 2013). In this paper, we propose Simple task-specific bilingual word embeddings (STBWE), a method for creating task-specific bilingual word embeddings using off-the-shelf word embedding algorithms. Our method does not require parallel training data or a large corpus, and can be easily adapted to a wide range of tasks by just defining the task-specific word equivalence classes. First, we derive a list of task-specific word equivalence classes by using existing dictionaries and knowledge bases. For example, if our task is POS tagging, we can use a pre-existing POS tagger on the source and target languages to obtain the mappings between POS tags in both languages. Off-the-shelf embedding tools such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) can then create monolingual word embeddings for both languages while the word equivalence classes act as the in-variant mapping that facilitates the creation of bilingual embeddings. More specifically, given an equivalence class, we create mixed context-target pairs, where the context (source language word) and target (target language word) are both in the same equivalence class but belong to different languages. For instance, if the equivalence class is "dog", we can create pairs like "sao (dog in Chinese) χ (dog in English)". However, this alone may not fully exploit the potential of the embedding algorithm or may result in poor embedding quality, as the original embedding algorithms are trained in the context of monolingual data. Our key contribution is the inclusion of additional word embedding examples that leverage the context from the task at hand but without requiring parallel data. For example, in the context of POS tagging, we can use byte-pair encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2016) for both languages to generate subword units, and then use those subword units as additional training examples for our embeddings. This not only uses real bilingual information (i.e., the BPE decoding and equivalence class mappings) but also creates more data points based on the specific linguistic patterns and subword regularities captured by these techniques.

Training natural language parsers typically involves maximizing likelihood and later decoding. A strict (combined) dependency parser additionally maximizes the joint likelihood of all involved factor functions. This is typically done using the max-product algorithm (or the more memory-efficient sum-product algorithm) which is quite computationally expensive for complex dependency structures and larger models. An alternative is to maximize the joint marginals which leads to a significantly lower computational and representational complexity (we obtain the best linear complexity with respect to the number of states and arcs). There is of course the issue that maximizing joint marginals can lead to very suboptimal results. Therefore, practitioners commonly solve for marginals with respect to most latent variables while keeping constraints dependent on some, typically those with a rich set of conditional dependencies. For example, verbal subcategorization frames are very well constrained from semantic knowledge and thus any consistent (or derived) model would among semantic features achieve a high weighted likelihood without fully marginalizing over them - which we call an instance of relaxed marginal inference. In our work, we want to systematically extend and evaluate this intuition with a theoretical and computational angle. Let us start with the theory. Let us assume that we have a distribution P over some variables X = (X1, ..., Xn), which we want to infer. Our goal is to perform a uniform relaxation of all the dependencies within the joint distribution but still maintain the most important structure in the initial distribution. We'll use this structure while the rest will be relaxed. If the entire graph G = (V, E) defining the joint distribution can be decomposed into a small set of carefully selected variables X (e.g., features related to specific grammar rules), we can then use these variables to provide a bound in accuracy: the correct inference should be within a certain bound of our relaxed inference result. One may think of a model approximation approach: doesn't this suggest that we should approximate the joint distribution with a simpler one which would allow for fast computation? Indeed, approximation is one approach if one is willing to pay the potential loss in accuracy. The point, however, is that a dependence graph, as often matched with a Bayesian network or a causal graph, is useful beyond just approximation but also for storing and maintaining structured probabilistic knowledge. We want to still refer to and maintain the probabilistic relationships as encoded in the graph but perform fast (approximate) inference.

Latent Topic Embedding (LTE) is a novel approach that combines topic modeling and word embedding. In particular, we address these two tasks together in a unified framework which can yield better latent semantics than using either technique alone. While general-purpose topic models can capture coarse-grained co-occurrence behavior at the document and sentence level, word embedding models exploit fine-grained local questions such as "What words often appear near a target word?". However, topic models do not "understand" word meaning and word embedding models often lack of generalization beyond small fractals. Table 1 (not included in text format) provides an overview of characteristics of popular topic modeling and word embedding methods. We propose LTE as a flexible, hybrid solution to capture rich structures in natural language data. LTE is built on a probabilistic framework that estimates word embedding and topic distributions simultaneously by leveraging inter-language relationships among semantic entities. The model estimates latent topics from bigrams observed in the corpus and each word's latent topic distribution. Then it generates a word embedding vector which is the average word embedding across all topics that the word participates in. The model uses a parametrized prior over bigrams and topics distribution, and explores this space using a novel Monte Carlo EM algorithm which is capable of varying computation granularity. By performing a single main loop which can be interpreted as alternating between local learning (word embeddings) and global learning (topics), our algorithm becomes highly efficient while retaining the flexibility benefits of EM. This single main loop performs updates over word topics and model parameters in a data-driven and integrated way. Our key innovation is to formalize the inference for MT (Mixture of Topic distributions, see Equation 1) and ME (word Embedding), jointly with an auxiliary variable (topic representation, see Equation 2). This formalization provides a clear model analysis leading to our novel Monte Carlo EM updates (see Equation 3 for an example of update for MT; and Equation 4 for an example of update for word Embedding) which are different from general methods used in prior work for topic models and word embeddings, as they explicitly interact with the other components of our model. By jointly optimizing both tasks within a unified probabilistic framework, LTE aims to accomplish several goals. From technical perspectives, the model aims for a better trade-off between model complexity and latent semantics. From a practical perspective, advanced features of topic models and word embeddings can now be used together in a single model, which can potentially increase overall utility.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated corpora. However, while such resources have been developed for many languages, their annotation is often incomplete and/or biased and may not cover all the phenomena talked about in less-studied texts. Moreover, annotated corpora are quite expensive to construct. A particular challenge comes from out-of-domain language, for instance when questions are posed on domain-specific conversations (e.g., IM chats, blogs) using web search access idioms (e.g., socialism + “in China”). This can confu fracture out-of-domain domain (e.g., economics) with in-domain context (e.g., political science or history) due to limited knowledge of web-specific word senses, new words introduced in web contexts, and colloquial language such as slang and jargon that may not be in standard lexicon or have been downplayed by standard annotation efforts. This paper presents a weighted graph-based approach that couples both rule-based and corpus-based methods, and is capable of capturing and generalizing these out-of-domain morpho-syntactic features during parsing with very small changes to the standard parser architectures. We conducted evaluation on both in-domain and out-of-domain Chinese SVO (Subject-Verb-Object) typed corpus. The proposed method demonstrated significant improvements on out-of-domain Chinese parsing over a uniform context-agnostic view as well as when compared to ground truth parsers running in heuristic mode. We specifically compare against CCG while adding distributed representation benefits. The paper contributes a detailed investigation on the sources and properties of out-of-domain features, an analysis of CCG's current design limitations in handling web-specific linguistic behaviors (Sect. 3), as well as a summarization of the different weighted graph strategies that were explored for each key syntactico-semantic component and their relative contributions (Sect. 4). For ease of readability and modularity, Section 4 further redesignates the discussion under subheadings: 4.1: Improving on VerbArgument Relationships; 4.2: On Dealing with the More Uncertain: NP/PP Structures; 4.3: Extending the CCG Formalism. These subsections are interwoven with rich quantitative and qualitative summary results for each stage of our approach, followed by ablation analyses to isolate changing components. 4. We wrap up with examples illustrating salient improvements on both in-domain and out-of-domain Chinese. Specifically, we show that for web-based out-of-domain Chinese, when compared to state-of-the-art results run in heuristic mode (usually reserved for real-time scenarios such as search engine queries), our method shows substantial improvement.

This is not surprising because human conversations contain repair events such as corrections, re-phrasings, back-trackings, and so on (Hovy, 1996). The precise identification of speech repairs in oral or transcribed texts has been an important area of study for decades (Grosz and Sidner, 1986;Choudhary et al., 2007;Miranda-Ribeiro and Nakov, 2013). Several studies have focused on the development of automatic parsing techniques or even grammar formalisms specifically for parsing speech with repairs (Dell and Nakov, 2010;Miranda-Ribeiro and Nakov, 2013;Nakov, 2010;Nakov and Walker, 2011). For instance, the SPEEL (Self-Experienced Engaging Ellipsis Repair Log) grammar (Nakov, 2010) is a Resource-based grammar that uses English speech with repairs to develop grammatical generalizations, and the Sound-Tagged and Branching (STaB) formalism (Nakov and Walker, 2011) models speech with repairs using branching and marked-up dependency structures. These earlier works have been done mainly manually, and in some less general cases the measured evaluation methods do not guarantee a higher level of statistical significance. The necessity for a more principled approach to speech parsing with repairs is explicitly mentioned in Miranda-Ribeiro's thesis (Miranda-Ribeiro, 2014). Building on earlier work, especially on the PARSEME project's resources (Borin et al., 2012a), for the multi-language and broadly definitional challenge of spoken language corpora (Borin et al., 2012b;Sebastian et al., 2014;Nakov and Bender, 2014;Tessler and Olsher, 2015), this paper proposes new syntactic models for parsing speech with repairs. Our key intuition is that repairs and other compositional disfluencies are not grammatical outliers created by independent syntactic rules that can often be disjoint from rules for fluent speech (Bolinger, 1989;Bresnan and Mennen, 2001;Fox Tree, 1995;Tessler, 2015;Post and Starosta, 2013). Rather, they are generated by a common mechanism at the syntactic level, similar albeit different functional successful complete clauses (Tessler, 2015). We also attempt to isolate the mechanism of repair recognition and rule changes from other variables, such as word order, word choice, or grammar consistency, to evaluate how much of the observed disfluency can be attributed to one or several independent factors.

Language models are widely used as features in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and machine translation. Probabilistic language models use algorithms that assign probabilities to all possible various sequences of words in a vocabulary, and are often trained on large and diverse text corpora. One kind of language model questions the status of word tokens and instead uses a latent variable space to group words into word clusters or "words" that are somewhat arbitrary. Language models using such latent word spaces are fractive language models, and experiments show that probabilistic LWLMs achieve better performance than simple n-gram language models in most NLP tasks. One essential feature of fractive language models is lazy learning – unlike many NLP systems that need to learn from a very large corpus from scratch, fractive language models can be derived directly from any unsupervised latent analysis of the input sample from which language models can be derived directly. LWLMs usually assume a latent variable space containing a certain number of clusters/words. This implies that if the data contains terms or expressions that cannot be represented in the rigid latent structure, those expressions are treated as if they were arbitrarily grouped. Thus, for achieving robust performance across varied domains or varying rarities of phenomena in the training data, this rigidity can prevent the models from adequately accounting for new or rare phenomena. These limitations significantly limit the capacity of traditional LWLMs in the modeling of natural language. In order to address this issue and achieve better generalization to out-of-domain data, this paper proposes the hierarchical latent word language model (h-LWLM). A multi-layer hierarchical latent space is introduced as an extension of traditional latent variable spaces. The model can be regarded as a generalized form of LWLMs. The key innovation is the introduction of hierarchical latent space through a two-layer approach: one layer for determining the candidates of the latent words and the other for selecting which latent word to use for a given input context. This hierarchical design makes the model more flexible and capable of generalizing to unseen or rare phenomena in the test data. The proposed model demonstrates the ability to model the complex dependencies in natural language better while maintaining advantages of probabilistic LWLMs such as lazy learning and less sensitivity to data rarity. From technical perspectives, the proposed model is defined by an iterative layer-wise construction and an updated learning procedure that appropriately adapts to out-of-domain data.

Underspecifying and Predicting Voice for Surface Realisation Ranking Surface realisation systems have been successfully applied to a variety of language generation tasks, including machine translation and spoken dialogue systems. These systems use a comprehensive grammar of natural language to generate many different possible phrasings from a single underlying semantic representation. However, most surface realization systems focus entirely on word order variants, because this kind of underspecification is relatively easy to make and analyze. A more challenging underspecification issue, with potentially greater payoff, is voice of verbs, as voice choice affects sentence meaning and contributes to nuance and style. For example, an active "John ate the pizza" is less routine than a passive "The pizza was eaten by John," and lazy or official writing may emphasize active or passive voice, respectively. Training a joint model for Chinese word segmentation (CWS) and new word detection (NWD) jointly is advantageous. It can improve performance of both tasks since CWS and NWD are interrelated tasks. For example, if a new word is not segmented correctly, it will also affect new word detection because new words are defined as a group of characters which are not correctly segmented according to existing dictionaries (Liu and Wong, 2007;Eick et al., 2006). On the other hand, the prediction of a new word can also affect the segmentation. However, this joint modeling will make training very costly because it has a large model and uses high-dimensional features to achieve accurate results. For example, Soga (Soga, 2007) first used very high-dimensional features in CWS. It used features based on characters, character bigrams, character trigrams, word bigrams, and word trigrams, and also used features based on CRF (Conditional Random Fields) edge labels. This made the standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) very slow in training the model, even given a small dataset. Offline training (i.e., batch training) would still be slow, and online or online-like training (i.e., using a small mini-batch and updating parameters after processing each mini-batch) is often preferred because it allows faster convergence and gives a better estimation of the model performance. However, even online learning with SGD is still slow because it uses the same learning rate for all the features. This can be inefficient because some features are much more frequent than others (e.g., the character '的', '是', etc. in Chinese are much more frequent than other characters or character bigrams). We propose a novel training method that adapts the learning rate for different features based on their frequency, and proves that this is the key to make online training much faster and still achieve high accuracies. This approach can be generalized to training any joint models or generalizable neural networks with extremely large feature spaces, a problem which arises in natural language processing applications. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present related work. In Section 3 and 4, we describe the proposed model for CWS and NWD, and the proposed training methods. In Section 5, we report on experimental results. Semi-supervised learning (SS) methods use additional unlabeled data to improve the accuracy of trained models, with the intuition that unlabeled samples can provide useful information as they are never independent of the observed data and thus can “inform” the supervised model (Chapelle et al., 2006). One way to optimize models using unlabeled examples is through feature learning using deep neural networks (Bengio et al., 2007). In recent years, semi-supervised learning has attracted significant attention in natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning research, especially in the context of deep neural networks (DNNs). Assuming access to a large corpus of unlabeled data, there are two common and complementary pathways through which unlabeled data can be used for training deep neural networks. One approach is the use of deep belief networks or autoencoders to learn unsupervised features (Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio et al., 2003, 2007; Coates et al., 2013). The other is by using semi-supervised learning methods within framework of deep neural networks (Weston et al., 2008; Blanchet et al., 2016). Deep architectures make it possible for these methods to model complex non-linear relationships, and recent works have confirmed their effectiveness over traditional shallow models such as SVMs or zero-order Gaussian mixture models (Blanchet et al., 2016; Pebesma, 2012). Five representative deep semi-supervised learning methods have been explored. Two, including stacked autoencoders (Sae) (Bengio et al., 2007) and Deep Generative Models (DGAs) (Le, 2013), are feature learning methods. For gradient-based optimization problems, it is standard practice to use adaptive learning rate methods to ensure convergence while keeping the training shallow. However, despite the success of ADAGRAD (and similarly designed adaptive learning rate methods like RMSProp and Adam) in a broad range of offline gradient optimization scenarios, they have been observed to underperform for online topic modeling (Bai et al., 2019, 2020; Wang and Blei, 2018). This inconsistency has caused puzzlement, as one would assume that a method as popular and robust as ADAGRAD would couple seamlessly with SVI, which is also designed to optimize and adapt to changing data. The purpose of this paper is to investigate the underperformance of ADAGRAD in online topic modeling. We hypothesize that the key issue stems from the way ADAGRAD accumulates gradients over time. In particular, ADAGRAD's learning rate is inversely proportional to the accumulation of squared gradients (in the case of ADAGRAD with the square root of the sum of squared gradients). For the variational objective of topic models, the gradients are typically large in magnitude, especially when topic probabilities are close to zero or one.

Grammatical error detection is key for a number of natural language processing (NLP) tasks including text normalization, automatic essay grading, and language learning assistant systems. This paper aims to identify and discuss these issues. We provide context and motivation for our approach by first showing how GED differs from error detection in other domains, then identifying the factors that complicate the evaluation of GED systems, and finally outlining best practices for evaluation in light of these issues. A primary reason GED is among the most difficult NLP tasks is its inherent nature. Unlike recognition or classification tasks where each instance belongs exclusively to a discrete category (e.g., a sentence is either grammatical or its grammatical error has a unique label), GED requires systems to identify errors in the context of entire sentences that can have multiple problems. Annotators may also vary in their error labeling, reflecting linguistic nuance or judgment, further complicating the comparison between a given system's output and the intended “correct” correction. For instance, an error in tense inconsistency could be labeled by one annotator while another may see the sentence as grammatical in context; the diversity in human evaluation makes it difficult to align annotations with a single gold standard. Traditional evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve), while widely used, can misrepresent the performance of a GED system due to the skewed distribution of errors versus non-errors in real texts (errors are typically rare). The inconsistent distribution impacts recall more significantly than precision and accuracy, leading to potential overestimation of system performance if these metrics are the sole or primary indicators used in evaluation. Another issue arises from the dependence of evaluation on the matched correction base. If a system is trained to recognize certain types of errors but the evaluation set contains different types of errors, the performance of the system in detecting its training-set errors may not generalize well to other errors. This is especially problematic if the evaluation set is smaller or comes from a different source than the training data.

We propose a method for Domain Adaptation with Latent Semantic Association (LaSA) for NER. The LaSA model learns the latent semantic association among words from the unlabeled corpus of the target domain. Words are grouped into concepts according to their contextually related snippets, which captures the semantic similarity but also accounts for the possibility of multiword expressions or collocations.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Traditionally, NER systems are trained and evaluated on specific domains such as news articles, academic papers, or webpages, and their performance degrades when applied to different domains. For instance, the NER system trained on news articles may not perform well on questions or queries asked on web search engines because these texts use different vocabulary and structure. This issue arises due to the domain shift that makes the pre-trained NER models fail to generalize to other domains. Cross-domain NER aims to overcome this challenge by enabling NER models to be adapted to or trained on multiple domains simultaneously. One way to adapt NER models to new domains is to utilize resources available in the target domain, but often such domain-specific resources are limited or not easily accessible. In addition to resource scarcity, adapting semantic models to new domains in the absence of labeled data is a significant challenge. Another challenge that has to be addressed while adapting NER models to new domains is the potential language shift. Different domains often have varying stylistic, syntactical, and lexicon usage, which can make the recognition of entities difficult. This problem is exacerbated in cross-domain NER as the NER model trained on one domain is often not equipped to handle the unique characteristics and nuances present in another domain. To address these challenges in the context of cross-domain NER, we propose the use of search engine results. Specifically, we submit the tokens and its context to a search engine and utilize the context in the search results to aid in entity recognition. By leveraging the diverse and abundant text snippets returned by search engines, we can gain insights into how entities are mentioned across various contexts, which is key to generalizing NER models to new domains. Our key idea is twofold: first, we learn a robust representation of the context surrounding each entity in the input text by analyzing how the search engine groups and presents similar contexts. We use these representations to inform the entity recognition process. Second, we analyze the search engine results to identify patterns, synonyms, and entity usage that can be useful for recognizing entities even when the training data is scarce or domain-specific. We refer to our framework as "Piggyback" because we benefit from the pre-existing work done by search engines to extract valuable context and patterns that aid in cross-domain NER.

Yet, these studies have glossed over the nature of the symbols (or signs) the agents use and how they relate these symbols to the images or objects in the world. Here, we focus on "visual representations," defined as the structures within the agent's cognitive system that map the visual world to symbols. Specifically, we ask the following question: Do agents in these communication games develop visual representations that are closely tied to human-like concepts about objects (e.g., features related to objects' material, shape, function, etc.)? To answer our question, we build upon the framework of Lazaridou et al. (2017), which introduces so-called "referential games." Two agents see a scene (comprised of multiple objects), and their goal is to communicate about the objects until they agree on which one of the objects the "teacher" (a human or another agent) is referring to.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Traditionally successful NER systems are trained and fine-tuned on large annotated corpora, and use sophisticated feature engineering and gazetteers. However, in low-resource transfer settings, training data is drastically limited, and this challenge is further compounded by the questions of cross-linguality (the task often needs to perform well in a new language with minimal annotated data) and phonological ambiguity (words often pronounced identically or very similarly may belong to different named entity categories). Many existing cross-lingual transfer solutions for NER rely on techniques such as multilingual embeddings, cross-lingual transfer of word embeddings, or jointly training for multiple languages. These methods are very successful in language similarity settings (e.g., languages belonging to the same language family) but perform poorly when transferring from a resource-rich language to a language with a significantly different writing system or phonology. In this paper, we introduce a phonologically aware neural model for NER that uses language universal phonological character representations in conjunction with word embeddings. Unlike orthographic representations which are inherently language specific and may not capture salient phonological similarities across languages (e.g., 'café' and 'coffee'), phonological representations encode symbols that are shared across languages for the same phoneme (even if the orthographic representation differs, like the 'café' and 'coffee' example). Furthermore, we incorporate the core attentional mechanism in the neural model to focus on salient parts of the sequence while performing inference. This is particularly important for named entities, which may be embedded deep in a sentence and may be preceded by substrings that carry strong semantic cues, but are not part of the entity itself. The proposed approach is evaluated on a set of low-resource transfer settings and the results are compared to several baselines and state of the art methods. Our approach significantly outperforms these baselines and demonstrates the value of phonological representations in facilitating transfer in low-data settings. The statistical efficiency of the model is further improved by incorporating both attentional and phonological features, leading to better generalization and performance in 0-shot transfer settings and low-data settings. While the model is not completely dependent on labeled data, our results show that phonological representations and attention contribute to a model’s ability to learn generalizable features across languages for NER tasks. We hope that this work contributes to the development of more robust NER systems for low-resource languages and cross-lingual transfer settings, demonstrating the theoretical and practical value of incorporating language universal phonological features and attentional mechanisms in the development of such systems.

Among these, lexico-semantic resources particularly have been well studied (Evert & Van Noord, 2001) and have proven to be very successful in various NLP questions. A kind of resources that seems to be missing in the field, however, are those linking words with the senses with which they are perceived and described, of which the five main ones are sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch. For example, how is "puff" associated with its senses? Puff could be associated with the vocals of a bird in the sense of hearing, or it could be associated with seeing smoke or clouds. Linking words to senses is a fundamental and valuable task for both understanding natural language and for various NLP applications, from sentiment analysis to image or event extraction. For instance, knowledge about the sensory aspects of words is crucial when trying to extract the intentions or emotions from textual data, as sometimes terms such as "tasty" might be used metaphorically, similar to "pleasing" (Pustejovsky & Jezek, 1995). However, there is a general lack of this kind of resources and only isolated attempts have been made towards their construction (e.g., Bellegarda et al., 2012;Rizzo et al., 2012). In this paper, we address this gap by presenting an automatically constructed sensorial lexicon, which we name Sensicon, associating English words with senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch. A Sensorial Lexicon A key question we answer in this work is: which senses are "proper" for a given word? For example, "dull" is primarily associated with sight (something might seem dull or be dull in color), but could also be associated with touch (e.g., a dull surface or pain). More specifically, together with each entry in the Sensicon lexicon comes a list of senses that describe the concept represented by the word or phrase. While this task might appear intuitive to humans, due to our commonsense knowledge, automating it is a complex challenge that requires large amounts of diverse examples illustrating how words are used with respect to senses, along with some general rules or heuristics for deciding between overlapping senses. This is particularly true when dealing with polysemous words, which might be associated with different senses depending on contexts (as in the case of "dull" mentioned above). Approach and Methodology To construct the Sensicon lexicon, we adopt a corpus-based and statistical approach, leveraging co-occurrence statistics to automatically generate examples of sense-word associations and then further refine and evaluate them using human-labeled data.

This limitation becomes particularly important for tasks where the data is annotated by hand, where large-scale language annotation can be impractical or out of economic reach (e.g. for many domains and even languages). Sentence compression, a task where a model generates a short summary of a text, is one such task. It is an important subproblem in various NLP tasks and applications, including text summarization (Rush et al., 2015), among others. While current methods based on LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) have achieved impressive results on some datasets (e.g. 20% BLEU on the widely used CNN/Daily Mail dataset (Hermann and Blunsom, 2014)), it is still far from what is required for general-purpose or even business applications. Current models are trained on this relatively small dataset and only see very generic domains (CNN news and Daily Mail). One solution to improve the domain adaptability of these models is to rely on additional syntactic features in the architecture of a model. This has been investigated, for example, for paraphrasing and text simplification (Sutskever et al., 2014;Holtzman et al., 2015). However, such features are typically auxiliary to grammaticality constraints, and they are not used to explicitly "help" a model to compress sentences in a more domain-specific, sub-syntactically inconsistent way that respects subject-verb agreement and other textual constraints. Our approach designates a model that not only consider the general syntactic structure of the sentence but also imposes a dependence between the words of the input sentence. The idea is that whenever a word is deleted or kept, this should affect the grammaticality of the sentence, or in our case, its overall informative value. Our hypothesis is that by using syntactic information we might improve domain adaptability of our model because syntax captures important structural information for any language. The intuition behind this is that irrespective of the domain-specific structure of words (blending of newly added terms for a domain with pre-existing concepts such as medical terminology), syntax still underpins the compositionality aspect of language.

The importance of this task is evident across a number of natural language processing (NLP) applications including information extraction, time-series data analysis and question answering. Current research efforts in this area face questions such as "What linguistic features are the most useful for predicting temporal relations?" (Molas and Li, 2016;Cohen et al., 2015), "Is there any structure in how temporal relations are expressed?" Temporal relations can be expressed in a number of ways. These include linguistic constructs that directly indicate a specific relation (e.g., connectives such as before, after, during), more implicit cues (such as verb tense, aspect, and tense) and discourse and semantic relations that provide context about potential relations (such as causality, coordination between events, or temporal landmarking or referencing). A challenge in the area is that this variety of expression and the variety of underlying domains and disciplines may make different sets of features relevant across different types of data and assumed world knowledge. Another challenge is that existing large scale sets of temporal relation labeled data (e.g., the TimeBank Corpus (Pustejovsky et al., 2003b), the MTurk English AMR Relation Corpus, and the Di-DeA Corpus (Granroth-Wilding and Clark, 2016)) all have inherent ambiguities and inconsistencies in how temporal relations are marked and annotated. These ambiguities and inconsistencies are due to a variety of factors including contextual dependencies and the need to make explicit implicit references to time or events in natural language. A further challenge is that the measured evaluation methods in this field are still in debate (Luo et al., 2014;Lemberger et al., 2016). Existing approaches to temporal relation classification generally fall into two main categories: (1) Morpho-syntactic approaches, which extract features such as tense, aspect, complementizer usage, preposition usage, and temporal adverbials (e.g., always, soon, eventually, later), and (2) Learning-based approaches, which are often based on machine learning and deep learning techniques applied to rich feature sets such as those just described, in conjunction with more superficial features such as word embedding and part-of-speech tagging (Cohen et al., 2015;Li and Ji, 2014;Makhoul and Modayil, 2015).

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models with seq2seq architecture using large datasets typically requires significant computational resources (both time and memory). Decoding such models generates a single most likely translation, and using this simple strategy gives low quality results. A better tactic is to generate a batch of translations, or a beam, and choose the best among them – a method called beam search. Beam search significantly improves the output quality but further increases the computational load. Training a very large NMT model that achieves near human-level translation quality, especially when paired with a beam search, can strain even very large systems with strong GPU memory configurations. Even if a large NMT model is trained, it is impractical for most practical scenarios due to its large size and training costs. These models need to be reduced to more manageable sizes in order to easily integrate with online services, devices, or among other computational limitations. However, reducing a large NMT model can lead to a significant drop in performance. Hence, there is a need to develop methods which reduce the model size without sacrificing translation quality. Knowledge distillation (Bucila et al., 2006;Hinton et al., 2015) is a common approach to create light weight or student models. It is often applied to reduce the complexity of image and language models. Knowledge distillation involves training a small model (student) with the objective of imitating the outputs of the large 'teacher' model. Traditionally, this imitation happens over the teacher model's predicted probabilities over the model's output at individual word level (so called word-level distillation). This latter approach has been less successful for NMT tasks, especially for large model-to-student model size ratios, because NMT typically has much longer context (sequences) and many-to-many and many-to-one mappings between source and target language words. We present a novel approach to apply knowledge distillation in NMT which we call 'sequence-level distillation'. This approach considers the teacher model's behavior over entire sequence decisions, or more specifically, the measured probabilities for each target token sequence. Our proposed method of sequence-level distillation foresees that NMT models can be simplified or scaled down without losing much accuracy by teaching the student to predict sequences of words (i.e., whole translations) instead of trying to predict individual target tokens (as done in traditional word-level distillation). An advantage of this approach is that it naturally encourages the student to learn multi-token predictions, just like the original NMT model, which results in better translations over zero shot or greedy outputs.

Rule-based systems naturally offer improved explainability over many deep learning models. Each decision made by our system can be traced back to a particular rule or a series of rules, making it easier to debug, audit, or fine-tune the system when needed.

Learning Multiview Embeddings for Assessing Dementia: A Canonical Correlation Approach We introduce a novel canonical correlation analysis (CCA)-based method to learn multiview embeddings for deep phenotyping and early detection of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). We first discuss the ideal properties for such embeddings and then motivate the use of CCA, a well-established statistical technique which captures canonical correlation between two or more multivariate datasets. We outline the CCM (Canonical Correlation Machine) framework that makes the inference and learning of CCAs efficient via the use of neural networks. To validate and apply our method, we extracted a dataset from DementiaBank, a unique corpus of natural speech samples collected to study early signs of cognitive decline in AD patients. After pre-processing the dataset with MMDS (Multiple Main Diagonal Singular Value Decomposition), we applied our CCM framework to learn multiple semantic correlations between speech and language content features from DementiaBank. We demonstrate the effectiveness of learned multiview embeddings in two important tasks: 1) distinguishing between Alzheimer's patients and healthy controls; and 2) predicting clinically relevant cognitive scores. In both tasks, we observe significant improvements in predictive accuracy and generalizability when compared to using either single-view features or existing state-of-the-art multitask learning approaches. Specifically, our multiview model provided an F1 score of 0.82 with an impressive positive predictive value (PPV) for the classification task. For the regression task, the mean absolute error (MAE) is significantly reduced by approximately 20% (from 4.25 to 3.42). In addition to DementiaBank, we demonstrated the feasibility of using our approach on a synthetic dataset based on another corpus of clinical data and a language corpus. This shows that our approach is model-agnostic and can learn multiview embeddings from different types of data that may be available for assessing dementia or other diseases. Our approach has several key advantages over traditional methods of biomedical natural language processing (BioNLP). First, it learns latent, compact representations that are simultaneously interpretable and discriminative. Second, by leveraging concurrent canonical correlations within and across data modalities, it can implicitly model various modes of cognitive and linguistic impairments that manifest differently across AD patients. These are potential advantages that we believe contribute to its improved performance in assessing dementia. This paper presents our CCA framework for multiview learning and demonstrates its utility on real-world AD data. We also provide insights on the challenges of applying deep learning to clinical datasets and future research directions for developing more generalizable models.

Training natural language processing (NLP) models with maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) objectives is currently the standard. These models are optimized to predict the nth step of the output sequence based on the previous n-1 steps and the various context features. However, despite the success of maximum-likelihood and its variants in sequence prediction, there are several issues questions remain open. For one thing, MLE emphasizes improving the model's prediction of the next word (or token) given the past sequence, and ignores other factors that contribute to better sequence-level quality (e.g., proper sentence structure, coherence, and even backwards prediction). This is a form of prediction bias. Another issue, and more importantly for our work, is that many NLP tasks are ultimately evaluated on sequence-level metrics. For instance in summarization, the ROUGE score is a sequence-level metric that assesses whether the generated summary contains enough “common” content with a reference summary, and does not properly penalize the model for producing a poor sequence of the included content. In translation, BLEU and its variants score how well the generated translation covers the content and surface forms of the reference translation. But because MLE optimizes the model to predict each word or token, it does not necessarily align with the expected sequence-level optimization. To alleviate both issues, several works have explored policy gradient methods, which directly optimize the sequence level metric while the model is still trained on the MLE objective. While these methods have shown improvements over the standard MLE training in some tasks, they suffer from high variance due to the non-differentiable policy (optimization is performed through sampling) and can struggle with large and complex datasets. Assuming that predicting the sequence is the outcome of a stochastic process, and that the "longest common subsequence" (LCS) between the candidates and the reference plays a role in that, we investigate the possibility of optimizing a differentiable variant of the LCS objective or its approximate during the training of the sequence prediction model. More specifically, in this paper, we present the CALCS (Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence) objective. The CALCS is derived from the observation that, if instead of the best possible LCS score, we continuously approximate the best possible sequence given our current model parameters, we might be able to mitigate some of the instability issues associated with policy gradient methods. In detail: - Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) is a well-known measure for capturing the similarity between two sequences.

For example, an input could be a document about a particular entity (e.g., Barack Obama) in a KB. Natural language inference (NLI), also known as text entailment or semantic text similarity, is the task of determining if one piece of text entails, contradicts, or is neutral towards another piece of text. It has become a benchmark for various NLP problems including language understanding, sentiment analysis, question answering, and dialogue systems. Current state-of-the-art models on questions such as "What is the most prevalent and successful attention mechanism in NLI?" would likely point at the attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, as fracturing out noteworthy winners in influential datasets such as SNLI , MultiNLI , and Quora . Attention mechanisms allow the NLI models to selectively focus on portions of one sentence when considering the other, offering a flexible way to capture dynamic relationships between words or phrases. However, in our view, the realm of interaction mechanisms is broad and among the most unexplored in NLI research. The recent trend of adopting "attention" as the go-to solution could lead to a narrow understanding of how we should model interaction in natural language. Our work proposes a creative yet very intuitive model, the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), which entirely explores this black box. CIN deviates from the traditional attention mechanisms in two significant ways. First, while attention focuses on identifying which parts of the sentence should be considered when evaluating the relationship with another sentence, CIN pushes the interaction further by dynamically generating filters through the entire process of interaction. The filters in CIN are learned at the same time as the model, based on the training data, providing an additional level of flexibility. This allows the model to capture more nuanced relationships between sentence constituents. Second, CIN can model interaction using filters in varying sizes, enabling it to learn from smaller, more local, and granular contexts, up to larger, overarching contexts. Essentially, CIN uses convolutional operations over the features of one sentence, with filters that are influenced by the features of another. This means if one sentence (X) contains a phrase that is crucial in understanding the relation with another sentence (Y), the filters of CIN are learned to specifically capture that relationship whenever such a phrase occurs. This does not mean CIN is static or that it predefines what relationship it is supposed to capture; on the contrary, the filters are learned dynamically on the fly. To further elucidate, let's consider a simplified scenario. Suppose we want to determine whether "John is sad because he lost his job" entails "John is depressed."

For queries, we hypothesize that users implicitly or explicitly consider a hierarchical structure of fact concepts when forming their queries. For entity representations, we build on the view that entities can be described through a series of factoid statements that capture different aspects of the entity’s nature and relationships in various information granularities. Certainly, here is my answer: Sentiment analysis or opinion mining is a rapidly growing area of research in natural language processing. It is often involved in determining the attitude of the writer towards a topic, product or service. This is usually achieved by classifying text into one of the sentiment categories (positive or negative), although the existence of a neutral category – which is questions or statements that do not express any subjectivity or emotional state – and the use of fine-grained labels (e.g., very positive, negative, minimal, etc.) have been argued for (Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010;Pang and Lee, 2005). One essential aspect of any practical sentiment analysis application is the use of ratings to validate the performance of sentiment detection models, despite the fact that in almost all cases, we cannot objectively measure the sentiment of text. This is because there is no universally agreed-upon unit of sentiment measurement. Instead, many choose to use human-generated ratings (Mani and Maybury, 2008) or user-generated ratings (Glied,2006) as the gold standard, expecting that these ratings accurately reflect the sentiment of the accompanying text. However, these ratings might not always achieve or even aim at objectivity For instance, a given review can elicit different viewpoints from different readers (our ground truth is often based on a shallow perspective of a single annotator), while the 'average' rating label is in practice more often a distillation of ratings coming from different, plausible, interpretations of the same text. This raises the important question: Can one predict the rating for a given text? Assuming the answer is yes, can we rely on ratings in practice: as a learning objective for sentiment analysis models, as well as a measure of performance? and how reliable is this model when human judgment doesn't come close to agreement (e.g., "strongly positive" versus "very positive")? The general sentiment understanding task, which involves rating or classifying text as the objective, depends critically on the measured evaluation methods: the test data and the evaluation metric. The most common metric used in evaluating sentiment analysis models is the Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA) score, measured by calculating the concordance and Cohen's Kappa (Landis and Koch, 1977). This is an indirect measure of how well human raters agree – on the assumption that if they don't agree well, then there's a problem with either the structure of the ratings (too many categories, or zero information gain by using them), or with the textual context leading to subjective judgments.

For example, in the example sentence, “There is no one more intelligent than Alison”, “Alison” is the only coreferent entity. Many methods for coreference resolution can be grouped into rule-based, statistical, or machine learning approaches. Rule-based methods rely on hand-crafted features and patterns, which limits the scalability of these systems (Johnston and Resnik, 1996; Kamp and Moldovan, 2005). Statistical or machine learning-based methods usually perform better than their rule-based counterparts or even human annotators in some cases (Pradhan et al., 2012). However, those hand-crafted features can't model the intricacies and nuanced language use effectively. For instance, the use of pronouns might not only depend on the textual cue but also on the context and the world knowledge (e.g., "U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson visited a country in the Middle East recently", where “a country” is a pronoun referring to another country mentioned explicitly or implicitly elsewhere in the text or discourse). Recent approaches in coreference resolution have incorporated deep learning models to benefit from the scalability and potential for capturing complex patterns in data without manual feature engineering. Deep learning techniques have achieved some of the best results in coreference resolution (Bansal et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Ghodsizadeh et al., 2017; Wang and Zhang, 2017), and the use of neural networks provides more flexibility and freedom in modeling text features inherently and implicitly. However, these approaches often require large amounts of training data and annotated gold standard data to function well.

RE are used to pick out individual objects, persons, and locations for further description or action, and are often constructed with reference to salient features and properties. However, this context isn't always available -- for instance, in the case of distributed cognition (Hollan et al., 2000), or when the speaker lacks expertise about the object being referred to. However, in many real-world applications, this "bazooka" approach may often fall short because the system doesn't have access to the entire set of available objects or because describing an object is not a trivial task. A more iterative, or "installment-based" approach might naturally be more effective (Clark, 1996; Riseman and Hanson, 1997). An installment-based approach would involve communicating a sequence of descriptions that together "narrow down" the set of potential referents until the correct object is identified (Matuski et al., 2016). This paper presents an investigation into using installments in referring expression generation for objects in photographs. The goal is to explore whether an iterative approach, similar to human communication strategies, can improve performance when generating RE. We argue that installments can be particularly useful in cases where the computational system confronts uncertainty and incomplete knowledge about object attributes and categories. Specifically, we extend our previous work on RE generation for objects in photographs (Gardner et al., 2018), where we previously proposed and evaluated a pipeline that generates strings of words grounded in image content. Here, we introduce a novel extension to this pipeline that enables generating referential installments and investigate how these improve the ability of the system to successfully identify objects within images.

This scenario is common not only to word segmentation and POS tagging in Chinese, but to many other annotation tasks as well, such as Wall Street Journal Penn Treebank 1.0 (Marcus et al., 1993), TDP (Huang et al., 1992), LDC05T07 (McDonald et al., 2005), and Universal Dependencies (Nivre et al., 2016). Training natural language parsers typically involves reranking candidate parse trees. A particular challenge in grounding language, as opposed to typical parsing applications, is that gold-standard references may not be available or may be difficult and expensive to obtain. Instead, feedback (e.g., success/fail in a language comprehension task or reward signal in reinforcement learning) can be used to set up a strong supervised signal that keeps learning grounded. This feedback is a form of weak supervision. In this paper, we show how discriminative reranking can be adapted to such situations, by designing reranking that only uses feedback in place of gold-standard references and by making the model compatible with semantic features beyond adjacency in the sample of parse trees to rerank. These features are particularly relevant in grounded language settings because they include perceptual descriptions of the environment. To this end, we propose a method for reranking parse trees using feedback (weak supervision) for grounded language acquisition. We then demonstrate experimentally that reranking with feedback achieves performance comparable to reranking with gold-standard references in the particular setting we investigate. For a parser to learn to follow navigational instructions from observation, it requires features beyond the surface syntactic structure of the instructions. A key innovation in our approach is the use of a latent-based reranking framework. This framework is designed to capture the richer, non-adjacent feature relationships and to incorporate the feedback signal into the reranking process in a robust manner. The latent variables used allow for expressive feature representations that go beyond the local textual context and include global features such as environmental state and navigation goals. We conduct experiments in a simulated environment where a model must learn to follow real-world navigation instructions matched with visual observations. The model is trained using weak supervision provided through feedback from successful or unsuccessful task completion. We confront several baselines including a systematic comparison with discriminative reranking trained on gold-standard references.

Training natural language understanding models to respond to navigation questions is one approach achieving interactive question answering systems. However, these models can still leave a performance gap between language and action and require the assumption that the routes talked about exist in the real world. A complete solution to map natural language instructions to a "navigable" spatial structure is still lacking. The task is to generate a high-level plan, which is a sequence of control commands for the robot to navigate from its current position to the goal location. The key idea is to represent the navigation plan as a line graph, which is a topological adjacency weighted graph without cycles (Dasgupta, 2014). The weights on the edges are used to enforce exploration, which is an important aspect of navigation especially when the robot is not familiar with the surrounding environment. The topology of the navigation plan is similar to the plan we conceptualize in our mind when we hear instructions like "turn left at the second corner, then go straight". Human navigators use spatial concepts such as corners, corners, turns, left-right, and straight to create a navigation plan. We encode these concepts in the line graph representation. For instance, in the example instruction "turn left at the second corner, then go straight", the line graph plan forms a "diagonal square" sequence (See Figure 1). In Figure 1, we see that the plan starts from a node, makes a "left" turn at another node which is represented as a left branch in the graph, and then "goes straight" along a single connected edge, which is the main "diagonal" of the square. The complete system we propose includes two main modules: (1) an embedding-based question answering module that extracts relevant variables and concepts from user instructions and (2) a planning module that converts the identified concepts into a line graph navigation plan.
