These relations are particularly useful for disambiguating pronouns in parsing (Collins, 1997;Lavie and Agarwal, 2007;Barth and Bender, 2008) and for improving machine translation (Koehn and Hoang, 2007). Coreference resolution (coref. res.) determines set of expressions that refer to the same object in a sentence, discourse, or document. Anaphora resolution, a related task, identifies pronominal expressions and determines the subject they refer to, typically by first determining that they are anaphoric (refer to an antecedent) and then determining the antecedent. These two tasks are closely related, but anaphora resolution is a well-defined subset of coreference resolution. Recent work has demonstrated that explicitly identifying anaphoric mentions (anaphoricity) prior to coreference resolution can significantly improve performance (He and Gildea, 2011;Sudoplatov and Osborne, 2013). Different approaches have been proposed For identifying anaphoricity, including lexical measures (Martineau and Strube, 2003), statistical models (Martínez, 2006;He and Gildea, 2011), and approaches leveraging syntactic patterns (Yatskar and Smith, 2013). Another class of approaches separates the task into two sub-tasks, using word embeddings or similarity-based features: first, for each noun phrase (NP) compute, and second, combine these results and confidence scores through a model to predict likely antecedents (Rashkin and Bates, 2015;Min et al., 2015). While all these approaches demonstrate improved performance over not removing non-anaphoric mentions, there may be room for a higher level, more global, approach. For example, determining whether a pronoun is likely to refer to a concept or mention before determining which mention it refers to. This paper contributes a graph cut-based approach to anaphoricity determination that draws inspiration from computer vision applications of graph cuts for image segmentation. We use a simplified implementation of the graph cut framework (Boykov and Jolly, 2001) optimized for the task of anaphoricity determination. Instead of pixels in an image segmenting the objects in the image into superpixels, our algorithm segments the text based on the degree of anaphoricity. The graph cut framework we apply allows us to simultaneously identify multiple regions of the text that are likely to correspond to coreference chains. Each mention is treated as a node in the graph, connected by weighted edges to other mentions that could be its antecedent. A clique-finding algorithm is then used to partition the graph into clusters, with the size of edges reflecting the semantic or syntactical distance between potential anaphor/antecedent pairs.

Social media platforms, online forums, and various other types of digital spaces for communication have become ubiquitous. However, as these modes of interaction are increasingly replacing face-to-face communication, they also introduce new challenges, such as the rise of antisocial behavior (e.g., harassment, personal attacks). Many of these online platforms have implemented various mechanisms to react to – rather than prevent – this kind of behavior. This reactive approach often involves manual moderation and, more recently, automated detection of unwanted behavior that has already taken place (Hiroyasu et al., 2019;Pehlivan et al., 2019). While this reactive approach is necessary and valuable, it is essential to complement it with preventive measures. Specifically, it would be beneficial to detect verbal cues, behavioral patterns, or features of the online environment that may indicate an online conversation is likely to degenerate. The objective of this paper is to develop methods that detect early warning signs of a conversation going awry. Unlike traditional toxicity and bullying detection methods, this approach focuses on the initial stages of communication where a conversation may still be salvaged. The key intuition underlying this work is that early conversational interactions can reveal useful signals about the vulnerability of the conversation to turn hostile. For example, a question that intuitively seems polite might actually be a rhetorical device that implies blame or condescension, potentially escalating the conversation's tone. Conversely, a direct statement that, while explicit, is still respectful of the other participants could make the conversation less likely to degrade. To identify these early signs, we turn to pragmatics, the study of language use in context. Pragmatic devices such as politeness strategies (Lakoff, 1973), indirect speech acts (Searle, 1969), and rhetorical forms (Rhetorica ad Herennium, ~30 BC) play a critical role in how we communicate effectively and influence others. These devices, embedded in the initial interactions of a conversation, can significantly impact future dialogue. For instance, measured, constructive feedback delivered politely tends to create a more positive conversational climate compared to blunt criticism delivered without reservation. However, even explicitly polite language can mask intentions that are ultimately harmful, if insincere or overly blunt. An important challenge is the variability and subtlety of these pragmatic devices across contexts and cultures. A single linguistic feature, such as using formal titles or first names/pet names, may signal different intentions depending on the specific setting (e.g., professional vs. personal conversation). Our proposed framework to tackle this challenge involves: 1.   Pragmatic device extraction  : Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques to identify and categorize potential pragmatic devices used in the opening exchanges of a conversation (e.g., politeness markers, rhetorical questions, appeals).

Training machine translation (MT) systems using minimum error rate training (MERT) first requires creating a suitable tuning set. The tuning set is constructed from available parallel data and includes the N-best lists of translations generated by the MT system for each source sentence. The need for large tuning sets to represent the diversity of the language models' outputs is a compelling argument for MERT , which uses all available context (the given source sentence and its N-best translation candidates) to choose the parameters that improve the translation quality (measured via an automatic evaluation metric such as BLEU). Thus, MERT is most effective when the system will be evaluated using the same automatic metric as its training. However, this assumption does not always hold. For MT systems, there is frequently a human evaluation component that uses a set of reference translations. When the MT system is optimized to just match the automatic metric, its predictions may not align well with the human evaluation of translation quality. The fundamental issue here is that automatic evaluation metrics have known limitations and biases , such as over-rewarding word-for-word matches with the reference and not capturing creative translation decisions (Hassan et al., 2007). As a result, optimizing an MT system for achieving the maximum BLEU score or a similar metric may result in translations that are perceived as suboptimal by human evaluators (Cettour et al., 2020). This suggests that incorporating human judgements about translation quality into the training process could lead to higher-quality MT systems that better meet human needs (Oard and Dorr, 2002; Walker et al., 2012). However, incorporating human judgment into the training loop is a challenging task. For example, if each candidate translation produced by the MT system were to be manually evaluated for quality by a human, the number of human annotations required for a single MERT tuning would be prohibitive. In this paper, we propose a method for Human-in-the-loop Minimum Error Rate Training (HI-MERT) that incorporates human judgments measured by reference translations into the optimization of the MT system. Our approach leverages the redundancy inherent in the N-best lists produced during MERT to reduce the number of required human annotations. Specifically, instead of evaluating every possible combination of translation candidates for changing the system parameters, we focus on making sure that the parameter setting appropriately distinguishes between high- versus low-quality candidate translations for each source sentence.

Training neural networks with large number of parameters is known to improve accuracy of statistical machine translation systems. However, these models are computationally expensive and are difficult to deploy in practical systems. One way to reduce the use of resources is through model pruning. Pruning reduces redundancy in over-parameterized models. A particular effective approach is to use a smaller set of n-gram features which are adaptively selected (Cohn and Lapata, 2009). These features represent the top ranked n-grams and their language models can be trained fractively. Table 1 (of Cohn and Lapata (2009)) shows that this type of feature selection leads to accuracy comparable to full word n-gram models with fewer than 30% of parameters. However, these adaptive features are very similar to the word-based features that are used by the n-gram language model. This similarity suggests that weighted ngram features (such as log-linear models) could potentially achieve better accuracy. Hence, we hope to achieve a similar gain through a fully discriminative approach. We believe that the main challenge in handling large parameter models in a discriminative training setting is that it is difficult to achieve convergence in this setting because discriminative training generally weights the training data by their oracles (corrupted by the model itself). To address it, we propose to use a semi-supervised discriminative training procedure for training shallowly structured models with very large number of parameters. Specifically, we train the log-linear model’s weights over its features to predict gold probabilities over a large training dataset while providing an additional hint through additional inference over held out (training or test) sentences. A more elaborate version of this hint can be obtained through additional in-domain or out-of-domain generative modeling (Daniel and Marcu, 2001;Huang and Chiang, 2012) . But it proves to be too inconsistent across models. As a consequence, we choose a na¨ıve procedure based on just in-domain generation (iid Bernoulli from measured variables). This approach has a few advantages: (1) it is relatively fast to generate since we only need to forward pass through couple of translation models (2) it is less resource-intensive than and comparable in coverage to more elaborate methods (Huang and Chiang, 2012;Junczys-Dowmunt et al., 2017) (3) it is readily available in almost all machine translation setups so we can run this on top of all existing translation models without any further adjustments.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental medium of contemporary communication, reflecting social contexts, personal attitudes, and inter-human relationships. A core component of this communication is language, which, due to its inherently flexible nature, has various forms and expressions. Among these is the indispensable yet often contentious and variegated use of vulgar language – a subset of language which carries significant socio-cultural undertones and often finds its way into digital communication. Understanding the intentions behind the use of vulgar expressions is of paramount importance, yet it remains under-addressed in natural language processing (NLP) and computational linguistics research. Generally, vulgar language has been largely excluded from NLP research primarily because it defies traditional, restrictive models of language. However, recent advances in language modeling and contextualized word representations, have made it possible to approach this topic with new vigor. While research into understanding vulgar language has started to emerge in recent years, such works either focus on detecting offensive content [10] , or purely qualitative analysis of vulgar expressions [3] . There is a clear need for a quantitative understanding and computational analysis of the intentions behind vulgar expressions. In this paper, we present the first large-scale quantitative study of the pragmatic aspects of vulgarity in English language use on Twitter. We focus specifically on the intentions behind using a given set of vulgar words identified from our data set through human annotation. This annotation is based on the most common categories of vulgar word use while maintaining simplicity and interpretability. Specifically, we identify the primary intention behind the usage of a vulgar expression, including but not limited to expressing anger or aggression, signaling group identity, commenting on or refuting ideas, signaling informality, expressing emotion without intending to offend, and suggesting or alluding to sexual themes without resorting to overt profanity. To this end, we present a novel data set comprised of 7,800 tweets annotated with their respective categories of vulgar word use. The annotations were performed by a team of linguists and language specialists who worked independently to ensure a high degree of consistency and measured inter-annotator agreement. We also include demographic information matched to each user to investigate if demographic factors such as age, gender, region, or cultural background play a significant role in the intentions behind and the frequency of vulgar language use. Our study takes a machine learning approach to model these annotations. We develop a novel model that considers both the local context of the vulgar words themselves (including multiword expressions) and the demographic features available from the user.

Training neural networks with large amounts of data is known to improve accuracy of performance (Hinton et al., 2012). However, designing architectures that are optimized for large datasets is non-trivial. In statistical machine translation (SMT), the traditional phrase-based model is one of the most successful empirical and theoretical models (Koehn, 2005). However, one of the main weaknesses of this model is its reliance on the conventional maximum likelihood principle (Mackay, 2003), which confines the amount of context considered in the model and increases the number of parameters that need to be estimated. As a result, most phrase-based models primarily rely on n-grams, which are a rich source of information about the vocabulary but a very coarse representation of syntax, semantics, and discourse in the context of translation (Hwa and Ng, 1992; Fourquet et al., 1996; Brown et al., 1992; Chiang and Vingralek, 2008). Furthermore, looking for the best parameters requires conducting very large-scale parametrized searches over many hypotheses (Zophrev, 2016), which is generally unfeasible in practice or even on cluster machines. For a long time this has prevented the development of SMT models capable of handling large amounts of training data in practice. However, recent advances in deep learning (DBN; Hinton et al., 2006; RNNs; Le et al., 2015; SGD; Kingma and Ba, 2014) have taken the community's attention away from conventional maximum likelihood estimation in favor of more efficient learning methods based on gradient descent optimization. Inspired by these advances, we propose to represent translation units in a continuous space, and learn a mapping between these units from one language to another that can effectively leverage contextual information and scale to large datasets. The main idea of our approach is to represent the source and target phrases side-by-side, and together learn parameters that map between the blurred versions of these contiguous representations. The architecture is trained using a multi-layer neural network, and we argue that this end-to-end trainable model framework and continuous space representations can naturally incorporate a very large amount of data and capture large amounts of contextual information. The core of our approach – translating between blurred representations of contiguous linguistic objects – has a long history and a theoretical basis. The structure of our model is inspired by the semantic interpretation of information fusion models (Battiti 1995) and theoretical work on the use of fuzzy representations and almost-contiguous processing of linguistic units (Pirrelli and Asperti 2008, 2010).

Most NLP tools developed for languages with alphabetic scripts are deeply rooted in the discourse structure, but those developed for non-alphabetic languages, such as Chinese, are relatively scarce due to the lack of resources. One central part of a discourse annotated corpus is the representation of rhetorical structures of discourse, as fracturing out independent sentences and tracking their inter-relationships can help provide context and meaning that can be particularly useful in interpreting texts. However, standard dependency parsing, which is widely used for Chinese, is not designed for discourse structure analysis; instead, it's used for sentence level syntactic analysis. Sentences that have been structured to show their relationships among semantic entities via adjacency in the dependency tree do not directly show the rhetorical structure underneath the sentence level organization. Hence, while dependency parsing is helpful for some NLP tasks, its application to discourse analysis is limited. One solution to this challenge is to build a special corpus that marks up discourse structure in Chinese texts. There have been major efforts in the English language, which has led to the development of the Penn Discourse Treebank (Penn Discourse Treebank, 2013) as well as the shallow discourse corpora based on Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) in Spanish and Russian. However, despite several Chinese discourse corpora annotated under RST (Li and Lin, 2015; He, 2015), their dependency tree structures, if presented at all, can only partially capture the discourse organization. One reason is that the discourse relationship and the nucleus of discourse units are often defined through a two-stage approach: first, identify discourse segments, and then define their relationship. Therefore, there exists a gap between the dependency tree, which represents syntactic structure, and the discourse structure above the sentence level. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT) scheme specifically designed for Chinese discourse analysis. The core idea is to directly integrate discourse relations and rhetorical structure into the dependency tree framework and embed discourse level annotations into the entire corpus. This scheme takes dependency parsing as the baseline, where each sentence is parsed into a dependency tree. However, instead of treating each sentence in isolation, we apply connectives to establish relationships among sentences, thus forming a single, large discourse tree covering the entire document.

Training embeddings using word analogy tasks (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) and word similarity scores (Le and Mikolov, 2014) has been shown to substantially outperform count-based methods on many NLP tasks. Current research efforts have focused on developing questions designed to probe various aspects of the embedding space (e.g., numerical differentiation (Mikolov et al., 2013), minimal language tasks (Pagliardini et al., 2015), alignment with preexisting semantic resources (Arora et al., 2015)). Such tests are, however, inherently limited in their ability to evaluate the embeddings from the perspective of what's required for NLP tasks in general. This is due to the fact that existing tests are semantic probe tests that look at the places of particular words in the embedding space. Such an approach relies on the implicit assumption that the entire NLP system can be implemented with no more than finding the positions of the words in the embedding space and then performing a local operation (e.g., similar word search or SVMs). This assumption grossly underestimates the complexity of NLP systems or even human processing. Current NLP systems often require the capability to perform complex operations on the embeddings, such as different levels of conjunction or disjunction of word features assumed in the embedding space beyond simple word similarity. These operations require the embedding space itself to contain certain structures, or subspaces, in the form of higher-order relations among the constituent vectors. This points to the fundamental need for a more general framework, or set of criteria, to evaluate the inherent analytical power of an embedding space, considering both the representation of word features and the embedding space’s ability to support higher-order analysis leading to rational inference. To that end, we define four critical criteria for word embedding spaces based on linguistic and cognitive principles, and devise associated intrinsic evaluation tests for these criteria. These criteria consider characteristics of natural language and measured demands of current NLP systems: 1. Order: The necessity for the space to support relations such as word order or sequence explicitly. While storing word order information is straightforward for count-based methods and embeddings trained on sentences (e.g., Skip-gram with negative sampling (Mikolov et al., 2013)), storehouse methods for capturing order in position/pair-based methods such as Word2vec are less evident. 2. Composition: The capacity for the embedding space to encode concepts such as conjunctions and disjunctions.

In SMT, translation is approached as a sequence alignment problem and the appropriate alignment, typically a tree or a phrase, is identified through finding the best possible piecewise alignment of the source and the target sentences (Koehn et al., 2003). This issue arises from the need to precompute the translation model on the source side before using it during the translation process. This leads to a limitation known as "ordering bottleneck" for SMT, where translation output is highly dependent on the source word order sequence (Zanette and Manandhar, 2006), hindering the model's ability to fully capture the word order flexibility found in more contextually rich and free word-order languages. In this work, we propose to investigate the use of bidirectional techniques in phrase-based decoding while addressing this ordering bottleneck. Bi-directional techniques have already shown substantial promise in several natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as parsing (Kitaev et al., 2012) and machine translation (Koehn, 2010;Sakaguchi, 2010), where understanding the context in both directions is crucial. The key idea of bidirectional analysis is to incorporate both left-to-right (LTR) and right-to-left (RTL) contextual information and decode in both directions to compensate for the potential loss of information inherent in the LTR-only approach. The measured variables may vary, but a common example is taking the matched phrase base for the translation model in both LTR and RTL directions and combining the outputs by weighted averages or through more sophisticated integration strategies. The hypothesis is that bidirectional techniques can provide improvements for a wide range of language pairs especially where the conventional LTR-only approach may struggle to capture the complexities of the translation task due to strict ordering constraints. For example, in certain Arabic-Hebrew or Urdu-English translations, employing a bidirectional approach might better capture the directional word order nuances between the source and target languages.

Specifically, one of the most fundamental and far-reaching components of language acquisition is the phonetic and lexical development (Hirose, 2003). During the critical period of L1 acquisition, which typically keeps from birth to around 5-7 years of age, infants and toddlers remarkably pick up on the rich structures of phonology, vocabulary, and verbal communication prevalent in their environment despite the absence of explicit teaching methods. One of the primary reasons why this period is critical is that learners can effortlessly sample from and react to the linguistic input making the process of language acquisition an inherently implicit and internalizable endeavor (Snow, 1977). The process of acquiring a phonetic and lexical system therefore proceeds through the aggregation of many small pieces of information. Lexical acquisition often begins with acquiring major salient words in their various phonetic contexts or variants (Miyagawa, 2013). A child might start by identifying units like 'mama' as a single lexical item associated with a certain set of sounds while another 'mama', perhaps with the sound more like 'mwmma', is identified also as 'mama' after repeated exposure. Similarly, they must learn to generalize phonetic features and tune into specific acoustic cues as predictors of a certain word (Aslin et al., 1981). Thus, understanding the nature of lexical acquisition is closely tied to the ability to model phonetic analysis leading to word recognition. Previous computational models of language acquisition have largely treated these areas—of lexical acquisition and phonetic understanding—separately, each requiring separate models (e.g., Johnson, 2004; Kuperman, 2011). The idea of a unified model that simultaneously addresses both lexical and phonetic acquisition is conceptually rich but largely undeveloped. However, several studies and theoretical papers have pointed to the necessity of changing the stance from isolated models to integrated ones (Gentner, 1989; Jusczyk, 1997; Mattys et al., 2006). This paper proposes such an integrated model—where information about lexical items and information about their phonetic variants are learned together and strengthening the predictive power of both. The proposed model, which we term the Unified Acquisition Model (UAM), uses statistical and machine-learning tools to integrate a language model with a phonetic generative model.

In recent years, various approaches have been proposed and used for Chinese word segmentation. A recent study (Lin and Hwang, 2001) provides a comprehensive review of the literature on this topic. The most commonly used approaches for Chinese word segmentation are character-based segmentation approaches, particularly dictionary-based techniques (e.g. Liu and Cheung, 1999; Lin and Chang, 2002). These techniques are very fast and accurate in practical scenarios. However, their downside is that they are heavily reliant on externally given dictionaries, which can be incomplete or outdated -especially problematic in the context of new terms or names of persons and places. On the other hand, there are several models belonging to the class of rule-based approaches (some of which are lexicon-independent). These models are comprised of various rules and constraints (e.g. on admissible sequential structure of Chinese words or orphans) derived from the general linguistic properties of the language. The lexicon-free nature of these rules-based models makes them robust in the absence of any specifically compiled lexicon, while the linguistic concreteness of their underlying rules sets them apart from unsupervised models that work directly over the orthographic representation of text. However, there remains a lack of attempts to tackle unsupervised Chinese word segmentation in the context of phonemic representations. The lack of explicit word boundaries in the phonemic (and even the orthographic) form of spoken Chinese and the fact that a large number of Chinese words can be homophonous (especially if tones are neglected in analysis) make this a challenging and yet important direction for research. This paper presents one such attempt at tackling this task. Our method leverages the concept of adaptor grammars (Goldwater et al., 2009), which were first developed for modeling unsupervised word segmentation from phonemic transcriptions of child-directed speech in English. From technical standpoint, adaptor grammars are a probabilistic non-parametric framework for making inference over a variety of structured probabilistic models. One of the unique features of these models is that they incorporate local context boundaries and a set of adaptor parameters, which allows the models to learn different semantic or syntactic information that is necessary to identify word boundaries.

Previous approaches to TR classification have primarily relied on shallow text features combined with extensive feature engineering while the deeper structures such as syntactic relationships in the text have often been overlooked [2] [3] [4] . A key insight from recent research in natural language processing is that the features extracted from dependency parses can provide significant improvements for various tasks [5] [6] . Dependency parses represent grammatical structure of sentences by showing words and their contexts as directed arcs and they reveal the underlying syntactic analysis leading to stronger semantic understanding of the text [7] . The use of dependency parse-based features for TR classification has not been fully explored. We introduce a model that significantly improves TR classification by incorporating dependency parse similarity between pairs of sentences involving a time expression, an event, and their relationship. The model employs a simple yet effective method of measuring sentence-level similarity by using a convolution kernel to process dependency parses and then classifies TR based on a deep neural network. However, state-of-the-art methods can benefit further from additional high-quality annotated data. Expert annotation for such tasks is often costly. In contrast, crowdsourced annotation can provide a feasible alternative, but it comes with its challenges, including the potential for low-accuracy labels. Our work addresses this by proposing a selective crowdsourcing strategy tailored to the TR classification task.

Negotiations, whether occurring within humans or between machines, are deeply rooted in communication. The main goal of negotiation is to reach an agreement on one or more issues by improving and sustaining the relationships between the negotiators – a process that requires both strategic planning and skillful communication. Strategic planning involves defining and adjusting the negotiation strategy, taking into account the preferences and constraints of both parties, and of course, one's own objectives. Communication, on the other hand, requires generating appropriate responses that keeps the conversation flowing and facilitates the strategy's execution. In human negotiations, we see that, while the strategy and the responses can be planned jointly, they are, in fact, logically separate – you can decide your strategy without necessarily having decided how to express it. This semantic separation between planning and generation can be particularly useful in the design of artificial agents specialized in negotiation. Hence, we explore a modular approach to negotiating dialogues that systematically decouples strategy and generation. In our approach, the negotiation strategy is determined in a separate component, which operates at a higher-level than the dialogue generation component. This allows us to separate the strategic decisions, which might or might not depend on the specific context of a given negotiation, from the mechanics of generating acceptable and contextually appropriate dialogue. This decoupling provides several benefits. First, it allows us to train or define the negotiation strategy independently of the dialogue generation process. Second, we can model the strategy with different methods, such as supervised learning (where strategic actions are predefined and labeled), reinforcement learning (if we want to allow agents to explore and refine strategies based on rewards in simulated or real negotiations), or even by domain-specific knowledge engineering, depending on the desired level of strategic "intelligence". Another key benefit of modularity is that it facilitates the analysis and the adaptation of strategies. By holding the dialogue generation separate, we can study the effectiveness of one’s negotiation strategy without the noise or bias introduced by the generation process itself. This is particularly important in the context of negotiation, where a poorly executed negotiation might erroneously lead to conclusions about the value of a strategy, even if that strategy was soundly chosen and only poorly expressed. While the previous work on negotiation generally takes an end-to-end approach where strategy and generation are trained together, such approaches can make it difficult to influence the strategy in meaningful ways.

Dialogue systems in HRI pose a particularly complex challenge due to the dynamic nature of human communication and the need for robots to interpret intentions and emotions (Williams, 2004). Usability evaluations therefore need to consider both objective and subjective metrics, which may capture different aspects of the interaction. Objective measures refer to quantitative data that can be directly obtained from the interaction itself, such as the amount of time it takes to perform a task, the number of errors or repetitions, and the types of user utterances. Subjective measures, on the other hand, involve collecting the users' opinions and feelings about the interaction (e.g., satisfaction ratings, Likert scales, or open-ended feedback). Both types of measures can provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of a system; however, in practice, subjective measures are more typically used to evaluate the usability of a system (Boa et al., 2017) likely due to their ease of collection and the direct relevance of the user's perspective. The influence of each type of measure on understanding and improving usability design can be different, and the relationship between them is not always straightforward. In this paper, we present the results of a study aimed at understanding the subjective and objective aspects of ease of use in a human-robot dialogue system for collaborative construction tasks. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of a robot that assists users in the construction of wooden toys using voice commands. The system allows the user to instruct the robot on how to build a toy, including providing complex instructions. Our goal is to explore whether objective metrics, collected from the interaction process, can effectively capture user satisfaction and usability as reported by humans (subjective measures).

Lexical composition refers to the way individual words are combined to form meaningful expressions such as phrases, sentences, or even poetic configurations (Linguistic and computational perspectives on creativity in text, 2020). The nuances of these combinations are deep and often tied to various aspects of human perception, language use, and cultural backgrounds. A computational approach that aims to quantify this subjective perception would need to handle issues of both lexical semantics and the subjective judgement of creativity. These measures can potentially give insights into the originality, interest, and "surprise value" perceived in word combinations (Hill et al., 2015). However, relying solely on these measures has limitations because creativity, as perceived by humans, can significantly depend on contextual and stylistic aspects that may not be fully captured by these methods (Yuan et al., 2015). Therefore, we also perform experiments using supervised learning techniques to gain further insights into how different aspects of lexical composition, such as word novelty, semantic distance, and stylistic features, collectively contribute to the perceived creativity. The core of our investigation involves a dual-sided approach. Dependency parsing is traditionally seen as a problem of finding a consistent labeling of a tree-like or graph-like structure over a sentence. The majority of approaches to this problem are based on the assumption that the deep structure of dependency trees can be modeled well by high-order features. For instance, one indispensable feature class is that of arc labels, which involve a kind of recursion on questions such as "What is the head of a given subphrase?" and "What are the children of a given parent node?", and which leads to constructing tree structures of arbitrary depth. This depth, in turn, combined with the facts that dependency parsing is a discrete and nondeterministic problem, makes the search space of possible derivations very large, often to the extent of being intractable to solve exactly with dynamic programming (DP) or even approximate with numerical optimization methods. One typical and successful approach is to use dynamic programming (DP) methods based on a dependency grammar, either through the Inside-Outside transition system (Klein and Manning, 2003; Nivre, 2006) or the graph-based version known as the Graph-Based Transition System (McDonald and Nivre, 2007). As proposed by Kaplan and Klein (2010), or as implemented in the C&C tools of this work, such methods can handle feature functions of arbitrary order. The attraction of this high-order shallowly-parsing approach is that, while the system must still explore all possible candidate structures, the dependency grammar can be used to model the plausible syntactic patterns of a language by exploiting higher-order features. However, while the inference for dependency parsers with high-order features has been shown to be akin to a convex optimization problem, its exact solution is often computationally too expensive. Hence much effort has been devoted to developing "proper" approximation algorithms for such systems (e.g., Nayak and Katz, 2015; Han et al., 2014, 2015; Xia et al., 2015; Koo et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2014), while another approach is explicitly to use randomized search algorithms (e.g., McDonald and Nivre, 2010). The latter approach draws inspiration from the observation that most DP problems for dependency parsing are over-constrained, such that the globally optimal solution for a given set of input features is often represented by a vanishingly small fraction of the search space. For over-constrained DP problems, algorithms such as greedy decoding and even sampling could perhaps converge to good solutions almost as fast as or faster than the complex optimization methods.

Paraphrase acquisition is the study of automatically identifying paraphrases of a given sentence or idea. To increase the size and coverage of an existing set of paraphrase seeds, various researchers have proposed pattern-based methods that generalize the original seed paraphrases into larger sets of candidate paraphrases (e.g., Wang and Manning, 2013; Wang and Lease, 2013; Liu et al., 2013). These pattern generalization methods vary in the degree of structural generality they can capture, as well as in their exploitation of observed paraphrase examples. The most general methods use an entailment-based approach, where a paraphrase pattern is considered an entailment of the seed. For example, S1: "The tractor broke down just before harvest" can entail S2: "Just before harvest, the tractor failed" because S2 makes the semantic point of S1 in a different way. The limitations of these entailment-based methods are twofold. First, they require a collection of human-annotated entailment pairs between sentences, which is challenging to scale up and maintain. Second, even when available, such pairings are limited in structure and often capture only very general or superficial relationships. Other methods or variants thereof cluster paraphrase examples based on a given similarity metric on word or n-gram units (e.g., cosine similarity of the set of most informative words or bigrams). These methods typically generate paraphrases in sets that are at least partially syntactically similar, but their generalizability is limited by the choice of similarity metric or n-gram units. Our previous work (Kurata, 2015a) exploited the observation that for each paraphrase seed, we can also consider lexical variants as candidate paraphrases that can also be perceived as likely paraphrases in context. A lexical variant can be thought of as a form or synonym of a word (e.g., "amendment" and "amending" or "document" and "record"). This observation extends a basic intuition, which suggests that paraphrase seeds can be generalized by considering alternative wordings. For example, "amendment" and "amending" are likely to co-occur in similar sentences and thus qualify as paraphrases in some contexts (e.g., "a plan to amending the document was presented" and "presented a document requiring amendment"). Unfortunately, just because two word strings co-occur as synonyms doesn't mean they are paraphrases. The association between two words like "modify" and "amend" can be more about almost-synonyms or related concepts rather than real paraphrase examples. Our previous work, while innovative, came with certain limitations.

Training natural language parsers has historically required large amounts of annotated training data to achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, many languages have few or no available annotated resources and for languages with resources, deep syntactic annotation may not be available. To address this, we need to move away from dependency-based parsing approaches that are highly sensitive to this annotation and towards models that leverage questions or features that can be estimated from the given data. Besides improving numerical efficiency, this permits access to more data and thus potentially makes the inference more robust and of better quality as the amount of independent word pairs observed increases. Among these data-driven approaches, language model-based architectures are well-suited candidates. They can be trained to predict, for example, a tag for each word without assuming a particular hierarchical structure, thus avoiding the need for features that directly encode syntactical relations (as is common in standard parser architectures) - instead relying on weighted sums of word bigrams or -grams making the model well-suited to handle the multitude of possible dependencies in a relatively free word-ordered language such as Hebrew (Babič et al.,2009, Tsarfaty et al., 2015). Unfortunately, the proposed model will suffer greatly if the language features (such as words, tags) are treated as isolated events without context. One remedy is to connect the units through syntax - using different levels of the parse tree. A traditional dependency parsing approach would typically build a parse tree based on the annotated training data, and then use features that rely on the resulting syntactic structure. For example, an "IN" tag (e.g., a preposition tag) would take its own identity as well as the head of its dependent and in some cases, its modifier (argument) into account when used in a features set. However, such approaches are model-specific and likely doesn't learn a robust, generalizable representation from "minimal" input which would allow adaptation to different languages, tagsets and corpora without extensive retraining or handcrafting of features. More specifically, in the case of dependence syntax, if we treat a base syntactic unit as a position with identity (denoted as head) and type (denoted as label type), we can insure that features for each dependnt or governed word position reflect the dependency structure. This is known as a Relational Realizational (RR) model (Tsarfaty and Sima'an, 2008). The RR model structure is truly general as it assumes no particular syntactic theory or structure over which the dependencies are to be projected.

The STREUSLE task specifically highlights the fact that while the 'average' error can be corrected effectively by MT at over 90% accuracy, there are specific subsets of errors that still elude correction technology. These subsets are often associated with context-dependent or 'nuanced' errors, mistakes that require an understanding of text in context or nuanced understanding of grammatical structure (Firat et al., 2014). Examples include errors in tense agreement, subject-verb agreement in complex sentences where the subject is not the grammatical subject, subject-verb agreement influenced by aspect, and understanding of discourse structure (such as pronoun referencing in the scope of less than or more than clause). These are areas where MT methods, which often rely on base-pair translation patterns, may struggle unless the parallel corpora explicitly contain or can be engineered to include these less common or more nuanced error-correction patterns. From a practical standpoint, MT-based approaches require large amounts of parallel data, which may not be readily available for all languages or for specific contexts in which GEC operates. On the other hand, classifier-based approaches can be robust with smaller datasets, relying instead on patterns derived from the structure of the language itself through machine learning algorithms and potentially with the use of heuristic rules and resources like treebanks or linguistic databases (Gimpel and Smith, 2010; Dozat and Manning, 2017).

Web search engines typically optimize search for the global best result, which returns similar results to all users. Personalization, on the other hand, aims to customize the search result list based on a user's specific query and background information. Personalized search should consider user-specific cues and preferences to serve relevant results, which often leads to improved user experience and engagement. Traditional personalization strategies, however, rely solely on the user's past activities such as search queries or click data (Salton & Buckley, 1988; Buckley & Salton, 1990; Teevan et al., 2005; Riordan & Bruzzone, 2012). The effectiveness of these methods is limited when the user has little or no prior activity with the search system, or when the user's interests evolve over time. Furthermore, current personalization models often ignore the broader web of user interests as well as their social connections, both of which are rich sources of information suggesting what the user is interested in and what is of value to them. Social data offers a different perspective that can complement traditional personalization approaches. Specifically, it leverages the collective wisdom and user-generated content that reflects diverse user interests and preferences. The recent surge in social media platforms has created extensive datasets containing social annotations from users. This data includes people's personal preferences, expressed as likes, shares, favorites, and bookmarks on a wide range of web content. Different from usage data, social data is often independent of user search behaviors within a specific web search system but can represent a broader view of the user's interests acquired from their diverse online activities. A challenge in using social data for personalization is that each user's social footprint may not capture all of their interests relevant for search.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models with a prohibitive number of parameters requires an efficient search algorithm to ensure successful decoding. As of now, beam search (BS) remains the most widely adopted approach due to its efficiency and reliability. However, a well-documented curse is that larger beam sizes (which are necessary to capture more potential translations) often do not result in higher translation quality and may instead degrade it (Ehret and Ngai, 2016; Sennrich et al., 2016b). This apparent paradox occurs despite the observed fact that larger hypotheses generally yield better translations (Koehn, 2004; Nye et al., 2011). Some explanations have been proposed for this phenomenon. Birch and van den Oord (2017) argue that, due to the inherent uncertainty among the chosen hypotheses at each step, a larger beam size does not necessarily lead to better final outputs. They suggest using length-normalized re-scoring of hypotheses which results in better performance when used alongside standard length-normalized decoding. However, the appropriate length normalization factor for a given beam size remains an open question and it has been empirically found that it should be tuned on a per-task basis or even on a per-model basis (Jiang et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2016). In addition to this issue of appropriate re-scoring of hypotheses, another problem lies in the uncertainty of when to stop the search process to obtain plausible translations. This problem is exacerbated by the high computational cost of running beam search longer, potentially for no additional gain in translation quality. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the interaction between beam search and neural machine translation models. Specifically, we focus on two aspects: 1.   Re-scoring Methods  : How can we better evaluate candidates in the beam search process to avoid the curse of larger beam sizes and obtain better translations? We study the effectiveness of different re-scoring methods, including length normalization and more sophisticated approaches, such as using additional language models or fine-tuning the scoring function. 2.   Stopping Criteria  : When to stop beam search optimally? We analyze various heuristics and methods and investigate how they perform under different beam sizes and re-scoring schemes. We aim to identify which methods can yield the best balance between translation quality and computational cost. Our work is motivated by the goal of developing more broadly applicable, hyperparameter-free methods for training robust NMT models, specifically for translation tasks with limited available resources such as Chinese-English.

These include the form and content of the messages (brief, terse in early platforms), the source (anyone is an author, not limited to professional journalists), the language of authorship (user-generated content making each source potentially distinct from traditional sources), and the time frame of collection (real-time, not retrospective). Social media platforms are also sometimes called “trending topics”) in a given time window. Clustering these various news items (both traditional news articles and social media messages) into coherent groups or “stories,” intuitively defined as sets of articles which report on the same event or topic, is a core task for media monitoring (Chien, 2015;Yasuhara, 2010). For a substantial volume of news content to be plausible, the technique employed must be able to manage high volumes of data (e.g., scale to millions of individual articles), must be computationally efficient to handle real-time streaming data in practice, and must be able to operate across multiple languages. Attempts have been made in traditional NLP to tackle the first two requirements (e.g., candidates 2010;Yasuhara and Yamada, 2010), but these approaches often fall short when applied to multi-language streams or streams of user-generated content in social media. Specifically, the blurred boundaries between news articles and casual social media banter, the informal language use in user-generated content, and the wide variety of topics reported in different languages (e.g., cultural concepts, humor, sports, and politics) require sophisticated and robust clustering methods. To accommodate these challenges, a series of aggregations methods for streaming news content have been proposed previously (Bizer et al. 2011;Bittner, 2015;Bollmann 2015; Blei 2012; Chien 2015; Drew 2013; Grimmer 2013; Lin 2016; Nadeau 2015; Qu and Cui 2016; Sakaki 2010). Training embeddings using all the data available can optimize them for any of the available domains or tasks. To compensate for this, task-specific embeddings and domain-specific embeddings have been proposed separately to improve the performance (Surdeanu and Tibshirani, 2014;HuggingFace, 2018;Zhong et al., 2018). However, constructing domain-specific embeddings and task-specific embeddings requires labeled data (e.g., labeled sentiment sentences and labeled language of origin, as in domain adaptation tasks) and thereby assumes that data for all domains and tasks are available (Chen et al., 2013;Fang et al., 2014). Lack of labeled data for all domains and tasks, often makes it challenging to construct task-specific embeddings. On the other hand, to capture both domain-specific semantic features and task-specific features in a single embedding, task-specific or domain-specific fine-tuning methods have been proposed (Wen et al., 2015;Jain and Wallace, 2014;Iyyer et al., 2015;Zhong et al., 2018). Domain adaptation techniques have also been used or proposed for capturing domain-specific semantic features using unlabeled domain data (Zhong et al., 2017;Lebret and Collobert, 2015;Rae et al., 2016). However, these techniques either ignore or do not effectively use the shared information (e.g., common language families) between the source and target domains. A more promising direction, especially for word embeddings, can be learned using all the available data without any domain or task information, and later optimized for domain-specific and task-specific learning. First, the unsupervised learnable embeddings should capture the domain and the task that they were learned on; and second, they should contain global features allowing them to be adapted to any new domain or task. More specifically, in this paper, we present an unsupervised learning method for cross-domain word representations. We specifically focus on learning representations that can be adapted to different domains while keeping track of domain-specific and domain-shared features. We first present a simple yet effective method for learning such embeddings. Then, we introduce a novel heuristic for pruning the embedding space for domain adaptation. The new heuristic reduces the computation cost of our method without compromising its performance. To the best of our knowledge, our paper is one of the first to propose learning cross-domain word embeddings using unsupervised methods aiming to capture both common and domain-specific semantics. We evaluate our method on four domain adaptation datasets, including sentiment analysis datasets with different language and domain labels (e.g. fine-grained English sentiment and English movie reviews).

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Knowledge-Based Semantic Embedding for Machine Translation: Machine Translation (MT) aims at automatically translating text from one language (source language) to another language (target language). Over years of development, MT has gone through different paradigm shifts from rule-based approaches (Klein et al., 1993), statistical methods (Koehn, 2005), and recently deep learning-based systems (Sutskever et al., 2014;Vinyals et al., 2015). However, despite these improvements, MT keeps facing challenges due to the complexity of human languages. One of the most essential challenges is to understand the semantics of source sentences and generate the corresponding sentences with correct meanings in the target language. To this end, knowledge-based approaches have been widely applied to MT to incorporate world semantic knowledge (Knight and Graesser, 1997;Tatu et al., 2002;Ko and Ney, 2003). Knowledge-based MT (kbMT) systems rely on external knowledge (e.g., dictionaries, ontologies, taxonomies) to guide the translation process. Past research mainly relies on linguistic knowledge, which has shown limited effectiveness. For a long time, the core idea of kbMT systems remains unchanged: transfer knowledge into different levels of the translation system. A traditional knowledge-based approach would typically include a component designed to acquire the knowledge and another component designed to interpret and apply it to the translation process. This knowledge is used to enrich or adjust the translation output (e.g., to resolve ambiguities, to select the right translations, to rephrase sentences). However, there remains a gap for more direct and effective integration of the knowledge and the language modeling. To tackle these challenges, deep learning approaches, especially neural networks, have been successfully applied to MT (Sutskever et al., 2014;Vinyals et al., 2015;Wu et al., 2016). At the heart of these approaches is a learned model that can generate the target sentences from source sentences. However, directly applying these models often falls short because they implicitly model semantics and fail to explicitly leverage structured knowledge provided by human-expertly curated resources. This is where our proposed Knowledge-Based Semantic Embedding comes into play. Specifically, we aim to incorporate structured knowledge from external sources (e.g., knowledge bases) into the process of machine translation. Unlike traditional kbMT where knowledge is used to adjust the output, we integrate it into the very spaces where language semantics are learned and modeled. This approach allows the translation system to learn semantic representations that are explicitly grounded in knowledge, thereby inherently enabling a more robust and accurate understanding of language semantics.

However, current NMT models are still imperfect. One limitation of NMT is that they do not take phrases into account, although research on questions such as "What is the translation of a phrase in a sentence?" indicates that this is a very real issue in NLP. Phrase translation is a common practice in human translation and there are many phrase-based Statistical Machine Translation systems (SMT) that keeps a large number of verbs or idioms in their phrase knowledge base. At first glance, it seems lazy or unfair to not integrate such existing knowledge into NMT. The problem arises because NMT reads and writes word by word. While SMT can directly incorporate the phrase knowledge, NMT uses word embeddings to represent the "phrases as bags-of-words" and does not inherently account for phrase-based semantic meaning. There are a number of NMT models which attempt to address this, most notably the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) and the structure-aware NMT or ATL (Zhang et al., 2018) which have shown some improvements over standard word-level NMT models by keeping the encoder and/or decoder aware of sentence structure through position embeddings and other techniques. However, these solutions are still limited and do not effectively model the long-range dependencies or specialized language used in phrases or idioms. In this work, we propose an extension to NMT that allows it to explicitly model phrases. Central to our approach is a novel phrase memory that is integrated into the encoder-decoder framework. This phrase memory complements the standard model by adding phrase-based knowledge from a phrase-based SMT system (Moses; Koehn et al., 2007). The phrase memory acts as a kind of "phrase dictionary" that is dynamic and contextually aware: it is a list of target language phrases matched with their source language counterparts that our SMT system would typically use to generate translations. A key innovation of our approach is that the phrase memory is not simply a fixed look-up table. Instead, it is re-written on-the-fly by the phrase-based SMT model, which injects relevant target phrases into the memory. For example, if we're translating a sentence containing a verb phrase such as 'bring to a boil', the SMT would re-write the phrase memory with target phrases like 'bring the water to a boil', 'heat until boiling', 'boil the liquid', etc.

The requirement for supervision limits the number of languages for which parsers are available, and makes it difficult to use these resources for the many unrealized NLP tasks. In this work, we describe a method for improving fully unsupervised parsing by adapting the size of the training data. Our method, Zoomed Learning, stays within the constraints of the fully unsupervised paradigm but allows us to choose the best subset of the language of interest to be used for training. The best subset is chosen by evaluating parser performance on extracted test subsets and backwards selecting the most informative training set. This simple idea improves parsing accuracy on three different English domains by up to 4.47% F-score, compared to training with the full available language. Sentence structure (as commonly derived by statistical parsers) is one of the most useful pieces of information in language recognition, information extraction, question answering and machine translation. Fully unsupervised parsers aim to learn the structure of natural language without any annotated data. This is a challenging task because in the absence of supervision, the parser needs to discover the rules of language by discerning patterns in the structure of sentences. Despite the challenges or even because of them, fully unsupervised parser research has seen great improvements over the past few years, driven by different training algorithms and heuristic techniques. A few of these methods now rival the performance of their fully supervised counterparts in limited settings, at least according to several measures (Lin and Pantel, 2001;Seki et al., 2002;Curran and Clark, 2007;Atsushi and Nagata, 2006;Seginer, 2007;Darwiche and Marquis, 2004;Collins, 2000;Collins, 2004;Miyao and Tsujii, 2004;Goldberg and Nivre, 2008a;Goldberg and Nivre, 2008b). However, even when performance is comparable to or even surpasses fully supervised methods for certain metrics in limited domains, fully unsupervised methods suffer from a lack of flexibility. The parsers themselves are often domain or language-specific, and because of the inability to boot-strap against existing annotated data, scalability and transfer of models across different domains is limited. Moreover, because the only data available is raw text, the induction of linguistic structure often requires a great number of distinct sentences.
