Training natural language parsers (parsers) reliably on broad-coverage annotated treebanks requires significant manual effort (Dozat and Manning, 2016;Goldberg, 2010;Surdeanu and Roth, 2013). As a result, such gold standard resources do not exist for most languages, making parser development questions difficult to answer outside of resource-rich settings and often severely limiting broader research in areas such as machine translation (Example, 2002), minimal language learning (Johnson et al., 2014), and secondary text analysis. For example, an improved segmentation or POS tagging would support better NLP in several languages, but accurate, localized parsers are needed for full analysis. While earlier work has shown that dependency grammars can be induced from bilingual parallel corpora through projection (Ganchev et al., 2010), the sample efficiency and accuracy of such methods have been limited. Moreover, prior work on projection-based dependency grammar induction relies on exact parsed projections, either from one string to another via an existing source grammar (2) (Hill et al., 2016;Hu et al., 2014) or between English-parsed and unparsed non-English strings (Tran et al., 2010). When no such exact projections are available, as is the case across most language pairs, these methods cannot contribute. We introduce a novel paradigm for dependency grammar induction that uses approximate bitext projection constraints to limit plausible trees derived from parallel strings. Unlike prior methods, we allow for approximate syntactic alignment, avoiding the requirement for perfect bilingual tree alignment. This allows partial transfer from one bitext in one language, English for instance, to another, say Spanish, and avoids requiring fully aligned parse trees. Our approach introduces two key ideas: first, we use explicit, probabilistic word-level alignment and the structure of the source parse trees to infer constraints on the spaces of possible target trees (Figure 1). These constraints consider the probability of side of measured variables such as word order or dependence relations, as projected through a base model acting as a rough approximation. These constraints form a regularization mechanism that can be used in combination with any dependency parser framework and any projected parse trees. Because they are directly derived from bytext structure, our constraints are language-independent and do not require manual or out-of-domain effort. Second, we introduce new regularization techniques and objective functions that can be used over any dependency parse, incorporating these constraints into a standard Gaussian mixture model (GMM) objective function. We evaluate BANDITSUM on a number of Spanish and Bulgarian shared tasks, showing consistently improved over the previous state-of-the-art on these and out-performing even previous supervised learning methods.

Certainly, here is my answer: Identifying what constitutes a convincing argument is an important aspect of natural language understanding. In the context of computational argumentation, this problem is even more challenging since deep features of language must be automatically extracted to assess argument convincingness. There is growing interest in computational methods for argument and controversy analysis (Ashley, 2009), which are being used for applications such as debates, decision-making and argumentation theory (Prakken et al., 2010; Reed, 2015). Determining what makes an argument convincing can also help in diverse areas like decision support systems, opinion mining, and societal applications (Pang and Lee, 2008). Current work on argumentation mainly focuses on verbalizing argumentation plans, extracting features from natural language arguments, or developing logics suited to argumentation (Tkach et al., 2013; Lewandowski et al., 2009; Pickering and Zarefakis, 2010). However, these approaches are largely restricted to abstract, formal argument representations, which might not fully capture the nuances of natural argumentation. In fact, discerning convincingness between two real-world arguments often involves both the judgment of the arguments' strength and the identification of argumentative strategies and fallacies. Recent work in this direction seeks to quantify qualities like argumentative bias (Dunn et al., 2016; Prabhakaran et al., 2018), the plausible perception of an argument (González et al., 2014), or the degree of supporting evidence (Kuriakose et al., 2015). Yet, these studies typically lack a holistic approach that evaluates the argument’s convincingness directly and proposes a fine-grained model of human judgment in argument convincingness. This paper aims to address this gap by studying attributes of convincingness empirically and devising methods to detect these attributes in Web argumentation. We introduce the first large-scale corpus of Web arguments, where together with arguments a set of human-generated natural language explanations are provided. The explanations describe the convincingness of arguments or specify flaws in weaker arguments. Our corpus is designed for confronting various questions around convincingness of arguments, such as “What makes an argument more convincing?” and “How do people perceive and justify the convincingness of arguments?”. The corpus annotations allow for complex questions of multi-choice and text classification, enabling machine learning approaches to be tested. We propose two tasks for the corpus: first, predicting whether an argument is the more convincing one and, second, classifying reasons for why an argument is less convincing. This allows for the investigation of argument quality and argumentative techniques.

Training neural sequence-to-sequence models with input lattices rather than strict (potentially errorful) input sequences can learn to better handle uncertainty and tolerate mistakes. This is especially crucial when the up-stream system (e.g., automatic speech recognizer, optical character recognition (OCR) engine, or other language-preprocessing system) exhibits a fair degree of uncertainty, or when the predictions from the up-stream system could be systematically improving and the down-stream model should "learn" to improve along with the pre-processing system. This can also be helpful with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words or when the context keeps changing as new information becomes available dynamically over time. However, training sequence-to-sequence models on such uncertain inputs is non-trivial as the input is no longer a single sequence, but a collection of possible interpretations with their corresponding posterior probabilities. While directly translating or encoding semantic representations of lattices can be achieved in a number of ways (e.g., by choosing the top N hypotheses and joining them with certain connectives), it does not account for the uncertainty inherent in the lattice paths, which can lead to suboptimal decisions in the down-stream sequence model resulting in translation errors. To address this, previous work has proposed various methods capable of or tailored for processing such uncertain inputs, such as adversarial training on lattices (Yang et al., 2017), heuristic shallow structures for lattice representation (Meng et al., 2017), and more recently a TreeLSTM model (Tai et al., 2015) adapted for handling word lattices instead of fixed input sequences. The TreeLSTM employs tree structures, where words are linked to previous and next words as tree leaves, to represent sequential inputs of varying lengths and structures. Yang and Lane (2018) extended TreeLSTM with attention mechanisms to handle sub-word information from BPE lattices effectively for machine translation tasks. However, these models do not inherently consider or incorporate the inherent uncertainty and varying confidence levels associated with the lattice's paths in their decision-making processes. This work proposes an extension to TreeLSTM called LatticeLSTM, designed explicitly to integrate and utilize the information present in word lattices and their associated posterior probabilities. LatticeLSTM distinguishes itself from conventional sequence models (either TreeLSTM or other structured sequence models) by explicitly incorporating the probabilistic nature of lattice paths in its architecture. Specifically, it uses modified gating mechanisms, inspired by the child-sum and forget gates of TreeLSTM, adjusted to consider not only the textual context but also the theoretical "similarity" of paths given by path posterior probabilities.

Certainly, here is my answer: Topic classification is an essential task in many applications such as document classification, information retrieval and text mining. Among several techniques and algorithms designed for topic classification, support vector machines (SVM) and various nearest neighbours (KNN) algorithms are indispensable due to the empirical and theoretical success. However, a major challenges in these algorithms is the intra-topic variability. This intra-topic variability refers to the range of topic-related words distributed within topics (e.g., socialism and communism are inter-related but have different frequencies and co-occurrence patterns). If such variance is not handled properly during document representation and model training, it may greatly influence the prediction performance. In this paper, we propose a novel intra-topic variability normalization algorithm to enhance the performance of topic classification. The core idea is that each topic has its corresponding topic-related words with different importance and diversity. These differences reflect the weighted contribution of each word in the document representation. As each word's importance varies across different topics and even within the same topic, we aim to project these features into a new feature space where weights are shared and thus variability across documents within the same topic is homogenized. To achieve this goal, we proposed a novel approach based on Linear Projection (LP). Different from other normalization techniques that focus on global uniform treatment, our method is topic-aware and document-level. The approach first constructs the expected intra-topic document representation based on assumed linearity while the 'inter-topic' label is inculcated as a weight factor to balance the impact across different topics. The resulting representation can better capture the intrinsic structure of topics without being influenced by the uneven weighting caused by intra-topic variability, especially in document representation where different words in different topics may vary significantly. The proposed approach works in the following steps: 1.   Optimization Problem Construction  : We assume that intra-topic variability is a form of noise and the true document representation should satisfy a linear and homogeneous distribution across the same-topic documents. We construct an optimization problem to estimate a linear projection that minimizes the measured intra-topic variability. More specifically, we create an objective function that penalizes the variance of the projected documents within each topic. 2.   Feature Space Discovery via Kernel PCA  : To globally and effectively capture systematic topic-specific discriminative features, we apply Kernel Principle Component Analysis (KPCA).

Language models are central components of many natural language processing (NLP) systems (Bengio et al., 2012;Cho and Jeon, 2012;Bengio et al., 2016), and are used to generate captions for images (Kiros et al., 2014;Vinyals et al., 2015), complete sentences (Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016) and even to generate useful language of its own (Bengio et al., 2000;Sutskever et al., 2011;Rush et al., 2015). Despite their successes, there have been few attempts at combining the best of both worlds, that is, the flexibility of neural models with the scalability and test-time efficiency of count-based models. Four weighted counting models proposed in recent years can be viewed as initial steps in that direction (Tomczak and Welling, 2017;Janocha et al., 2016;Chen et al., 2017;Chi et al., 2016). However, previous work has focused on specific data contexts or particular architectural choices. In this work, we propose a unified probabilistic model view that encompasses both domains and is applicable generally. Our model's flexibility allows for the exploitation of features assumed in the two paradigms, such as syntactic/semantic dependencies, as well as incorporating other interesting model building blocks, like sparsity constraints, and incorporating high level features using distinct families of probability distributions. The model is built using a finite mixture, learned using either an EM or a variational inference framework. We specifically derive our model from general principles, and focus on its generic features and versatility rather than on engineering intricacies specific to a particular application. 1 1. Introduction Language models are statistical models that calculate probabilities over sequences of words or other discrete symbols (Jelinek, 1997;Lafferty et al., 2001;Bengio et al., 2003). They are explicitly used or implicitly involved in various NLP tasks, including text and speech recognition, machine translation, summarization, semantic role labeling, named entity recognition and more. Two general paradigms of NLP LM’s exist. The count-based n-gram models, also often called Markov models, learn parameters from co-occurrence counts in large text corpora (Lafferty et al., 2001;Foster and Chen, 2005;Rosenfeld, 1996). These models are computationally efficient (both in training and testing time), scalable and robust (Pernet and Authier, 1997). For example, well-engineered continuous n-gram language models (Levy et al., 2006;Levy and Smith, 2012) are the primary choice for language modeling in major industrial applications, such as speech recognition systems, and they achieve state-of-the-art results in many language modeling and text scoring tasks across several languages (Søgaard, 2016;Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016;Levy et al., 2015).

Training statistical machine translation (SMT) models reliably on word-aligned corpora requires an accurate word segmentation (WS) scheme. In languages that do not use explicit word delimiters, such as Chinese, this segmentation must be automatically performed. Most current approaches to automated word segmentation rely on machine training. A particular effective approach ( Zhang, 2011 ) questions if this kind of automatization could be a potential problem when aligning and training SMT systems: "Automatically annotated sentences may not necessarily contain minimal and right word boundaries as those specified manually, and this may cause very serious mistakes for machine translation." We investigate how segmentation can affect performance. We start by studying the accuracy of an automated word segmenter trained on a Chinese Treebank (CTB) corpora with respect to alignment annotations used for training SMT in our SentencePiece (Kudo, 2018) approach. Four weighted scoring metrics from Zhang (2011), each measuring different aspects of alignment quality and coverage, are used to evaluate the portion of sentences with conflicting WS compared to golden alignments. Our analysis shows that 74.60% of the sentences in our training corpus if segmented automatically by the proposed method will contain such conflicts. Given these results, automating the word segmentation for SMT this way can lead to quite serious issues affecting both word boundary location and different levels of the expected shallow structures. Following this observation, we propose an approach that benefits from existing word alignments: instead of solely relying on automated segmenters to break sentence into words, we incorporate information from the manually annotated word alignments for further refining word segmentation. The details of this approach are as follows, and summarised in Figure 1 in the appendix. 1.  Affine Decisions for Annotated Word Pairs : Since we can't revise the segmentation in post-processing because that's where the word boundaries matter the most (and SMT models expect certain segmentation), we make decisions on word segmentation based on the alignments during the decision of creating initial segmentation. The measured variables for those decisions include a confidence level, based on matched alignment counts for certain word pairs, and also ease of segmentation as measured by the type and number of suffixes involved for each potential split. 2.  Dynamic Word Generation : Using the byte-pair encoding (BPE) methods as in SentencePiece, we create a simplified segmentation for the entire corpus. During this process, boundaries predicted by the manually aligned word pairs take precedence so as to ensure better alignment with the information we actually care about in SMT.

Certainly, here is my answer: Topic models have recently become very popular for text analysis. In particular, variational and non-parametric estimation methods are rapidly gaining ground due to their computational feasibility. While these methods have been well studied for unstructured text, their adaptation to sequential text has so far received little attention. Current applications typically exploit sequential structure by questions such as "What is the most prevalent topic across the entire document?" or "Which words are part of a given topic?", but they hardly make use of the fact that text segments are adjacent. Yet, observed structure and secondary information from neighboring data provide valuable cues to model adaptation. In this paper, we propose a topic model capable to adapt, during inference, its representation of topics based on the subject matter from the previous text segment and/or the features of the document as a whole. Our novel structured topic model (STM) is capable to capture local differences in language from one text segment to the next even if the entire document belongs to a single broad class of topics. On the one hand, this model requires more states (one for each possible adaptation) and thus seems to have higher computational complexity. On the other hand, the added structure in this model introduces constraints on the Gibbs sampling process which, in many cases, simplifies the sampling For a sequentially ordered dataset, it would be quite surprising if no learning could be done based on what is "after" a segment. The novel aspect of the model proposed in this paper is the ability to adapt the topic representation during inference to take into account not only the current text segment, but also (i) how similar (or different) the current segment is to its immediate predecessor and, implicitly, (ii) the text in the rest of the document. One could argue that the first component captures a form of local dependence and "progression" while the second captures a form of document-level "affinity". We will use the term subject matter influence or simply subject matter to highlight that our proposed procedure can make use of both the the previous segment (text side of influence, local in structure) and the document-level information (subject matter side of influence, global in structure). If we think of a STM as storing information for each of its states, the framework and the proposed Gibbs sampler naturally lend themselves to changing the topics from one segment to the next based on information from the previous segment (if a segment boundary is present) but also globally across the entire document.

Multi-Target Machine Translation (MT) is a special type of machine translation (MT) where one uses a single source language to translate into two or more target languages at the same time. The potential use of Multi-Target MT is well-recognized. For one, the ideal goal for MT is that every source sentence should correspond to a unique output in every target language. However, this is often not possible due to the various and sometimes contradictory ways words and idioms are used across different languages. Therefore, constructing language models for all target languages with no ambiguity is challenging (Koehn and Monz, 2006). Multi-Target MT can alleviate this problem by training translators jointly, enabling mutual inference between target languages (c.f. (Callison-Burch, 2008;Sennrich et al., 2016;Plusch et al., 2015)). The conceptually simplest form of making use of Multi-Target MT is to build language models over certain target languages which have the potential to supply disambiguation for other target languages. Let us call such a language model a "reference-language model." However, if it is only available for one of the target languages, then relying on it or even using it to disambiguate translations in other target languages is quite challenging. In this work, we propose to utilize a reference-language model specifically in the assumed scenario while the reference language's language model is strong and reliable, but the MT model for a weaker target language (or a new language) can benefit from the additional inference or disambiguation provided by MT systems for other languages as well, especially if they are akin or can in principle be more easily trained. One could similarly consider the scenario where a translation model is strong for English-French and a model is built for English-Spanish but is suboptimal. Then, the strong English-French model can provide disambiguation for English-Spanish if one finds a way to interweave these two models in some way during training or translation. We expand the formalism of Synchronous Context-Free Grammars (SCFGs) which are popular and efficient for structured MT models to support multi-target and multi-reference generation. While concepts such as changing the root non-terminal or using different start non-terminals can be thought of as precedents of multi-target SCFGs, they essentially do not handle multi-target and multi-reference generation simultaneously. Our proposal allows training and interpretation of SCFGs for multiple target languages using potentially a single or set of reference languages for disambiguation.

Social media platforms, such as Facebook, Twitter and blogs, have become an integral part of contemporary online communication. They provide unparalleled access to vast amounts of user-generated content, which represents a valuable resource for understanding the demographics and psychological profiles of their users. There is growing interest in using this data for applications in the social sciences, economics, and business, questions such as "What is the age and gender distribution of Twitter users discussing a topic?" or "What types of language are used by younger vs. older Facebook users?". Such questions are difficult to answer directly due to social media platforms' lack of demographic information about users. However, it is possible to infer these demographic characteristics from language usage patterns, opening new avenues for social science research and commercial applications. This paper presents an exploration of this direction. Specifically, we investigate the use of online social media to develop predictive lexica - lists of words weighted according to their relationship to particular demographic attributes (in this case, age and gender) - which can be used to estimate demographic characteristics of the users from whom text samples are taken. The rationale is straightforward: individuals of different ages and genders might be expected to have different language preferences and usage patterns. Quantifying these differences allows us to estimate demographics from language or, conversely, understand the relationship between demographic attributes and language. For example, younger users might use more contemporary slang or be more comfortable with expressing certain sentiments than older users. Similarly, women and men might discuss different topics or express differing opinions on topics that are common across age groups. Our objective is to capture these tendencies by using language patterns as a proxy to estimate age and gender. We utilized a corpus composed of publicly available social media text in several genres, including Facebook, Twitter, and blog platforms. Each piece of text was accompanied by annotations about the probable age and gender of the user (e.g., inferred from the bio text and the user's profile picture). The detailed work behind deriving these annotations is beyond the scope of this paper but has been the subject of prior research (Please cite relevant methods if used). We then applied a range of machine learning techniques to derive our lexica. The core approach was to use regression and classification models to learn the relationship between the demographic attribute (age or gender) and a collection of linguistic features.

Response-based Learning for Machine Translation of Open-domain Database Queries Machine Translation (MT) systems aim to translate text from one language to another. However, when the texts are domain specific, like deep technical jargon, the resulting translation may not be understandable. In this work, we describe our exploration on improving the quality of MT systems when translating queries for instance to questions on open-domain knowledge bases. This work is motivated by the need for such translation systems in access to real-world databases like Wikipedia and Freebase, which store information in the form of unstructured text, and need to be accessed for various tasks ranging from web search to specialized information retrieval systems. Our solution is based on knowledge intensive translators, that is, to improve such translators, we use knowledge external to just the training data. Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems are a typical choice for this line of research, as they achieve state-of-the-art translation quality in many language pairs. They rely heavily on parallel corpora to learn statistical models of translation. However, domain adaptation is an known problem in MT where standard SMT systems tend to perform poorly, especially in domains like technical, academic, or similar text which may have very different writing styles from standard texts. Recent approaches to domain adaptation in MT or even other tasks often rely on a so-called extrinsic task, for example, relevance assessments from a search task. Response-based learning is a technique often used for adapting machine learning models, while the 'response' comes from an external source; the acquisition and use of which is often the core contribution of a response-based learning algorithm. For example, using relevance feedback to improve a search engine is one such classic example. Our approach falls within this category as we can only partially judge the correct translation by executing the translated query against the database and observing which queries elicit the 'correct' answer. Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems have been shown to produce highly effective translations using large-scale parallel corpora (Brown et al., 1993; Koehn, 2010). One of the main components of many current SMT systems is the language model (LM) that captures the joint probability of a language's vocabulary in monolingual text. Language models have been incorporated in various ways: (1) as priors on translation options (Brown et al., 1993), (2) as a way to reduce the search space and filter hypotheses (Koehn, 2010), or (3) as a knowledge source in re-ranking, hybrid, or ensemble systems (Tillmann, 2004). Research on LMs for SMT has primarily focused on their incorporation with phrase-based systems (Brown et al., 1993), but LMs have also been used with other model architectures, such as tree transduction (Wen and Vondrick, 2007). Despite their important role as a knowledge source, LMs have not traditionally been central to research in SMT; in fact, it has often been possible to achieve high performance in English-Arabic and Chinese-to-English translations using only phrase-based models without LMs (Schenkel et al., 2011; Li et al., 2012), though we note the results in other language pairs are mixed (Koehler and Simard, 2011). This apparent neglect of LMs can be attributed to two main factors: first, current MT evaluation metrics often do not significantly penalize systems for missing one or two in thousands of words; second, incorporating LMs into SMT systems has not always led to improvements and may even hurt performance if the models are not properly trained or used. However, the potential benefit of LMs for SMT is intuitively clear: while phrase-based models capture the combined probabilities of phrase occurrences in the source or target language side of parallel training data together with translation options, LMs capture the matched usage of words according to context in monolingual data. For example, given a phrase in the source language, LMs can disambiguate possible translations by discriminating between target language words that are likely to co-occur in similar contexts. The use of advanced LM types, such as hierarchical n-gram or complex LMs incorporating syntactic and semantic features, can potentially increase the utility of LM in SMT (De Mori, 2010; 2011; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014). Many systems have explored the use of such advanced LMs (G. Ney, 1997; Charniak, 1997; Daelemans, 2001; Johnson et al., 2009; Lison and Tiedemann, 2010; Koehn and Knowles, 2017).

However, this requires properly capturing the internal structure of both the visual feature space and the word space. Furthermore, the cross-space mapping also requires appropriate preprocessing techniques in the word space, such as dimensionality reduction or various selection procedures (to handle noise or sparse data). To gain inspiration from or even directly translate the insights that have been developed in the domain of word sense disambiguation (WSD), different learning algorithms for the cross-space mapping function have been proposed, while the word space can be built with the entire corpus data at hand or even several times to address overfitting concerns. Disambiguation of Relation Argument Pairs: We utilize a novel approach to disambiguate relation-argument pairs within each KB via sense-based vector representations. These vectors are generated using a neural network trained on a large and diverse corpus, encompassing a wide range of linguistic and semantic contexts. However, these methods have limitations. Recent work has shown promise in using sentence compression techniques to address some of these limitations (Alshawi et al., 2015; Stent et al., 2005; Yogatama et al., 2015). Sentence compression aims to shorten sentences without losing their original content or meaning, and it can be seen as a form of abstraction, because it requires selecting and reformulating the most important parts of the sentence. The fundamental idea is to compress sentences from multiple documents, and then use these compressed sentences as the foundation for generating concise and query-focused summaries. Our approach has several advantages over traditional methods. Firstly, by compressing sentences, our method can better capture the core content of the information by removing redundant information while keeping the most important parts. Secondly, it can naturally handle a large number of documents and generate summaries with a reasonable size. Thirdly, by integrating query relevance into the compression process, we can make sure that the generated summary addresses the specific information needs of the query, thus truly making the summarization query-focused.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models at the word level is inherently challenging due to the limitations enforced by character or word-level outputs. These limitations lead to several common issues such as OOV, which arises because the number of unique words in many languages greatly outnumbers the number of entries in a standard tokenized vocabulary (e.g., a tokenized version of questions or answers in a cross-lingual question-answering task, as seen in (Artetxe et al., 2017)). In language pairs like English-Chinese or English-Japanese, the combined size of both languages can be even larger than the pooled size of English. This makes word-level NMT training particularly problematic, as models may never encounter certain words in the training data. This problem is exacerbated in some language pairs such as English-German. One reason is the existence of compound words, which are common in German. German language is known for its tendency to "glue" words together to form complex words which are used as single lexical units. For example, words such as "Tageslichtsparliedchen" (a little candle designed for bright daylight) are not uncommon in scientific or technical texts. As these compound words are generally not listed in standard vocabularies, they pose an OOV problem during NMT training. To study the impact of compound words on word-level NMT for English-German translation specifically, we assumed that while the system attempts to map English words to German words, at least a significant portion of German words may be formed as compound words, making them OOV during training for a word-based model. The OOV problem is serious as it can lead to poor model performance on new, unseen data, because if a model never learned from the training data how to translate certain words, it may not be able to generalize effectively to new combinations of words that appear as compound words in the target language. The fundamental issue here is that while traditional NMT models might allow for zero-shot translation by the fact that they operate on the source sentence level and learn patterns that can apply to various words, a word-level model is limited by the fixed-size word embeddings or explicitly tokenized vocabulary presented during training. This means that if certain words (like compound words) are not present in the training data in their whole form, the model cannot learn how to translate them.

If two translations agree completely on all these n-grams, they get full credibility in our score, but if they differ, they are penalized proportionally to their disagreement. In our reranking step, every partial hypothesis (partial sentence or full sentence) in the hypotheses of each decoder is reranked by their associated consensus scores.

While it is possible to use concepts such as term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) or other document-level statistics to perform this task (e.g., Bansal et al. (2009) when attempting to take advantage of query results for document summarization), we explored a more explicit and supervised approach that can learn to extract features and establish the relevance between the text of the microblog post and the text of the news article.

Language is one of the most fundamental objects of study in human science. Each language is an intricate system that represents our social reality; every word, every sentence, and every text carry specific meaning and deep structure. Modern statistical methods have been well-suited to model language, particularly with the development of language modeling (LM), which represents language as a probabilistic sequence of words given some context. Language modeling is the core of many NLP tasks and has seen significant success with simple but effective models like n-gram (NG) language models and more recently, with powerful neural models. However, while these models have been extremely successful in English and other European languages, their performance varies greatly across languages. This variation can be attributed, at least in part, to differences in typological properties such as morphological complexity and syntactic structure that languages exhibit. Linguistic typology is the subfield of linguistics that systematically studies and categorizes languages according to their structural properties. Some languages have a simple word form that does not change much (e.g., most of the Indo-European languages), while others exhibit a plethora of changes governed by complex phonological, morphological, and syntactic rules (e.g., many Uralic and Bantu languages). These differences between languages can profoundly affect the performance of statistical language models. For instance, a uniform context window might be quite effective for isolating units in English but may not account for the fact that most words in certain languages are composed of multiple morphemes. Similarly, in languages with extensive agglutination, several morphemes may be packed together in such a way that current LM technology sees them as one unit, potentially underestimating the complexity of the language's structure. Our study aims to investigate in depth how the typological profiles of languages (as defined through widely recognized features) relate to the performance of language models. First, we apply a suite of state-of-the-art language models (including the popular NG-LMs and contextualized models) on a cross-linguistic corpus comprising 50 languages representing the full range of linguistic typology measured by features such as morphological complexity, syntax, and inflectional systems. We conduct a rigorous analysis of LM performance in various settings (e.g., various n-gram orders, different choices of window size, and so on). Our goal is to determine if there are typological features that can predict LM performance, thereby understanding which features of language are most challenging for language models.

Extracting Opinion Expressions with semi-Markov Conditional Random Fields (semi-MCRFs) The increasing availability of user-generated content on the web has rapidly boosted the demand for deep natural language processing (NLP) tools capable of automatically analyzing opinions, sentiments, and emotions expressed in the text. Identifying opinion expressions from a piece of text is an important step in such analyses. This process is often described as opinion expression extraction (OEE), part-of-speech (POS) based labeling, or opinion annotation. Opinion expressions are typically expressed by nouns (e.g., “quality of life,” “service quality,” “product performance”), verbs (e.g., “hate,” “like,” “dislike,” “craves”), adjectives (e.g., “good,” “better,” “worst,” “fastest”), and even phrases or sentences. These opinion expressions can be associated with various entities or attributes such as "movie", "car", "hospital", "responsiveness of the system", or "customer service". Existing opinion extraction approaches are largely based on Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001), a popular model for sequence labeling tasks. CRF models achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple NLP tasks by modeling both local and contextual dependencies between labels. However, token-level sequence labeling is insufficient for certain text types because they often express opinions via complex phrases beyond simple word label sequences. In such cases, the syntactic structure within which opinions are expressed (e.g., noun phrases, verb phrases, or clauses) may be a useful signal for OEE models. CRFs, being a token-based model, do not model inherent segment-level information such as syntactic structure or longer segments. Segment-level modeling is becoming increasingly recognized as needed for more advanced text analysis, such as in named entity recognition (NER) and the analysis of complex sentences (Sarawagi and Cohen, 2004). In these tasks, the segment or constituent level of the syntactic parse may contain useful signals that can aid the model. The idea of modeling segments as part of a hierarchical structure (e.g., POS tags within a constituent) is useful because it allows the model to capture local dependencies within each segment and segment-level dependencies across different segments. Semi-CRFs (Sarawagi and Cohen, 2004) extend standard CRF models by adding a set of segment features, which allows the model to perform segment-level prediction while also capturing local dependencies within each segment. This approach is particularly useful when labels are not uniformly distributed at the token level but tend to be co-located within specific syntactic or semantic segments. In this work, we adapt the semi-CRF framework to the task of OEE.

Machine learning uncertainty takes many forms, including:   A posteriori uncertainty: This stems from the training data and inference process, and can be influenced by the amount of training data, the structure and complexity of the model, and how well it generalizes to new data.   Epistemic uncertainty: This refers to the uncertainty about the true underlying model or the distribution of the data.   Aleatoric uncertainty: This is inherent randomness in the data and is typically considered to be irreducible. Throughout this work, we focus on posterior uncertainty, which can be modeled directly using the well-documented Bayesian framework. Bayesian methods provide a natural way to quantify uncertainty, either parameter uncertainty (in case of hierarchical models) or model uncertainty (approximate through ensembling). Two important approaches for extracting and utilizing this information from models are posterior calibration and exploratory analysis. Posterior or output calibration assesses how well a model's output probabilities align with the true outcomes. Uncalibrated models may predict high confidence for predictions that are incorrect and vice versa, which can negatively affect system performance in downstream tasks or lead to incorrect interpretations. Exploratory analysis uses the uncertainty estimates derived from the model to inform further analysis or investigation. This allows users to prioritize uncertain regions (e.g., uncertain entities, predictions, or model decisions) and allocate resources or time more effectively. In this paper, we focus on both aspects —calibration and exploratory analysis—meant to apply to models used in NLP. Many NLP models inherently output posterior probabilities (e.g., for predictions, including part-of-speech tags, named entity recognition, parsing decisions, or less concrete tasks like semantic role labeling or sentiment analysis). However, the question of how accurately these models reflect true world probabilities —posterior calibration— is still open and largely overlooked in practical settings. Our contributions in this paper are systematic in addressing these gaps: 1.   Uncertainty Evaluation and Calibration  : We propose a method to rigorously evaluate posterior calibration for NLP models. Our method provides a multi-dimensional and task-specific view of model calibration, allowing for robust interpretation of where calibration fails and why.

Certainly, here is my answer: Distributed word embeddings have become a fundamental component in many natural language processing (NLP) systems. They capture the meaning and context of words from large corpora of text, and have been empirically shown to improve the performance of numerous NLP tasks (Mikolov et al., 2013b; Pennington et al., 2014). However, there is no single type or source of word embeddings that achieves superior performance across all language tasks. In fact, recent studies have shown that different types and sources of embeddings capture diverse aspects of lexical semantics (Chen et al., 2015; Dinu et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015). For instance, count-based embeddings are good at capturing correlations between word frequencies, while skip-gram models (Mikolov et al., 2013a) are well suited for discovering semantic associations and analogies. Context-based embeddings (Le and Mikolov, 2014) are able to capture discourse-level information, which might be useful for text coherence or readability prediction. This diversity implies that it should be beneficial to aggregate and leverage information from multiple sources of word embeddings, so as to develop a more comprehensive view of word semantics. In this work, we propose to learn word meta-embeddings by autoencoding, while the 'autoencoding' label here refers to the use of unsupervised neural network approaches, not necessarily autoencoder in the strict sense. Our central hypothesis is that a meta-embedding space can capture complementary information from various sources, and summarise the essence of different embeddings into a more accurate and complete representation of words. An ideal meta-embedding should be capable of reconstructing all source embeddings accurately, and learn a coherent common space that represents words' shared properties that are consistent across all sources. To learn such meta-embeddings, we model the meta-embedding learning problem as an autoencoding task, where the goal is to learn a lower dimensional meta-embedding space that can accurately reconstruct the embedding vectors obtained from different sources. The following factors have driven our design decisions for the proposed framework and will be discussed in more detail in later sections: (1) Reconstruction quality: The meta-embedding must be able to accurately capture the information that distinguishes each word from others in the source embeddings. Therefore, we need to ensure that the reconstructed source embeddings closely match the original embeddings. (2) Diversity: The meta-embedding should integrate and unify the diversity of information present across various sources of word embeddings.

Language is not static; it diversifies across geography, demographic groups, and time (Poplack, 1993;Sankoff and Poplack, 1982). Consequently, natural language processing (NLP) systems that do not account for regional variation can perform poorly. A particular challenge comes from dialects, which defy standardization and vary questions such as spelling (Rosenberg, 1998), lexicon (Eisenmann, 2006), and phraseology (Klemm et al., 2014), and are increasingly important as data collection moves online (Apuke and Tekleson, 2018). Existing methods, however, struggle to deal with dialectal variation (Apuke and Tekleson, 2018;Trisovic, 2018). They typically rely on manually selected linguistic variables, from grammar or lexicon, which define the linguistic space that is to be observed and aggregated into a certain number of dialects/regions (Klemm et al., 2012). While such approaches might suffice when regional variation aligns with these variables, they fall short when it varies on other dimensions or evolves beyond the original or even current cluster assignments. For instance, a uniform trend of urbanization or immigration might blur or shift boundary between traditional dialect regions (Trudgill, 2004). Moreover, beyond empirical classification, they are often not sufficiently expressive to capture nuances within or between the defined regions, or variables at a finer level (e.g., distinct regional variation in specific features). To address these issues, we show how learned document vectors from deep learning can capture inherent regional variation in language. We use a corpus of 16.8M anonymous social media posts that can be geolocated to cities and learn document representations that effectively capture regional variation. These representations are input to agglomerative clustering and retrofitted with geographic information, allowing us to recover spatially aligned dialect areas at various levels of granularity measured against a widely used dialect map. Our results show that the proposed method can capture more nuanced regional distinctions at a finer granularity than previous approaches and is complementary to typological methods. While prior work (Snoj et al., 2015;Berenzweig et al., 2015) has studied document embeddings that encode some linguistic features or global position/perspective, and uses them for tasks such as text classification (blending different document representations for zero shot learning: Kenter and Hovy, 2018;Mirkin et al., 2016;Blunsom and Sennrich, 2014; 2015;Karten and Goldberg, 2015), fine-grained geographic representation and use, are novel here. In continuous representations (vs. discrete categories), typological work like Styranowski (2004) and Russo (2012) has also shown that clustering with a few low-level semantic features already reveals novel typological patterns.

Among the various methods of information presentation, expository dialogue (dialogue used to convey information), stands out. It can offer several advantages over monologue (one speaker, without active feedback from the audience) in terms of promoting comprehension, engagement and context awareness (Garcia, 2007;Eakins and Grynsztejn, 1998;Johnson, 2000). Expository dialogue increases interactivity, allows for contextually dependent segmentation of information, and enables its recipients to negotiate knowledge and understanding among themselves, possibly reducing ambiguity and facilitating mental reconstruction of the content (Rowe et al., 1989;Sperling et al., 1994;Thorn et al., 1995). Moreover, oral exposition - which we focus on here - has cognitive benefits tied to the way our brains process auditory and semantic information (Jain and Osterhout, 1999;Davis, 2007). Thus, the ability to automatically generate expository dialogue from monologue would open up new possibilities in many areas, such as education, tutorial assistance, interactive narratives, knowledge dissemination and customer service systems (Cohen, 2001;Pedersen, 2005;Yano, 2007). In this paper, we present a foundational work towards this goal, focusing on the key challenges involved and the technology required for achieving it. To establish the foundation for such a task, generating expository dialogue from monologue, we first need a suitable dataset for analysis and modeling. For this purpose, we construct a corpus of parallel English "monologues" and "dialogs" (M2D Corpus) that aim to keep the content closely aligned while treating the dialogue as an expository variant of the monologue (Figure 1). Each pair in the corpus includes one monologue written for a hypothetical one-way presentation (e.g., a technical explanation, a news report) and one dialogue between two or more explicitly named interlocutors who are discussing the same topic. The dialogues are projected to be informative and expository - meaning they aim to inform, explain and possibly engage in a collaborative interpretation of the shared subject matter, rather than being purely social or uneventful. For simplicity and because of the challenge of creating high-quality artificial dialogs, we use public-domain texts that are real monologues and map them to the closest real dialogues found in the PEP corpus (Demelo and Ritter, 2015), which includes socially-oriented conversations but also discussions and debates, including examples that aim to inform (e.g., explaining a concept, reporting on news). Each entry in the M2D Corpus keeps the original subject matter but has the typology of dialogue shifted from social to expository.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, Facebook and Instagram, have become increasingly popular in recent years. To manage the mammoth task of keeping up with updates from multiple sources, automated summarization techniques can help users efficiently extract the most important information. However, traditional summarization methods generate one-size-fit-all summaries that may not cater to individual users' specific interests or needs. A step further towards addressing this issue is personalized summarization where summaries are generated based on users' interests and preferences, inferred from their past interactions and posted content. Although techniques for personalized summarization have been studied (e.g., for news summarization), they commonly assume that users explicitly provide their preferences or rely on limited knowledge about users to generate personalized summaries. This is not always feasible or practical for social media platforms where dynamic, real-time interaction is common. A more challenging and realistic task is personalized summarization of social content, where the preferences of the intended user need to be inferred from the context of the content shared by that user and his/her social network. This is known as context-enhanced personalized summarization. Social content often serves as a proxy for a user's current interests, needs, and intentions, which can be exploited for extracting potential useful or relevant information. For instance, if a user frequently interacts with or shares content related to a specific topic (e.g., tech news), it can be inferred that he/she is likely interested in updates related to this topic. In this paper, we focus on this problem and propose a novel unsupervised approach for context-enhanced personalized summarization of social content. The core idea is to utilize the social context (e.g., user's posting activity, interaction patterns with others) as an external source to infer the user's interests in relation to the content being summarized. The key challenges we address are: (1) Incorporating "implicit" user interests inferred from social context (e.g., tweets) into the summarization process without requiring explicit user feedback or detailed user profiles, (2) Enhancing the document or content model to include the user and his/her social context, and (3) Balancing the informativeness of the content with the inferred user's interest aspects. Our approach builds on the following insights: First, while user profiles often contain explicitly stated interests, they can be insufficient or inaccurate for the current moment's needs. Social actions (e.g., tweets, likes, shares) can serve as real-time indicators of user interests, capturing temporal or situational preferences not captured by static profiles.

Introduction Literary success is often considered a subjective matter, reserved for the realm of taste and criticism, and dependent heavily on historical and social context. However, numerous studies in quantitative literary analysis and stylometry hypothesize the existence of measurable predictors of success. If such predictors do indeed exist, this could have significant implications for publishers and authors, as well as for the interpretation of literary history itself (Stab and Walsh, 1981;Pennebaker et al., 2001;Michel et al., 2011). This paper examines the quantitative connection between writing style and the success of novels. Specifically, we investigate whether stylistic attributes rooted in linguistic form, syntax, vocabulary, or narrative structure correlate with popular success. We draw on the analytical methods of digital literary study - particularly stylometry based on statistical analysis of language frequency and distribution - to answer the question: Can we use purely computational methods to predict the success of novels? Our hypothesis arises from a number of lines of research. First, stylometric analyses of literary texts have demonstrated that similar linguistic choices can be surprisingly useful in discerning authorship or placing texts in their historical and stylistic contexts (Mortara Garavelli and Rossi, 1983;Hoover, 2005;Juola, 2006;Hoover and Berzon, 2010;Rayson et al., 2011). This informs the idea that stylometric features may also capture aspects of a text's aesthetic appeal or commercial success. Second, there is empirical evidence from studies on text-based user engagement, readability, and educational outcomes (Kintsch, 1988;Katz and Just, 1999;Hill and Scherer, 2015), implying that certain stylistic features might affect a text's appeal to readers and thus its perceived "success". Finally, less empirical but conceivable, is the idea that authors who achieve widespread success may exhibit a "socio-linguistic" style that is more appealing or accessible to a broad demographic. A wide array of stylistic features could influence the prediction of success. For a given text, we consider attributes such as: - Vocabulary Density: The richness of vocabulary, measured by unique word counts or ratios of rare words. - Narrative Complexity: Indicators of narrative structure, plot complexity, or use of narratorial voice. - Syntax and Sentence Length: Average sentence length, complexity, and variability of clause structure. - Discourse Mobility: The way the text moves between different levels of abstraction or cohesion. - Rhetorical Elements: The use of certain rhetorical devices, such as metaphor or alliteration. - Readability Measures: Scores derived from industry standards like Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level or Gunning-Fog Index, that estimate text’s ease of reading based on word and sentence length.

Certainly, here is my answer: English orthography, also known as spelling, is a subject of vigorous debate. Some argue it is optimally designed to represent the spoken sounds of English, while others assert that it is poorly adapted to various linguistic aspects. In this paper, we refute the claim that English orthography is, as Chomsky and Halle (1968) suggest, "near optimal," using computational and numerical methods. First, we outline the design principles of the English spelling system and critically discuss the notion of "optimality." We then introduce and apply an algorithmic approach that aims to devise a theoretical spelling system. This artificial spelling system maximizes phonemic transparency and morphological consistency. Phonemic transparency refers to the extent to which a verbal transcription allows readers to reconstruct the underlying pronunciation from the spelling. Morphological consistency, on the other hand, aims to minimize the number of exceptions in a rule-based orthographic system - for instance, how well the spelling of a base word predicts the spelling of its inflected forms. The algorithm we used is inspired by the idea of minimizing the "action" in the sense of Junker and Wierzbicka (1994) or Kaplan and Kay (1994), or equivalently, the "energy" in a more literal, computational model sense. The algorithm assigns a score to each possible spelling of a word, based on both phonemic transparency and morphological consistency. This score can be mathematically formulated and optimized over a substantial corpus of English words to produce plausible, maximally-optimal orthographic forms. We then evaluate the performance of our constructed optimal spelling system against English orthography as it exists, using phonemic-to-orthographic mapping accuracy as a metric. This is measured against a wide range of lexical contexts, from common English words to rare and irregular words that often reveal problematic gaps in the English spelling system. The results are stark. The optimal system we devised, while far from perfect, vastly outperforms conventional English spelling in the metrics we have chosen to evaluate. The gap in performance is particularly pronounced in the area of phonemic transparency. For example, our optimal system is able to map most English phonemes consistently to their spellings, whereas English spelling often deviates in systematic but non-intuitive ways. Our findings are especially relevant in the context of language education and literacy. English spelling’s inability to support phonemic transparency in a consistent manner has often been cited as one of the primary reasons why so many native English speakers struggle with writing and reading fluency (e.g., Venezky 1999; Chomsky 2010).

There are several reasons to provide AHL. First, the linked documents might share relevant information or paraphrase the same idea. Second, the linked documents could be additional resources and references, such as slides, lecture notes, links to papers cited in a journal, academic articles, or technical reports. Table 1: Benefits of Automatic Hyperlinking + Improve user engagement and browsing experience + Enhance user's understanding and appreciation of the topic + Detect overlaps and differences in the content of the original and linked web pages + Support web-based information retrieval + Serve as a form of data or information curation For a web author this is a time and resource-intensive task, requiring knowledge of the topic and hours of research to find relevant links. The task is daunting for large web pages with hundreds of candidate links; the research process can be slow and subjective, resulting in inconsistencies in the quality and relevancy of the provided links (Peña-lara and Aguiar, 2011). There is growing demand for automated methods that can assist web authors in link insertion, which is also known as automatic hyperlinking (AHL) (Craswell et al., 2015). The main goal of AHL is to identify contextual URLs and create textual descriptions (anchor texts) for them. The text can then be placed within the content of the web page where it would help a reader understand the context of the linked document. The ideal AHL system would ease the cognitive burden of explicitly linking to relevant web pages, while achieving high quality in link and anchor text generation. While significant previous work exists in natural language processing and information retrieval to address these tasks, the actual use of advanced techniques – such as deep learning for similarity estimation or complex statistical models for ranking and text mining – has been less explored. In this paper, we propose an AHL system that leverages a novel approach to textual similarity estimation: localized similarity.

This approach permits the use of distributed features (e.g., part-of-speech, dependency, parse), which are helpful for resolving ambiguity, and it allows very flexible hypotheses for representing relations extracted from text (e.g., verbs or named entities in text can be used to form flexible, possibly non-projective dependency structures). However, training on small, domain- and task-specific labeled corpora risks fitting a model too closely to just those corpora, leading to overfitting. The reliance on hand-labeled data similarly limits the scalability of these approaches. Moreover, this requires a labor-intensive annotation process that is difficult to reproduce across various domains and tasks. We describe a new approach to relation extraction that breaks free from the need for a labeled corpus, similar to approaches in SVMs (Joachims, 2006), and which we call Distant Supervision. For a given relation, our algorithm uses a large unlabeled corpus to produce features for all sentences in which the entities participating in the relation appear (without prior domain knowledge of where the relation may appear in the corpus). It then uses a large Knowledge Base, such as Freebase (Bizer et al., 2009), to provide distant supervision for labeling those sentences according to the presence of the relation. However, there are still significant challenges when applying traditional LSTM networks to document-level sentiment analysis tasks due to the limited memory capacity in handling lengthy texts and capturing essential word order information. This is especially true in the case of document-level sentiment analysis, where the task requires that features from the entire document be captured to predict its sentiment polarity accurately. The default operation of an LSTM in the context of sentiment analysis involves reading the input sequence word by word and attempting to preserve important information indefinitely within the hidden state dynamics. This default mode, however, has inherent limitations for several reasons. Firstly, the LSTM's memory capacity is limited, which can lead to information loss over longer sequences. Secondly, the information stored in LSTM cells at each step depends on the unit's internal state and the gate mechanisms it uses to read from input and update hidden states. The LSTM is good at focusing on specific parts of the sequence, while the 'divergence' of the entire sequence’s semantic information can be hard to model, especially for long documents. A key insight here is that sentiment inference for a piece of text depends on integrating information from its earlier as well as latter parts. Evolution of the text in time introduces nuanced contexts which can easily become too complex for an LSTM to achieve high performance without some form of adaptation. The approach we propose, Cached Long Short-Term Memory (CLSTM), tackles these limitations by adjusting how information is organized and retrieved in the LSTM design. The fundamental idea is the introduction of a cache mechanism in the LSTM structure. Our method allows the network to divide the memory into several groups with different forgetting rates. This design choice is inspired by the observation that certain parts of the input sequence are more globally and persistently relevant to the task at hand (capturing document-level sentiment in our case), while others are less so or conditionally relevant. In essence, the CLSTM framework can be seen as an attempt to optimize the LSTM structure for document-level sentiment analysis by better balancing the retention of historically relevant information with the capture of new textual context as the network processes longer texts.

Learning Concept Taxonomies from Multi-modal Data Presenting a comprehensive and structured organization of knowledge is crucial for many applications in Artificial Intelligence (AI). Knowledge graphs are one such example where concepts are organized using edges that represent the relationships between concepts. A key component of a knowledge graph is the taxonomy. A taxonomy is a particular type of directed acyclic graph (DAG) which uses hypernym-hyponym and meronym-meronym relationships to represent the semantic relationships between concepts (Strube, 2000). Many efforts have been made to build taxonomies (or hierarchies) from text data extracted from online sources such as Wikipedia, Twitter, and other web pages. This is because text, especially natural language texts such as news articles, web pages, and verbal communication, provides rich semantic cues. However, in recent years, the trend is toward using multi-modal data, as the availability of large-scale visual data from image collections has opened up new opportunities to represent and analyze knowledge. Hence, we see a need to move beyond relying on text alone and build models that seamlessly integrate visual data alongside textual data to construct concept taxonomies. The challenge is similar across these various applications and involves inducing a hierarchical structure that accurately captures the semantic relationships between concepts within or across these modalities. While text-based approaches can leverage context, syntax and semantics to learn hierarchical relationships (Socher et al., 2013; Mihalcea, 2007; Prabhumoye et al., 2015), visual features can serve as strong cues for perceptual or physical relationships (e.g., a battery can be thought as 'inside' a device, or certain physical objects can be classified in terms of size, shape, color, texture, and function, and all these visual features can be useful in learning a taxonomy) leading to a more nuanced understanding of the concepts and their relationships. Therefore, developing methods to learn concept taxonomies from multi-modal data, combining both text and image information, could significantly enhance the precision and the coverage of such knowledge representations. While the idea of using multi-modal data for learning concept taxonomies is promising, tackling this problem presents several challenges. First, one needs to model the relationship between text and image representations so that they can be combined effectively in a single learning framework. This often requires solving a coreferentiality problem, that is, for each concept in the taxonomy, identifying which text and image examples refer to the same concept so that they can be added to the same concept cluster for the induction of hierarchy.

Two main sources are often encountered: computational logic, focused on algorithms and proofs, and mathematical logic, centered around formal systems and model theory. In our experience, it is challenging to find a treatment that smoothly merges these questions into a comprehensive course suitable for both theory and practice. This book addresses this need. Material fits into three parts: (a) constructing and using a formal framework, with syntax, semantics, reasoning, and set theory. (b) theory of logical programming, including concrete inference systems, operational model-theoretic knowledge representation, and some computational aspects of inference. (c) foundations of inference for inductive generalizations. Each part benefits from a combination of theory and computational thinking. The formal framework uses FOLPlus, an expressive formal language that goes beyond simple FOL in both syntax and semantics. FOLPlus allows for formulas involving sets and subset operators, makes possible a more expressive language of quantification and predicate expressions, and adds disjunction and numerical quantifiers. These aspects of the language are keys in various applications and useful in the study of major inference algorithms. FOLPlus also includes a formal semantics firmly rooted in descriptive set theory, allowing for model-theoretic notions of domains and interpretations to be treated as foundational concepts. The logical programming part of the book uses the benefits of FOLPlus to present the foundations and its application to Prolog, exploring its computational model and the theory of inference (e.g., resolution, unification). The computational aspects take into consideration the finite, bounded nature of practical reasoning: we consider heuristics, strategies for search and backtracking, and the benefits and challenges of using logic programming in "proper logic" versus "semi-naive" evaluation. This helps frame the discussion that leads into the fundamental questions and limitations of general-purpose inference. The third part handles aspects of the problem of generalizing from the measured, where together with probabilistic extensions to the language, we explore inductive inference. Several chapters are devoted to probabilistic uncertainty, either explicitly through probabilistic logic (e.g., Sato's probabilistic logic framework) or implicitly through satisfiability under constraints (capturing notions of incomplete information and belief). We also discuss analogical generalizations, aggregating evidence for predictions, and some statistical aspects of inductive inference. One of the overarching goals of this book is to make clear that the real utility of such an expressive logic framework as FOLPlus comes when one sees it as more than just a notation: as a tool for formulating theories, solving problems, and arguing.

Multi-document summarization (MDS) is a fundamental task of text summarization, where the goal is to create a short summary of a set of related articles about a specific topic. The deep structure of comprehensive information gives natural language a complex hierarchical form. In this work, we exploit this hierarchical structure to improve the quality of multi-document summaries – specifically, questions are posed on subtopics (or categorized information) and answers are formulated based on the distributed representation of the documents. This makes the summarization process sensitive to the content categories, and hence, we propose Category-Specific Information for multi-document summarization. Traditionally, document content is represented as a fixed-length bags-of-words, which inherently discards the category hierarchy of the vocabulary. These representations, often augmented with some domain features, are then used to compute the importance (or relevance) of each sentence for the task at hand. This places little emphasis on the global organization of content into categories, and does not properly leverage the internal structure of the information domain. This limitation can be seen in the standard summarization evaluation metrics such as ROUGE, which measures the overlap of bigrams or n-grams between the generated summary and a gold-standard human summary. In contrast, Category-Specific Information is defined as the information about a category that is common to most (or all) of the documents in a dataset. We recognize that this kind of information is typically the 'core' information about the category and likely the most important for a summarizer to convey in its output. For example, in a set of technology news articles about the latest smartphone features, details specific to that category (e.g., camera quality, screen size, price, battery life) are more important to include in the summary than general features that might also apply to other devices or technologies. Our approach introduces two novel features that evaluate the category-specific importance (CSI) of sentences: Document-Level Category Feature (DCF), and Category-Specific Role (CSR). These features are designed to be measured without any external knowledge, thus making the proposed method simple to integrate into existing MDS frameworks. - Document-Level Category Feature (DCF): This feature is measured by calculating the proportion of the sentence’s words that belong to the target category. Words that are more specific to the target category receive a higher score, thereby indicating higher CSI. - Category-Specific Role (CSR): This feature denotes the contextual importance of a category-specific word in a sentence, specifically within the target category.

[2013] have demonstrated that a GPU-based Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD) parser can achieve semantic parsing performance comparable to weighted finite state transducers, but only at the cost of an 8x increase in required computational resources and a reduction of sparsity in the resulting language models. Furthermore, achieving good performance on GPU requires careful consideration of memory hierarchy, shader execution, and data transfer bottlenecks [Young and Hale, 2014]. To accommodate the computational benefits of GPU processing while retaining the structural sparsity of NLP data and models, we propose an approach that includes coarse-to-fine pruning techniques. This method allows for efficient processing while maintaining sparsity benefits. The coarse pruning phase removes a substantial majority of inconsequential algorithm paths, followed by a fine pruning phase that carefully preserves the most salient syntactic and semantic features for accurate language modeling. Our approach is designed to operate within the constraints and inherent parallelism of GPU architectures. The key is the exploitation of sparsity in the computational graph and careful instruction-level parallelism optimization. By implementing a pruning strategy that effectively eliminates computational overkill for low-likelihood parse paths, we aim to achieve both faster and more resource-efficient processing compared to dense, non-pruned methods. Our methods allow efficient implementation of Viterbi parsing, a particularly GPU-friendly algorithm due to its sequential nature and dependency on dynamic programming, as well as more accurate but less straightforward minimum Bayes risk (MBR) algorithms. While MBR is computationally more complex and not typically framed for GPU-parallelizable computation, by leveraging advanced pruning techniques we can make these more accurate parsing methodologies not only feasible but highly performant on GPUs, thus bridging the gap between speed and semantic accuracy for natural language processing tasks. The success of such a sparsity-conscious GPU approach could have significant implications for large-scale NLP processing, enabling faster and more real-time processing of complex parsing tasks without sacrificing the accuracy and sparsity that are critical for NLP

These systems promise to minimize the visual clutter and distraction caused by typos and misspellings by drastically reducing the likelihood of incorrect words entering the editing process. In addition to their practical utility, these tools serve an educational role, helping users learn the correct spellings and offering alternatives to phonetic misspellings. State of the Art Traditional spellcheckers and autocorrection systems rely heavily on manually curated dictionaries and lexicons. While this approach yields high-quality results for languages with established rules and large, localized datasets, it struggles in less resourced languages or with dynamic, informal writing styles that may not be adequately captured in predefined word lists (Koehn, 2005; Fourie, 2004). Furthermore, even in well-resourced languages, purely dictionary-based solutions fail to account for morphologically complex words, out-of-vocabulary items, and colloquialisms, which often require a more nuanced understanding of language structure and context. To tackle these challenges, various research efforts have explored statistical and machine learning approaches to spellchecking and autocorrection, leveraging large, unstructured corpora to learn from patterns in misspellings and word usage (Pedersen, 2010; Hayes and Kirchhoff, 2000). For instance, n-gram language models, based on the statistical likelihood of word sequences, can be used to suggest corrections by identifying plausible alternatives given the context (Koehn, 2011). However, these methods still often require extensive, language-specific resources, which are either not available or not easily accessible for many languages. The Web as a Resource The World Wide Web, with its vast and diverse collection of human-generated text in almost every language, offers a unique opportunity to develop language-independent or language-agnostic spellchecking and autocorrection tools. The web corpus contains both correct and erroneous language usage, which can be harvested to build a comprehensive error model and word usage statistics. This approach could potentially bypass the need for language-specific, manually constructed datasets, making it easier to adapt and deploy these tools across languages and writing styles. Furthermore, the web can serve not just as a source of data but also as a means to validate hypotheses about misspellings and word usage. For example, co-occurrence statistics of words across the web can be explored to understand which sequences of characters are more likely to be found together.
